Dismiss alert {{ message }} VikOlliver RepRapMicron Repository navigation Code Issues 1 ( 1 ) Pull requests Actions Projects Wiki Security and quality Insights More items Home Jump to bottom Vik Olliver edited this page Oct 13, 2026 · 37 revisions μRepRap - The RepRapMicron The µRepRap is intended to be a RepRap (a replicating 3D printer) capable of micron (1/1000th of a millimetre, or 1µm) and sub-micron fabrication, made with only common and easily accessible materials. This degree of accuracy was initially made possible by 3D printed microscope platforms designed by The OpenFlexure Project. Variations more suitable for prototyping and fabrication have since been developed, but kudos to them. Expectations for the initial μRepRap prototype were to demonstrate repeatable positioning to better than 3µm on a work area 10mm across and to produce a probe tip in lieu of a print head that is suitable for manufacture in a simple home workshop. This goal has effectively been achieved. 0.5mm "Benchy" 3D test model printed with μRepRap, 4μm layer height PIKA Version "PIKA" V0.02 hardware is producing repeatable positioning of approximately 1μm and reliable 10μm or better accuracy in an approximately 8mm cubic volume. Using a fine probe etched with the PIKA mechanism itself, UV resin droplets as small as 4μm have been deposited. With a fibre optic probe 9μm resin lines have been cured. This is the current recommended build. PIKA V0.02 Complete Circa May 2026 MAUS Version (Deprecated) This was devised as a testbed for flexure components, and is only mentioned because it has been thoroughly documented with a bill of materials etc. It was updated to V0.05 to give compatibility with PIKA Axis Drivers, but the full documentation is for the "MAUS C" V0.04 (essentially a debugged V0.03). This achieved approximately 5μm positioning best case over a 4mm square, though motion is not linear. Maus-C-Build-Process instructions have been created. If you want to download the pre-built STL files go here to Printables and day-to-day progress is detailed on the RepRap blog . MAUS 'L' V0.05 μRepRap, in development Feb 2026 Overview Microelectronics and Micro-electromechanical Systems (MEMS) are essential components of most of the electronic wizardry we use in our everyday lives, whether we realise it or not. In the way that RepRap brought Open 3D fabrication to the masses, the aim of the µRepRap Project is to bring users the same capabilities on a much smaller scale and allow those components to evolve in the same way. The solution is effectively a very precise and compact CNC machine. The objective has two related parts: To create a macro scale 3D printed micron fabrication and manipulation system, and while doing this develop the techniques needed to reproduce a similar system printed at the micron scale. Background A 1.3mm "Hello World" mechanically etched in Sharpie Marker on glass slide mid-2025 Precision manufacturing began somewhere in the 1700's, and the first micron scale electronic devices were fabricated from silicon in the 1960’s. The Intel 4004 , for example, was made with a feature size of 10μm. Ever since then the technology focused largely on silicon, with fabrication systems becoming ever more complex, esoteric, and costly. The techniques used are difficult for the average hobbyist to manage, and in many cases are downright dangerous. In biology and medicine, equipment to measure and manipulate objects on the micron scale are relatively common - though these devices tend to be large, specialized, and expensive. Recently though, microscope platforms capable of sub-micron resolution were developed by The OpenFlexure Project , and these have created an interesting opportunity for developing micron scale fabrication. If micron scale manufacturing can be achieved by RepRap-like technology, it is likely that these fields will be advanced in the same way that desktop fabrication was by the RepRap. The biological sciences will gain from inexpensive, rapidly-evolving equipment. The microelectronics field will regain the potential for independent communities develop on the micron scale, and break away from its fixation on silicon as its main platform. As with 3D printing, there will certainly be new developments in fields that do not currently even exist. There is also the possibility (and intent) that this technology could replicate in the future at a yet smaller scale. Requirements Micron scale 3D printing has many of the same requirements that The RepRap Project developed when initially printing on the macro scale: A 3-axis positioning system CAD/CAM software Axis zeroing sensors A deposition system Building material In addition there is the practical aspect that humans are unable to directly manipulate micron scale assemblies and sub-assemblies. Novel systems are therefore needed to: Detach printed items Transport items Rotate and position items Conduct micron scale maintenance tasks Operate and interface with items Similar issues will exist if and when a micron scale system is developed. Optics While conventional optics are readily available to allow humans to initiate and inspect the fabrication processes, it is likely that some customisation of the optics will be desirable. For the moment two USB microscopes are sufficient. One to observe the initial Z probe height during setup, and one for the XY positioning of the probe when commencing a print. A minimum of 8Mpixel resolution is recommended. Additionally a conventional bench microscope of 100x to 200x will be needed to examine the output. "Hello, World" and a 100μm square set in resin using UV and a 125/9 optical fibre Additionally, an optical fibre may be attached as the probe. This can be used to cure UV resin by projecting a sufficiently powerful UV source down the probe. This section describes how a 125/9 optical fibre patch lead and 3W UV LED module can be attached to the μRepRap as a print head. 3-Axis Control The axes are driven by 400-step NEMA17 stepper motors, but 200-step motors will get quite close to 1μm. The driving hardware and firmware is left to user preference, though existing developments assume interactive control using GCODE on a serial connection. Arduino GRBL is adequate. Probe Print Head The probe is used as a Z touch sensor, engraving tool, and deposition head. A robust probe for initial testing can be made from a 0.5mm hypodermic needle or 0.25mm accupuncture needle. These are sufficiently robust to use subtractively on resist-covered surfaces such as Sharpie marker on a glass slide. For fine deposition an electrochemically etched wire point is recommended. Instructions for fabrication with minimal equipment are in the Probe documentation. The PIKA is capable of etching its own probes. Building Materials Additive fabrication is currently implemented by transferring minute quantities of "Top Coat" UV nail gel resin with the probe. The reservoir is a smeared layer of resin. The probe accepts this resin by capillary action. When depositing, capillary action forms relatively consistent droplets. The number of consecutively deposited droplets and their consistency depend on the qualities of the resin and probe, but sub-15μm droplets are achievable. Other resins and ionic gels may also be used. A UV LED in the print bed operated by the hardware controller sets the resin. Note: Thin layers of 3D printer UV resin do not readily set in air as oxygen neutralises the activated photoinitiator. Other substances may be transferred. They key limitation is that their solvent should not evaporate during deposition. Materials that readily adhere to the resin (which may be partially cured first) such as gold leaf may be added. Summary The current μRepRap 3D printer is intended to provide a platform for further hardware and software development on the micron scale. Much work remains to be done in determining what can be printed and in what materials. If objects cannot be printed high enough, or with overhangs, folded structures, hinges, and flexures will need to be developed to produce complex 3D shapes and mechanisms. It is hoped that μRepRap may be used to eventually construct useful devices in its own right, and an ecosystem of fabrication utilities that operate on a yet smaller scale. title: DeepSeek search and fetch – $0.75 per 1000 successful requests
body_text: Search & Fetch | DeepSeek API Docs Skip to main content Search / Fetch API is now available, powered by our in-house search engine and supporting web search and fetch. Click here to view the guide. DeepSeek API Docs Resources Integrations API Status FAQ English English ä¸­æï¼ä¸­å½ï¼ DeepSeek Platform ä¸­ Quick Start API Guides API Reference News Change Log Vision Thinking Mode Multi-round Conversation Chat Prefix Completion (Beta) FIM Completion (Beta) JSON Output Tool Calls Files API Search & Fetch Context Caching Using the Responses API Using the Anthropic API Search & Fetch On this page Search & Fetch The Search API and the Fetch API give agents and RAG applications access to live web content: Search API finds web pages for a query and returns structured results. It is powered by DeepSeek's in-house search engine. Fetch API retrieves a single web page and returns its content as Markdown. Both are raw JSON APIs. They use the same bearer authentication as the DeepSeek API. The base URL is https://api.deepseek.com : API Endpoint Search POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search Fetch POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch See the Search API Reference and Fetch API Reference for the complete request and response schemas. Authentication â Send your API key and the JSON content type in the request headers: Header Required Value Authorization Yes Bearer <DeepSeek API Key> Content-Type Yes application/json Search API â Request â curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "query": "DeepSeek V4 release", "count": 5, "need_content": true }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "query" : "DeepSeek V4 release" , "count" : 5 , "need_content" : True , } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) for result in response . json ( ) [ "results" ] : print ( result [ "title" ] , result [ "url" ] ) print ( result [ "summary" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Default Description query string Yes - The search query must contain 1 to 128 Unicode characters, cannot be all whitespace, and supports the query operators listed below. count integer No 10 The number of results to return, between 1 and 50. ori_question string No - The user's original question that triggered the search, between 1 and 128 characters, to improve query understanding, with null treated as not provided. localization string No "" An optional IP address used to localize search results. need_content boolean No false Whether to return page content in content , which is always an empty string when false . Unknown fields in the request body are ignored. Query Operators â The query is forwarded with its search syntax intact. The examples below combine operators with a search term; you can combine multiple operators in one query. Operator Example Description site: DeepSeek site:github.com Restrict results to the given site, and to target multiple sites, separate the site: clauses with spaces and join them with OR , for example DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co . -site: DeepSeek -site:example.com Exclude the given site, and separate multiple sites with spaces. - DeepSeek -advertisement Exclude pages containing the term, and separate multiple terms with spaces. -"..." DeepSeek -"release notes" Exclude pages containing the exact phrase, which can contain spaces, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. "..." DeepSeek "exact phrase" Match an exact phrase, and separate multiple phrases with spaces. lang: DeepSeek lang:zh,en Restrict results to the given language codes, separating multiple codes with commas, for example lang:zh,en . after: DeepSeek after:2025 or DeepSeek after:2025-01-01 Restrict results to pages published after a date. before: DeepSeek before:2026 or DeepSeek before:2026-06-01 Restrict results to pages published before a date. For example: { "query": "DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co lang:en after:2025", "count": 10 } Response â A successful request returns HTTP 200 with a results array. A normal search with no matches returns an empty array. { "results": [ { "rerank_score": 2.4, "title": "DeepSeek V4 model released", "url": "https://example.com/deepseek-v4", "snippet": "DeepSeek V4 is now available, with tool calling and long-context support.", "summary": "DeepSeek has released the V4 model. The release adds improved tool calling and long-context support for agent workflows.", "content": "DeepSeek V4 is now generally available...", "site_name": "Example News", "site_icon": "https://example.com/favicon.ico", "date": "2026-06-01T00:00:00+00:00", "authority": 3 } ] } Each item in results contains: Field Type Description rerank_score number A relevance score from 0 to 3 that combines signals such as relevance, authority, and freshness, with scores of 1.5 or above considered high-quality results. title string The title of the result. url string The URL of the result. snippet string A short summary related to the query, typically 100 to 200 characters, intended for display in a UI. summary string A long summary related to the query, typically 600 to 800 characters, intended to be read by a model. content string The page content, which is empty when need_content is false or when the content is unavailable. site_name string or null The name of the site, or null when unavailable. site_icon string or null The URL of the site icon, or null when unavailable. date string or null The publication time in UTC, formatted as RFC 3339, or null when unknown. authority integer The authority tier of the page, 0 to 4 ( -1 means unknown), with values of 3 or above indicating highly authoritative sources. Fetch API â Request â curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch \ -H "Authorization: Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "url": "https://example.com/article" }' import requests response = requests . post ( "https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch" , headers = { "Authorization" : "Bearer <DeepSeek API Key>" , } , json = { "url" : "https://example.com/article" } , ) response . raise_for_status ( ) page = response . json ( ) print ( page [ "title" ] ) print ( page [ "content" ] ) Request fields: Field Type Required Description url string Yes The page URL to fetch, which must be at most 8192 characters, an HTTP or HTTPS URL with a host, and must not contain a username or password. Response â { "title": "Example article", "content": "# Example article\n\nArticle content." } Field Type Description title string The title of the page, empty when the title is unavailable. content string The fetched page content as Markdown text. Fetching is subject to the target site's availability and access policies. Errors â Errors follow the OpenAI-compatible error format. The param field is always null . { "error": { "message": "'count' must be between 1 and 50", "type": "invalid_request_error", "param": null, "code": "invalid_request_error" } } HTTP Status Description 400 The request headers or body are invalid, including malformed JSON or an invalid field value. 401 The API key is missing or invalid. 402 The account has insufficient balance. 403 The Fetch request was rejected by the security policy. 404 Fetch could not retrieve usable page content, for example due to an unavailable URL, a URL blocked by site policy, an error from the target site, an unsupported content type, or a page with no extractable Markdown content. 408 Reading the request body timed out. 413 The request body is too large. 429 The Search or Fetch QPS limit was exceeded. 500 An internal server error occurred. 504 A downstream request timed out. Search and Fetch are read-only. For HTTP 408, 429, or 5xx errors, wait and retry. For HTTP 402, top up your account before retrying. Do not retry other 4xx errors without changing the request. Billing â Search and Fetch are billed per successful request, not by tokens or by the number of returned results: API Unit Price Search Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 Fetch Per 1,000 successful requests $0.75 A request is billable only when it returns HTTP 200 and produces a result (Search must return a non-empty results array, and Fetch must return page content). Failed requests, empty search results, and timeouts are not billed. count only controls how many results are returned and does not affect the per-request price. Note: when you use the DeepSeek API through DeepSeek Harness, Claude Code, or Codex, server-side tool calls already hit the Search and Fetch APIs. These calls are currently free of charge; per-request billing starts at 00:00 Beijing time on November 1, 2026. Rate Limits â For each account, Search and Fetch are limited independently, and traffic to one does not consume the other's quota: API QPS Limit Search 5 Fetch 5 The QPS (requests per second) limits are calculated at the account level, regardless of which API key is used, and are separate from the model concurrency limits. Requests above the account-level QPS limit receive HTTP 429. In addition to the account-level limit, Fetch is also subject to a per-domain QPS limit, and requests above that limit also receive HTTP 429. title: Someone behind the software
body_text: Someone behind the software · Karri Saarinen Karri Saarinen RSS 𝕏 ☾ Someone behind the software October 15, 2026 I think good products carry something of the people who make them. Their experience, what they care about, and how they think things should work. You might not know who those people are, but you can feel their perspective in the product. The industry often talks about software as though it comes out of a factory. You collect requirements, build features, and measure whether they work. Follow the process and you should get a good result. Now we're talking automating this whole pipeline with agents. But two teams can talk to similar customers, have access to the same technology, and make very different things. The difference comes from how they understand what they see and the style they go about building it. The founder background or company DNA also shapes this a lot. At Linear , we have always valued intuition over process or data. I think people sometimes understand that as making decisions based on personal preference, without much thought or evidence. What we mean by it is that your intuition develops through experience and understanding. You work on something, talk to customers, make mistakes, and learn what to pay attention to. The intuition is your point of view on something, and forcing to use your judgment, not hide behind faceless data. Before we launched, we talked to people across companies and roles about how they worked. We had our own frustrations with this type software, but those conversations helped us understand what mattered beyond our own experience. Our perspective got better after those conversations. So eventually the products develops a character through what its makers pay attention to, what they decide not to do and what they keep working on after it technically works. I sometimes think of this as the soul of a product. You feel that someone cares about how the whole thing comes together. A feature can work perfectly well on its own and still make the product worse. Recognizing that requires some belief about what the product should be. Someone has to make the call, then stay close enough to customers to see whether they were right. Recently, many products are starting to feel messy to me, including products from very successful companies. There seems to be more thought going into what the technology can do and what can be added than the form it should take. The product changes are primarily additive, not improving the core problem. I think the reasons for this is that it's lot easier to add new capabilities, than rethink existing capabilities. So each product becomes a collection of abilities, without actually having unified point of view. I wonder whether some of this comes from how the work is organized. Individuals work with agents to produce changes independently, each operating a small software factory. Each change might make sense on its own, but together they start to resemble Frankenstein’s monster rather than a carefully shaped sculpture. Without the shared perspective, soul, or thought, the product becomes an average of all those outputs. The choices that once gave it character are being diluted by day. More things work, but it becomes harder to feel someone or even something behind them. Making software is getting easier. I hope that gives people more room to develop a perspective and follow it further. To understand a problem deeply and keep shaping an answer until the pieces belong together. I want to feel the creator behind the software, not the factories. ← →

The Elizabeth Holmes documentary “You Can See Everything” is deceiving
body_text: How the Elizabeth Holmes Doc 'You Can See Everything' Is Deceiving You The Profile Subscribe Sign in How the Elizabeth Holmes Doc 'You Can See Everything' Is Deceiving You Did you realize the film was actually manipulating *you*? Polina Pompliano Oct 16, 2026 65 17 19 Share Holy freaking cow. I saw the new Elizabeth Holmes documentary, You Can See Everything , last night, and I genuinely can’t type fast enough to express how mind-bending it was. I’ve seen a lot of chatter online about whether Elizabeth Holmes is a liar, whether she deserves to be in prison for her failed startup Theranos, and whether the documentary is too sympathetic to her. But that’s not even remotely close to what I took away from it. As we walked out, my husband asked me, “So what did you think?” And I just responded with, “Forget Elizabeth Holmes. That was a masterpiece in storytelling.” Subscribe I walked in expecting that the filmmakers were going to tell us a story about deception. What I did not expect is that they were deceiving us — the viewers — in real time. An entire theater full of grown adults was falling for it. At one point, people were shouting so loudly at the screen that I couldn’t hear the dialogue. I heard a woman yell, “Criminal!” — and it wasn’t directed at Elizabeth Holmes. I’ve never experienced anything like that in a movie theater. It was emotion, and it was visceral. What makes the documentary so brilliant is that it forces you to confront how much of what you believe about another person comes how their story has been told to you. And we are so so susceptible to this that it’s scary. Think about Elizabeth Holmes. How much of your opinion of her comes from the facts of her criminal case & how much comes from the images and/or videos and/or TV dramas you’ve seen over the years? I remember one Halloween when the Theranos scandal was at its peak, it seemed like everyone was dressed in a black turtleneck carrying tiny vials of fake blood. Holmes was everywhere. But the thing that often gets lost in the retelling of her story is that Holmes was actually acquitted of all four charges related to defrauding patients. She’s in prison because a jury found that she knowingly misled investors who poured more than $700 million into the startup. That’s a significant distinction, but as a society, we don’t love nuance. Just tell us — is she good or is she bad? Is she a liar or is she not? I recently wrote about a fascinating experiment Canon conducted in 2015. Six photographers were asked to photograph the same man in the same location. The twist was that each photographer was given a different description of him: a millionaire, a convict, a fisherman, an alcoholic, a psychic, and a lifesaver. The resulting portraits were wildly different. A Canon rep said, “A photograph is shaped more by the person behind the camera than by what’s in front of it.” Now imagine that principle applied to an entire three-hour documentary. Over the course of the film, directors Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder managed to make a theater full of people with fully developed pre-frontal cortexes repeatedly reconsider what they believed about the people on screen. They did it through camera angles, close-ups, editing, and the order in which information was revealed. The framing of Elizabeth and those around her changed little by little until it became obvious, and as soon as our brains detected a narrative shift, our feelings about it followed. It was like watching a magic show … or one continuous reality TV show in which someone gets the villain edit, the victim edit, the manipulator edit, and all of us just falling for it again and again. Subscribe We like to believe that we form our opinions by gathering evidence, weighing facts, and arriving at reasonable conclusions. Be for real. No we do not. Here’s how it actually goes: We form an emotional impression first, then we build a belief around it, and then we go looking for facts that support it. This is my theory as to why we’re so divided in this country. Beliefs built on emotion are nearly impossible to reason with. The psychology behind the film’s manipulation should be studied. First, a close-up shot of an unblinking Elizabeth Holmes: She’s sinister. Then, a wider shot of her bouncing her baby: Wait a second, she’s a mom, she’s human! Then, her husband’s painstakingly long pause: Wait, is he the puppeteer? Then, a smile! “No, no, that can’t be genuine.” And then there’s Fielder himself, who moved in with the couple for a whole month before Holmes headed to prison. How reliable of a narrator is he? Does he care a bit too much for Elizabeth that he’s willing to lie to the viewer? How much can we trust his perception of events? I’m telling you, it’'ll break your brain. You Can See Everything does a good job explaining the phenomenon of psychological manipulation, but it also makes you participate in it. It evokes emotion, and all of the greatest pieces of art evoke emotion. You sit there believing you’re watching a documentary about a woman who deceived the world, only to discover that you’re also watching a demonstration of how easy it is to deceive you. (This was really hard to write without giving away any spoilers, but watch the film, and let me know what you think!) At one point I had to readjust my brain and consciously consider that maybe I was watching a feature film about a documentary about a feature film. My head is spinning. It was so clever. PING 1.1.1.1 (1.1.1.1) 56(84) bytes of data. 64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=1 ttl=52 time=389 ms 64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=2 ttl=52 time=68.7 ms 64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=3 ttl=52 time=47.1 ms 64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=4 ttl=52 time=48.6 ms 64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=5 ttl=52 time=85.8 ms 64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=6 ttl=52 time=84.8 ms 64 bytes from 1.1.1.1: icmp_seq=7 ttl=52 time=87.4 ms --- 1.1.1.1 ping statistics --- 8 packets transmitted, 7 received, 12.5% packet loss, time 7008ms rtt min/avg/max/mdev = 47.129/115.880/388.750/112.515 ms { header: { targetIp: "1.1.1.1", resolvedIp: "1.1.1.1", icmpPayloadSize: 56, totalPacketSize: 84 }, packets: [ { byteCount: 64, from: "1.1.1.1", seq: 1, ttl: 52, time: 389 }, { byteCount: 64, from: "1.1.1.1", seq: 2, ttl: 52, time: 68.7 }, { byteCount: 64, from: "1.1.1.1", seq: 3, ttl: 52, time: 47.1 }, { byteCount: 64, from: "1.1.1.1", seq: 4, ttl: 52, time: 48.6 }, { byteCount: 64, from: "1.1.1.1", seq: 5, ttl: 52, time: 85.8 }, { byteCount: 64, from: "1.1.1.1", seq: 6, ttl: 52, time: 84.8 }, { byteCount: 64, from: "1.1.1.1", seq: 7, ttl: 52, time: 87.4 }, ], statistics: { packetsTransmitted: 8, packetsReceived: 7, packetLoss: 12.5, time: 7008, rtt: { min: 47.129, avg: 115.88, max: 388.75, mdev: 112.515 }, }, } Fold const result = list.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n) ["Hello", " ", 100] → "Hello 100" Unfold const result = pSeq(...)("Hello 100") "Hello 100" → ["Hello", " ", 100] T string Parser Combinators Parsing is the act of taking less structured input like text, and turning it into more structured data, like objects. Many of you will be familiar with using regex to parse text, and some of you might know about tree-sitter, a heavy-duty parsing library which powers the syntax highlighting in your code editor. But regex gets messy on complex tasks, and tree-sitter often is overkill — for this middle ground, parser combinators are perfect. Not many people know about them, so allow me to show you! The partial parser The smallest unit of parsing we’ll be looking at is the partial parser . It gets to decide where to cut the input string, and then it returns a tuple consisting of whatever and the rest of the string. It can be any old function, as long as it returns such a tuple! It can even use regex inside. ▸ Code definition · pInteger const pInteger : Parser < number > = ( input : string ) => { const match = input . match ( / ^ \d + / ); if ( match == null ) throw new Error (); const digits = match [ 0 ]; return [ Number ( digits ), input . substring ( digits . length )]; }; Chaining A single parser function won’t do much on its own; but by applying multiple parsers in sequence, we can consume the entire input step by step. ▸ Code definition · pHello const pHello : Parser < string > = ( input : string ) => { if ( ! input . startsWith ( "Hello" )) throw new Error (); return [ "Hello" , input . substring ( 5 )]; }; ▸ Code definition · pIgnoreWhitespace const pIgnoreWhitespace : Parser < null > = ( input : string ) => { const match = input . match ( / ^ \s + / ); if ( match == null ) throw new Error (); const spaces = match [ 0 ]; return [ null , input . substring ( spaces . length )]; }; ▸ Code definition · pInteger const pInteger : Parser < number > = ( input : string ) => { const match = input . match ( / ^ \d + / ); if ( match == null ) throw new Error (); const digits = match [ 0 ]; return [ Number ( digits ), input . substring ( digits . length )]; }; const [ token1 , input2 ] = pHello ( "Hello 100" ); const [ token2 , input3 ] = pIgnoreWhitespace ( input2 ); const [ token3 , input4 ] = pInteger ( input3 ); console . log ( token1 , token2 , token3 ); // "Hello", null, 100 console . log ( input4 ); // empty! Chaining Or, and this is where the real power of partial parsers comes in: we wrap the chain up as a new parser of its own. ▸ Code definition · pHello100 const pHello100 : Parser <[ string , null , number ]> = ( input : string ) => { const [ hello , rest1 ] = pHello ( input ); const [ space , rest2 ] = pIgnoreWhitespace ( rest1 ); const [ number , rest3 ] = pInteger ( rest2 ); return [[ hello , space , number ], rest3 ]; }; pSeq Or we generalize even further and provide a function that does the chaining! “Feeding the rest of the string into the next parser” is super generic after all, and doesn’t really depend on what any single parser does. Getting the types right is tricky, but TypeScript is perfectly capable of expressing these complex variadic types. ▸ Code definition · pSeq type Parsers < T extends unknown []> = { [ K in keyof T ]: Parser < T [ K ]> }; const pSeq = < T extends unknown []>(... parsers : Parsers < T >): Parser < T > => ( input ) => { const results = [] as unknown as T ; let rest = input ; for ( const p of parsers ) { const [ val , next ] = ( p as Parser < unknown >)( rest ); results . push ( val ); rest = next ; } return [ results , rest ]; }; Combinators Since pSeq combines many parsers into a new parser, we call it a parser combinator . Take a moment to appreciate the functional madness going on: pSeq is a function that takes parsers, which are functions, and it returns another parser, which is also a function. And only then do we actually start the parsing, by calling the resulting function with data. It’s like we are building up this construct of nested functions to create a complex program. Kinda cool! By the way If splitting a string into many tokens feels somehow related to .reduce then you have good instincts. What we are doing here is actually the dual, which is called an unfold in functional circles ( reduce is referred to as a fold ). While a fold uses intermediate state — the accumulator — to combine a list of things into one, an unfold uses intermediate state to split one thing into many. Yay, maths! Tuples are unwieldy If the point of parsing is to get structured, often human-readable data out of raw strings, then a tuple of values like ["Hello", null, 100] can hardly be the end goal. We could of course map over the result to transform it into a more convenient shape. const pHello100 = pSeq (...); const [ result , rest ] = pHello100 ( "Hello 100" ); console . log ( result ); // ["Hello", null, 100] const parsed = { greeting : result [ 0 ], who : result [ 2 ], }; pMap But this is not in the spirit of parser combinators! Like before, we can also wrap the mapping into a new parser combinator itself. pMap takes a parser and a function; the function will be applied to the eventual result after parsing. ▸ Code definition · pMap const pMap = < T , R >( parser : Parser < T >, fn : ( value : T ) => R ): Parser < R > => ( input : string ) => { const [ value , rest ] = parser ( input ); return [ fn ( value ), rest ]; }; const pGreeting = pMap ( pHello100 , ([ greeting , _ , who ]) => ({ greeting , who }), ); const [ parsed , rest ] = pGreeting ( "Hello 100" ); console . log ( parsed ); // { greeting: "Hello", who: 100 } pRepeat Before we hop into a practical example, let me show the third fundamental parser combinator: pRepeat — it takes a given parser and applies it over and over again until it can’t. It’s the * of regex, as a combinator! ▸ Code definition · pRepeat const pRepeat = < T >( parser : Parser < T >): Parser < T []> => ( input : string ) => { const values : T [] = []; let rest = input ; while ( true ) { try { const [ value , next ] = parser ( rest ); values . push ( value ); rest = next ; } catch { return [ values , rest ]; } } }; ▸ Code definition · pNumber const pNumber : Parser < number > = ( input : string ) => { const match = input . match ( / ^ \d + / ); if ( match == null ) throw new Error (); const digits = match [ 0 ]; return [ Number ( digits ), input . substring ( digits . length )]; }; ▸ Code definition · pSemicolon const pSemicolon : Parser < string > = ( input : string ) => { if ( ! input . startsWith ( ";" )) throw new Error (); return [ ";" , input . substring ( 1 )]; }; const pNumberCsv = pRepeat ( pSeq ( pNumber , pSemicolon )); pNumberCsv ( "10;20;30;" ); // [[[10, ";"], [20, ";"], [30, ";"]], ""] Let’s build a parser! We have enough tools now to start parsing actual, real-world data! Above is a sample output of me pinging Cloudflare. There’s tons of useful info in there, so let’s parse it into structured data — how about this: type PingResult = { header : PingHeader ; packets : IcmpPacket []; statistics : PingStatistics ; }; type IcmpPacket = { byteCount : number ; from : string ; seq : number ; ttl : number ; time : number ; }; type PingHeader = { targetIp : string ; // 1.1.1.1 resolvedIp : string ; // 1.1.1.1 but in parentheses icmpPayloadSize : number ; // 56 totalPacketSize : number ; // 84 }; type PingStatistics = { packetsTransmitted : number ; packetsReceived : number ; packetLoss : number ; time : number ; rtt : { min : number ; avg : number ; max : number ; mdev : number }; }; Bits and Bobs We have some recurring things in this output like decimal numbers or IP addresses. So let’s set those up first. ▸ Code definition · pString // Exact text, like "PING" const pString = ( text : string ): Parser < string > => ( input : string ) => { if ( ! input . startsWith ( text )) throw new Error (); return [ text , input . substring ( text . length )]; }; ▸ Code definition · pInteger // Whole numbers, like 64 const pInteger : Parser < number > = ( input : string ) => { const match = input . match ( / ^ \d + / ); if ( match == null ) throw new Error (); const digits = match [ 0 ]; return [ Number ( digits ), input . substring ( digits . length )]; }; ▸ Code definition · pDecimal // Numbers with an optional fraction, like 68.7 const pDecimal : Parser < number > = ( input : string ) => { const match = input . match ( / ^ \d + ( \. \d + ) ? / ); if ( match == null ) throw new Error (); const digits = match [ 0 ]; return [ Number ( digits ), input . substring ( digits . length )]; }; ▸ Code definition · pIpV4Address // Four bytes and three dots, like 1.1.1.1 const pByte = pMap ( pInteger , ( n ) => { if ( n > 255 ) throw new Error (); return n ; }); const pDot = pString ( "." ); const pIpV4Address = pMap ( pSeq ( pByte , pDot , pByte , pDot , pByte , pDot , pByte ), ([ a , _1 , b , _2 , c , _3 , d ]) => ` ${ a } . ${ b } . ${ c } . ${ d } ` , ); ▸ Code definition · pWhitespace // At least one space const pWhitespace : Parser < null > = ( input : string ) => { const match = input . match ( / ^ \s + / ); if ( match == null ) throw new Error (); return [ null , input . substring ( match [ 0 ]. length )]; }; The header The first line should be easy, it’s just some pSeq of parsers and then a pMap to finagle it into PingHeader shape. ▸ Code definition · pPingHeaderParts const pPingHeaderParts = pSeq ( pString ( "PING" ), pWhitespace , pIpV4Address , pWhitespace , pString ( "(" ), pIpV4Address , pString ( ")" ), pWhitespace , pInteger , pString ( "(" ), pInteger , pString ( ")" ), pString ( " bytes of data." ), ); ▸ Code definition · pPingHeader const pPingHeader = pMap ( pPingHeaderParts , ([ a , b , c , d , e , f , g , h , i , j , k , l , m ]) => ({ targetIp : c , resolvedIp : f , icmpPayloadSize : i , totalPacketSize : k , }), ); A packet Actually the packets are also a pSeq of parsers, followed by a pMap . This parsing stuff is really easy, hey! ▸ Code definition · pIcmpPacketParts const pIcmpPacketParts = pSeq ( pInteger , pString ( " bytes from " ), pIpV4Address , pString ( ": icmp_seq=" ), pInteger , pString ( " ttl=" ), pInteger , pString ( " time=" ), pDecimal , pString ( " ms" ), ); ▸ Code definition · pIcmpPacket const pIcmpPacket = pMap ( pIcmpPacketParts , ([ a , b , c , d , e , f , g , h , i , j ]) => ({ byteCount : a , from : c , seq : e , ttl : g , time : i , }), ); \\d+) packets transmitted, (? \\d+) received, (? [\\d.]+)% packet loss, time (? \\d+)ms"},{"p":"pWhitespace","re":"\\s+"},{"p":"pStatsLine2","re":"rtt min/avg/max/mdev = (? [\\d.]+)/(? [\\d.]+)/(? [\\d.]+)/(? [\\d.]+) ms"}]}" data-astro-cid-msrwk2gl> The statistics Could you imagine doing this in regex by the way? ▸ Code definition · pUselessLine const pUselessLine = pSeq ( pString ( "--- " ), pIpV4Address , pString ( " ping statistics ---" ), ); ▸ Code definition · pStatsLine1 const pStatsLine1 = pSeq ( pInteger , pString ( " packets transmitted, " ), pInteger , pString ( " received, " ), pDecimal , pString ( "% packet loss, time " ), pInteger , pString ( "ms" ), ); ▸ Code definition · pStatsLine2 const pStatsLine2 = pSeq ( pString ( "rtt min/avg/max/mdev = " ), pDecimal , pString ( "/" ), pDecimal , pString ( "/" ), pDecimal , pString ( "/" ), pDecimal , pString ( " ms" ), ); ▸ Code definition · pPingStatistics const pPingStatistics = pMap ( pSeq ( pUselessLine , pWhitespace , pStatsLine1 , pWhitespace , pStatsLine2 ), ([ _1 , _2 , [ a , b , c , d , e , f , g , h ], _3 , [ i , j , k , l , m , n , o , p , q ]]) => ({ packetsTransmitted : a , packetsReceived : c , packetLoss : e , time : g , rtt : { min : j , avg : l , max : n , mdev : p }, }), ); Ping packets, parsed! And boom, that’s pretty much it! Just one more pSeq and pMap to wrap all the parts together, and we have built a complete parser for the ping command. That was super easy, right? ▸ Code definition · pPingSummary const pPingSummary : Parser < PingResult > = pMap ( pSeq ( pPingHeader , pRepeat ( pMap ( pSeq ( pWhitespace , pIcmpPacket ), ([ _ , packet ]) => packet )), pWhitespace , pPingStatistics , ), ([ header , packets , _ , statistics ]) => ({ header , packets , statistics }), ); Go give it a try In a single post we built a fairly complicated parser from literally zero, and a hand-rolled parser combinator library along the way! It’s much easier to create correct and maintainable parsers this way than with a regex; once you start nesting pSeq calls, the equivalent regex would become an unreadable mess, while the combinator approach gives you something squeaky clean. In case you are missing fancier features like backtracking or lookahead, rest assured that parser combinators can handle those scenarios as well, since at the end of the day it’s all just functions composed together. Go give them a try next time you have to parse something — parser combinators are a really elegant solution to the parser problem, and many more people should use them! ‹ ›

title: Show HN: Sphinx – A hook that quizzes you on your AI's code before shipping
body_text: Sphinx — you can outsource your thinking, but not your understanding sphinx Install GitHub Free FOSS “You can outsource your thinking, but not your understanding .” — Sun Tzu Sphinx is a Git hook for agent-assisted development. Before your agent’s code ships, it asks you a question about what that code actually does. $ npm install -g sphinx-understand Copy Built to run on minimal tokens, from your existing coding agent, OpenRouter, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. $ git push origin main sphinx · understanding check for main 11 files changed · +5,012 −3,147 Sphinx Your webhook handler now saves the event ID before calling charge() . Stripe times out and sends the same event again. What happens on the retry? You It runs twice, so the customer is charged twice. Sphinx Not quite. The retry finds the saved ID and returns 200 without charging. But that ID is stored before the charge succeeds. If charge() fails, what does the next retry do? You It skips the charge, so the customer is never billed. ✓ Understood. Pushing to origin/main. An illustrative exchange. Real questions come from your diff. 01 You push. Or your agent does. Git pauses on the branches you protect. 02 Sphinx asks. A reviewer that never saw your chat reads the diff and asks what the change does when things go wrong. 03 You answer. Get it wrong and you learn why, then try a new scenario. Get it right and the push continues. The real questionnaire: a push waits, you answer, Git continues. Works with Codex, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenCode, and Pi , or plain Git. Your answers never reach the coding agent, and .env files and keys are never opened. In a hurry? sphinx yolo lets pushes through, and every skip is logged. Start in a minute. # Node 22.19+ · macOS, Linux, or WSL npm install -g sphinx-understand sphinx install # then push as usual git push sphinx install connects Git and your coding agents and asks which model should review. Read the docs for everything else. sphinx · MIT licensed GitHub npm

title: Legal experts warn Meta's new terms still grant broad scraping permissions

Meta-owned platforms include Facebook, WhatsApp, Oculus, Threads, Instagram, and Messenger. (Adobe Stock) By Andrew Deck and Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 17, 2026, 2:49 p.m. Meta has removed the word “train” from its upcoming terms of service for business accounts. The company revised its terms after Nieman Lab’s story on Thursday exposed that the new terms would permit broad scraping of websites “associated with” business accounts, and possibly allow Meta to use that scraped content to train its AI models. In its revision, published Friday afternoon, Meta removed the word “train” from a list of allowed use cases and limited those uses to “advertising and business products,” rather than all Meta products. But the revised terms will still allow for broad scraping of websites, potentially superseding robots.txt files, according to legal experts. On Saturday, a Meta spokesperson said the company revised the terms because “it wasn’t clear in the initial consolidation of terms that robots.txt preferences are respected. News sites, like all other content owners, still have the ability to disable the crawler via robots.txt flags. That has been the case, and it has not changed.” Meta has not included any specific language about respecting robots.txt preferences in its revised terms of services . The new terms are slated to go into effect on October 30. There is no option for business accounts to opt out of the new terms before then. RELATED ARTICLE Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Andrew Deck October 15, 2026 “I think publishers should remain concerned,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “The revised version of the new terms still allows Meta to use that scraped content to develop any ‘business product.’ That doesn’t seem to be a defined term, and presumably Meta is developing AI business products. I think ‘develop’ is broad enough to include ‘train.'” Meta currently lists examples of its business products as “ads, Meta Business Tools and Meta Business Suite.” Virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, which allows companies to manage Facebook Pages, Threads accounts, Instagram profiles, and WhatsApp channels from one place. As of publication time, the section reads (with changes in bold): You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs in order to provide, develop, improve, research, and maintain advertising and business products (including business, commercial and related products to help you create and deliver ads and other commercial content, provide users information about your products and services, and connect you with users who may be interested in your products and services) and maintain the integrity and security of Meta Company Products . Here’s the original text : You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains , web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train , and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” a spokesperson said in a statement, claiming publishers can still update their scraping preferences using robots.txt files. “This is not about scraping news sites, and these updates don’t give us new rights that supersede those preferences.” Meta’s current terms permit it to scrape websites associated with business accounts, but only in a very specific scenario. That language is found in its terms of service for when accounts use Meta’s generative AI features to run advertisements . The scraped content can only be used to “optimize your ads.” Adding this language to more general terms of service, and allowing scraped content to be used for all “advertising and business products,” is a substantial expansion of Meta’s scraping permissions. A Meta spokesperson said the company is incorporating its “ Ad Creative Generative AI Terms ” into its general commercial terms to make them easier to understand. Three legal experts Nieman Lab consulted were skeptical about the revised terms of service and Meta’s most recent statements. “[The update] doesn’t address my concerns,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “While it adds more language about the permitted uses, [the] ‘develop…advertising and business products’ [language] is still broad enough to drive a truck through. This does nothing to restrict the ‘associated with your products or services’ [language] that would let Meta scrape entire sites.” University of Wisconsin law professor Benjamin Sobel explained that robots.txt indicates a website’s preferences, but compliance with those is completely voluntary. He likened it to a homeowner putting up a sign saying, “Don’t look at my house.” Putting up that sign doesn’t give the homeowner an enforceable legal right to stop people from looking at the house. “You can still express the preference, and unless it’s a legally enforceable preference, it can still be ignored all the same,” he said. RELATED ARTICLE Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 At least three journalism organizations have publicly raised concerns about the forthcoming terms as a result of Nieman Lab’s reporting. Prior to the update on Friday, the European Publishers Council announced that it would formally petition the E.U.’s telecommunications regulatory authorities and its executive body, the European Commission, to “ scrutinize these terms urgently, including their implications for copyright, contractual fairness and abuse of market power .” The United Kingdom News Media Association , the trade organization representing British media, issued a statement on Friday calling for government officials to intervene. “This shameless landgrab attempt from Meta to scrape anything and everything from news publishers and business websites to train their AI products is the worst kind of arrogant tech platform bullying,” said chief executive Theo Bamber . “We urgently need Ministers and regulators to stand up for British creators and the business community by calling out this outrageous behaviour and preventing Meta from setting this dreadful precedent.” The News/Media Alliance — the largest news publishing trade association in the United States — denounced the terms, with president and CEO Danielle Coffey calling the update “ outrageous and probably illegal .” “The company’s decision to withhold access to its audience unless businesses allow Meta to scrape content from their websites is an appalling, bad-faith policy, and a clear abuse of the company’s market power,” Coffey said. “It cannot be allowed to be implemented on October 30.” This story has been updated to include comments from Meta. title: Bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour
body_text: ‘Incredible’: bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour | Nature Skip to main content Thank you for visiting nature.com. Advertisement View all journals Saved research Search Log in Content Explore content About the journal Publish with us Subscribe Sign up for alerts RSS feed nature news article NEWS 14 October 2026 ‘Incredible’: bleached corals thrive within days when touching healthy neighbour A coral fragment can form a tissue bridge with a dying counterpart — and provide it with crucial microalgae. By Sarah Wild 0 Sarah Wild Sarah Wild is a freelance journalist in Canterbury, UK. View author publications Search author on: PubMed   Google Scholar Email Bluesky Facebook LinkedIn Reddit Whatsapp X Save article View saved research This video shows a bleached coral fragment brought back to health within weeks through fusion with a vibrant fragment from the same individual. Credit: Danny Collins Scientists have rapidly restored bleached coral in a laboratory by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment, giving hope for reversing widespread coral decline. Rising sea temperatures are stressing corals, causing the animals to expel the symbiotic algae that live in their tissues and give them their colour — a process known as bleaching. Because the photosynthetic algae (Symbiodiniaceae) provide corals with most of their nutrients, without them, the marine organisms are likely to starve and die. A team of researchers has now shown that it is possible to fully reverse this bleaching process, in just days. It reported the findings in Science Advances on 14 October 1 . “This incredible new result — that fast and full recovery is possible in bleached coral — can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable,” says Fiorenza Micheli, a marine ecologist at Stanford University’s Center for Ocean Solutions in California and a co-author on the study. The healing touch In early 2025, marine scientist, and study co-author, Stephen Palumbi at Hopkins Marine Station in Pacific Grove, California, was working in the lab and noticed that two coral fragments in a tank were accidentally touching. Where the healthy and bleached fragment met, colour had begun to seep into the ghostly branch. “I’d never seen that before,” he remembers. Symbionts spread from the healthy into the bleached coral. Credit: Danny Collins Danny Collins, who was studying how disease spreads through coral contact as part of his PhD at Stanford, set out to investigate whether algae can also spread and, if so, how. He prepared ten pairs of coral fragments from the same animal ( Pocillopora damicornis )., Each pair had a bleached and a healthy fragment. He set up five pairs so that their fragments touched each other, and five with their fragments separated by a few millimetres. In the touching pairs, the bleached coral recovered within eight weeks. “We were blown away when we watched the colour of the algal symbionts transfer over to the bleached coral, reviving it in a very short period of time,” Collins says. By week two, the symbiont population was doubling every four days, which is much faster than the recovery times seen in studies of coral recovering naturally in the wild 2 , 3 . After touching the healthy fragment for a week, a bleached branch could fully recover on its own, even if separated from the healthy branch. In the slightly separated pairs, the bleached fragments died after 20 weeks. Using high-powered microscopy, the team showed that two coral fragments fuse together by creating a tissue bridge — enabling symbiont transfer. This only occurred for coral fragments taken from an individual of the same genetic make-up, called a genet. Fragments from different species and even different animals of the same species did not fuse together, and so did not nurse the bleached piece back to health. Enjoying our latest content? Dismiss alert {{ message }} antirez c64-hw-simulator Repository navigation Code Issues Pull requests 2 ( 2 ) Actions Projects Security and quality Insights More items c64-hw-simulator Public Notifications You must be signed in to change notification settings Fork 14 ( 14 ) Star 366 ( 366 ) You must be signed in to star a repository About Commodore 64 hardware simulator Resources Readme License Activity Stars 366 stars Watchers 9 watching Forks 14 forks Report repository main Branches Tags Go to file Code Open more actions menu Latest commit History 2 Commits 2 Commits Folders and files Name Name Last commit message Last commit date chips chips docs docs src src tests tests third_party third_party tools tools .gitignore .gitignore LICENSE LICENSE Makefile Makefile PLAN.md PLAN.md README.md README.md compile_flags.txt compile_flags.txt View all files Repository files navigation README License More items c64-hw-sim c64-hw-sim simulates the motherboard of the Commodore 64, ASSY 250407, pin by pin. You can lift the leg of a chip, short it to ground or to +5V, pull a chip out of its socket, or open a resistor. Then you watch what the machine does: the picture on the monitor, the keyboard, every signal on the board. The program knows the board's netlist (the electrical connections on the PCB) and how each chip behaves at its pins. It knows nothing about what a broken Commodore 64 looks like: when you simulate a broken part and the screen fills with garbage, that garbage was computed from the circuit, not chosen by someone who knew what to expect. Here is an example. Lift pin 17 (A7) of the color RAM before power on, and the machine boots and looks healthy. The CPU writes and the VIC reads with the same wrong address, so the RAM simply aliases. Put the leg back, and the half of the color RAM that was never written shows up as random colors. Lift it again, and the screen is clean. A real 2114 does the same. With this program you can do mainly two things: Learn how the Commodore 64 works at a more intimate level, in a way that is hard to reproduce on real hardware without the risk of damaging it (and on most boards many chips are soldered, not socketed). If you have a broken C64 and some hypothesis about what could be broken, simulate it with this program and perhaps gain clues, so that you can desolder chips in the most logical order, and desolder as few of them as possible (desoldering is a boring process, and every time it risks damaging the board...). A matching symptom is a clue, not a proof: different faults can look the same, and the simulation has its limits (see below). Please note that even on fast computers this program struggles to simulate the C64 hardware at real speed. A real C64 is simulated at 31% of its speed on an Apple M3 Max, 39% on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 495 (Gorgon Halo), and 48% on an Apple M5 Max. This is not a problem for the goals of this program, but be warned: it is not an emulator to play games with. Above: the classic 10 PRINT CHR$(205.5+RND(1));:GOTO 10 maze is running when the character ROM (U5) is pulled out of its socket, and later put back. The CPU, the RAM and the program keep working; only the shapes of the characters are lost, as repairers know well. The scope is on the data line D0 of the ROM socket: with the socket empty, the bus floats (the dotted segments) whenever the VIC fetches a character shape. Shown at C64 speed. Acknowledgements I (antirez) got the idea for this program while using and observing Andre Weissflog's (floooh) chips, emulators of the 6502, VIC-II, CIA, SID and friends that use pins as their interface. The next step was to take this approach, with his code as a starting point, to its logical extreme: pin-level models of every other part of the C64, the RAMs, the ROMs, the logic chips, the PLA, and so forth. The chip cores are floooh's chips, taken from c64-llm (zlib license). The board comes from bwack's C64-250407-Replica-KiCad (CERN OHL). The PLA equations come from the 82S100 read-out by Mark Smith and Marko Mäkelä. Building make ./c64-hw-sim [program.prg] It runs on macOS and Linux (X11), with OpenGL. The graphics library (sokol) and the interface library (nuklear) are in third_party/ . Using it The window shows the board, the monitor, a control panel and an oscilloscope. Chips are boxes named by role: RAM1 to RAM8 are the 4164 DRAMs. Each one holds a single bit of every byte: RAMn has data bit n-1. VRAM is the 2114 color RAM. BASIC, KERNAL and CHAR are the ROMs. PLA is the address decoder. Zoom in to see references and address ranges. Pins show their state as a logic probe would: red high, blue low, yellow pulsing, gray floating, magenta when two outputs fight. Click a pin to put it on the oscilloscope and to break it: floating, shorted to GND, or shorted to +5V. Click a chip to pull it out. Click a resistor, a ferrite bead or the crystal to open it. The control panel lists the faults, each with a repair button. The control panel also loads .prg files. They are written straight into the DRAM chips, as a freezer cartridge would do it, so loading works on a broken board too. Type on your keyboard as usual. ESC is RUN/STOP, PgUp is RESTORE, TAB is CTRL, and left ALT is C=. Command line ./c64-hw-sim --headless 200 --text --shot out.png --fault U17:removed This runs four seconds (200 frames) without a window. It prints the text read from the monitor picture, as a person would read it, and saves the picture. A fault is written REF:what or REF.PIN:what : U17:removed U21.14:gnd U12.14:vcc U9.2:open R51:open RP4:short Other options: --at 150:U6.17:open --at 300:repair breaks and repairs parts while the C64 runs. --nets reports the nets where outputs fought. C64HW_TYPE=$'PRINT 1+1\n' types text after boot. C64HW_CHECK=1 checks every KERNAL read and every VIC fetch against the ideal memory map. --record 900:DIR --frames 90 (graphical mode) saves the window 90 times, every 4 emulated frames from frame 900 on. This is how the GIF above was made. tests/faults.sh runs 31 common faults. The expected symptom of each one was written down before the simulator was run. How it works tools/kicad2c.py turns bwack's KiCad replica of the 250407 into C tables: 216 parts, their pads, and 249 nets. Every pin drives its net strongly, weakly (a pull-up), from a supply short, or not at all. The strongest drive wins. Two equal drives fighting are a contention, and low wins. A net that nobody drives keeps its charge, and then drifts: to about 1.4V within microseconds, if TTL inputs load it; toward 0V in a fraction of a second, if only MOS inputs are on it. MOS inputs compare that voltage, plus some noise, with their own threshold, so a floating line can read erratically. Power faults depend on the chip: A chip without VCC is dead. A chip without GND lets its outputs float high. A CMOS chip keeps running on phantom power, which reaches it through the protection diodes of its pins. The noise is seeded, so a run can be repeated exactly. src/parts.c models these parts at their pins: the glue logic; the ROMs; the DRAMs, which latch the row on /RAS and the column on /CAS; the color RAM; the PLA, with its real logic equations. The 6510, VIC-II, CIAs and SID are cycle-accurate cores from floooh's chips. In src/board.c each core sits in a socket that sees only its pins. Each half cycle runs in three steps: the row address, then /RAS falls, then /CAS falls. The whole board settles after each step. PLAN.md explains the reasoning behind these choices. Limits It is slow, between a third and half of real time on the computers listed above, because every pin of every chip is simulated. The floating and power models have the right shape, but their numbers (thresholds, drift times, crosstalk) are guesses. They are constants in src/sim.c . These analog parts are not simulated: the video output, the SID filter, the power supply, and the dot clock PLL. Faults inside a chip, such as bad DRAM cells or slow parts, and bridges between two nets are planned but not done. title: Gold is now the top U.S. export
body_text: Gold is Now the Top U.S. Export - Numismatic News Subscribe Shop Newsletters Buy, Sell & Trade MARKETPLACE See Future Events Here 2026 Summer Coin Show Calendar Listen to Our Podcast! Stay up-to-date on the market. Pricing Directory US Coins World Coins Paper Money Collecting 101 Coin Market Events Podcast Shop Home / Coin Market / Market Update Coin Market Gold is Now the Top U.S. Export Surging U.S. gold exports have overtaken traditional top exports, fueling speculation that rising global demand—particularly from foreign powers seeking alternatives to dollar-based reserves—is reshaping precious metals markets. Patrick A. Heller Updated May 15, 2026 6:39 AM PDT Share this story Image: AdobeStock Normally, America’s highest value exports are either oil, pharmaceuticals, or aircraft and their parts.  Not now.  Starting in October 2025, the value of gold exports has topped all other categories almost every month.  For information on U.S. nonmonetary gold exports through December 2025, go to https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/IEAXGG That’s not just because the price of gold reached record high prices.  In February 2026, the tons of gold exported may have set an all-time record. The majority of gold exports are going to Switzerland, almost certainly to the refiners there. The second greatest quantity is going to Hong Kong, which is the global destination for gold going to China. The third greatest quantity of exported gold is going to the United Kingdom, where the London Bullion Market Association is the world’s largest gold trading exchange. The U.S. government is still reporting that its gold reserves are unchanged, so these exports look to be coming from current mine output and recycling operations. Why is this happening? There is no official explanation of why U.S. gold exports have soared in recent months.  But here is my speculation. There are multiple foreign governments growing leery of the future loss of purchasing power of the U.S. dollar, where they would prefer a different reserve asset with a better track record. Among all foreign central banks combined, the value of their gold reserves now exceeds their holdings of U.S. Treasury debt. Most foreign nations do not have the economic and financial power when negotiating with the U.S. government or businesses to demand payments for goods and services other than in dollars. China does have the economic and financial clout to press for payment in gold instead of dollars. The Chinese Central Bank has a track record the past few years of reducing its holdings of U.S. Treasury debt, from $1.096.1 trillion in April 2021 to $784.3 billion in February 2025, and the latest reported at just $693.3 billion in February 2026. Much of the decrease in Bank of China U.S. Treasuries has been replaced with gold. The Chinese government is also working to decrease the use of the dollar in international commerce, through the creation of alternative payment systems and the promotion of the “unit” for transactions among the member nations of the BRICS consortium. When you add up the gold held by the Chinese central bank (which has a decades-long track record of underreporting gold reserves, Chinese sovereign investment funds, the Chinese military, the inventories held by companies owned directly by the Chinese government or the Chinese military, and private citizenry, there are multiple analysts who consider that nation effectively controls the greatest amount of gold of any government. When you put these factors together, my suspicion is that a high percentage of U.S. gold exports are going to China, though some must first detour through Swiss refineries to convert the gold into kilogram bars of acceptable purity. It is possible that the U.S. government may have acquiesced in this form of payment in return for other political concessions having to do with a number of global uncertainties. Can I prove this?  No.  But it does make sense, much more than any other explanation. Last column’s numismatic trivia question. Last time I asked— Why did the Coinage Act of 1834 reduce the gold content in U.S. coins? From the late 1700s to the 1830s, the relative value of gold to silver had increased. As a result, pre-1834 U.S. gold coins contained a higher value of gold than their face value. Many were being melted down. In 1834, the U.S. government reduced the gold content in coins to match the face value to the international value of the gold they contained. This week’s trivia question Here is this week’s question. Which denominations has the U.S government issued in both coin and currency? Come back next week for the answer. Patrick A. Heller was honored as a 2019 FUN Numismatic Ambassador. He is also the recipient of the American Numismatic Association 2018 Glenn Smedley Memorial Service Award, the 2017 Exemplary Service Award, the 2012 Harry Forman National Dealer of the Year Award, and the 2008 Presidential Award. Over the years, he has also been honored by the Numismatic Literary Guild, Professional Numismatists Guild, National Coin & Bullion Association, and the Michigan State Numismatic Society. He is the communications officer of Liberty Coin Service in Lansing, Michigan, and writes “ Liberty’s Outlook ,” a quarterly newsletter on rare coins and precious metals subjects. He now volunteers with the National Coin & Bullion Association as its Industry Issues Advisor. Past newsletter issues can be viewed at www.libertycoinservice.com . (Image credit: Tom's Hardware) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 35 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Rep. Ritchie Torres of New York's 15th congressional district has introduced the Power To The Players Act . This new legislation aims to protect consumers by directing the FTC to establish regulations on game ownership to curb anti-consumer business practices. "Under the bill, buying a video game would give the consumer ownership of the game rather than a license to play it," the release says. "Games with online functionality would also be required to provide an offline mode before the servers supporting them are shut down." Games having an expiration date despite being more expensive than ever has been scrutinized by players all over the world, along with aggressive monetization schemes within the games themselves. Rep. Ritchie Torres isn’t the first to fight for gamers, as Pennsylvania state senator John Kane also recently introduced the Protect Our Games Act , requiring publishers to provide an offline mode, community servers, or a 25% minimum refund. Players want to be able to enjoy their games even if the publisher decides to stop supporting the game, but Sony doesn’t think the players own their games and that they have the right to pull the rug from under them. Sony’s lawyers even recently said in a defense in an ongoing class action lawsuit that clicking on the “purchase” button would obviously not lead the consumer to think that they were acquiring a durable right to use the game instead of a revocable license; basically a one-time rent fee that Sony could take away at any moment that benefits them. One of the most prominent recent examples of players not owning their games came in 2024 with The Crew , an online-only racing game that Ubisoft shut down for server upkeep, making it unplayable even for those who had recently purchased it. Ubisoft had not provided a way for community servers to be set up, nor an offline mode, since even the single-player campaign depended on a connection to Ubisoft’s servers. Another is the notorious yearly sports games released by EA, 2K, and Sony, with NBA 2K25 specifically being cited by Rep. Torres in his announcement of the Power to the Players Act ; NBA 2K25 is being pulled from digital storefronts, with the online servers being shut down only two years after release, leaving players unable to use a main feature of the game they purchased, and new players unable to purchase the game at all. Overwatch 2’s release also killed the first Overwatch game, replacing it outright instead of the first game becoming a purchasable and separately playable game. Latest Videos From Tom's Hardware Watch full video here: The Crew’s shutdown prompted the Stop Killing Games movement, demanding that publishers leave the games functional after discontinuation in the form of an offline mode, peer-to-peer patching, and the ability to host community servers. The movement also pushes back against the industry standard of selling games as revocable licenses rather than outright ownership of the copy. Concrete definitions and details of the bill have yet to be released, but it aims to require publishers to provide an offline mode before shutting down servers and actual consumer ownership instead of a license that can be taken away, potentially satisfying the demands of the movement. We don’t know whether the right to transfer that Rep. Torres mentions is mandatory for digital purchases, but it will likely be relevant for physical copies. It is also important for the bill to strictly define what ownership is and what rights the owners have over their copy. One popular phrase against these practices is “If buying isn’t owning, piracy isn’t stealing,” pushing strongly against these revocable licenses that the companies want you to purchase. Piracy is often touted as a better experience by players, as it removes DRM that often slows games down and provides a permanent copy that the publishers cannot modify to be dysfunctional; many players say they would be more glad to purchase the game if it were actually a better experience. It is still yet to be known how well the bill will execute its aims, but this is a big step towards correcting the direction the gaming industry is currently on.
