Advertisement Markets & Policy See all Solar surpasses nuclear power globally for first time Solar and wind are increasingly outpacing nuclear power globally, with solar generation surpassing nuclear for the first time in 2025, according to WNISR 2026. The report highlights nuclear’s slow growth, lengthy construction timelines and limited small modular reactor deployment, contrasting them with rapid renewables and battery expansion. By Emiliano Bellini 29 Sep 2026 Markets & Policy Utility-scale Image: Hans Ott / Unsplash Advertisement The World Nuclear Industry Status Report (WNISR) 2026 , overseen by French nuclear energy consultant Mycle Schneider , shows that wind power alone surpassed nuclear generation on a monthly basis in March 2025, followed by solar in April – the first time global monthly solar generation exceeded nuclear output. From March 2025 through June 2026, either solar or wind individually generated more electricity than nuclear every month. In March, April and May 2026, both technologies independently surpassed nuclear generation. Increasing gap According to the report, the gap between renewables and nuclear widened substantially in 2025. Global solar capacity increased by 510 GW to 2,383 GW, up 27% year on year, while wind added a record 159 GW to reach 1,291 GW, an increase of 14%. By comparison, installed nuclear capacity rose by just 1.5 GW to 399.5 GW, while operating nuclear capacity declined by 0.5 GW to 368.6 GW. The report notes that nuclear capacity has remained essentially flat for more than 25 years, while wind and, particularly, solar have expanded rapidly. The report’s PV figures, however, are based on relatively conservative estimates. More recent data from IEA PVPS indicate that global PV additions reached around 690 GW in 2025 , about 180 GW more than the figure used by WNISR. This suggests the gap between solar and nuclear capacity – and their respective growth rates – was even wider than indicated in the report. “The reality of the nuclear industry on the ground is quite sobering for those who expected to find a booming sector,” Schneider told pv magazine . “Recently, U.S. nuclear company Holtec put an initial public offering (IPO) on hold just days before its planned stock market listing, through which it had hoped to raise almost $1 billion. Its peer, Fermi, has lost about 80% of its stock value since it was first listed in October 2025.” “The main reason? These companies have little or nothing to show on the ground to convince investors to continue providing cash,” he added. “Meanwhile, the world’s operating nuclear fleet increased output by 1.1% – with output declining outside China – while global solar power generation jumped by a stunning 30%, surpassing nuclear’s annual electricity production for the first time. One is tempted to say: It’s the growth rates, stupid!” The report identifies falling battery costs as a potential enabler of continued PV expansion, particularly as grids contend with growing volumes of variable renewable generation and periods of low or negative electricity prices. Grid-scale battery deployment accelerated sharply in 2025, with 104 GW and 257 GWh connected during the year. More than 78% of cumulative battery energy storage system (BESS) capacity was installed between 2023 and 2025. Slow expansion The report shows that the global nuclear sector is expanding slowly, with most new activity concentrated in China and Russia. As of July 1, 2026, 411 reactors were operating in 31 countries, excluding 30 units in long-term outage, with operating capacity at 374.7 GW. In 2025, nuclear plants generated 2,703 TWh, up 1.1% year on year, largely driven by a 7.6% increase in China. Outside China, nuclear generation declined by 0.2% and remained well below its 2006 level. Nuclear’s share of global electricity generation slipped to 8.8%, its lowest level in four and a half decades and roughly half its 1996 peak of 17.5%. Four reactors started supplying electricity in 2025, while seven closed, resulting in the first negative annual reactor balance since 2021. Between 2006 and 2025, 104 reactors started up and 106 closed. China accounted for 53 of those startups and no closures, meaning the rest of the world recorded a net decline of 55 reactors. Although global nuclear capacity increased by a net 21.5 GW over the two decades, China alone added 52.3 GW, while capacity outside the country fell by almost 30.7 GW. The construction pipeline has nevertheless expanded. Seventy-three reactors were under construction as of July 1, the highest number since 1987, with China accounting for 37. Russia remains the dominant international supplier, with Russian technology involved in 29 reactors under construction worldwide, including 22 outside Russia. Nine out of 10 reactors being built are in Asia or Eastern Europe. Long construction times and delays remain a feature of new nuclear projects, according to the report. None of the 16 reactors connected to the grid between 2023 and 2025 was completed on schedule, with an average construction period of 10.9 years. Of 13 reactors scheduled to start generating electricity in 2025, only four did so. Some projects have experienced exceptionally long timelines, including Slovakia’s Mochovce-4, where construction began more than 40 years ago, and Iran’s Bushehr-2, where construction originally started in 1976. Construction starts accelerated in 2025, however, reaching 12 units, the highest annual total since 2010. Nine were in China, two in Russia and one in South Korea. Of the 52 reactor construction starts recorded worldwide between 2020 and 2025, all but one involved the Chinese or Russian nuclear industries, either domestically or abroad. Limited progress on small modular reactors The report questions whether small modular reactors (SMRs) can deliver on their long-standing commercial promises, noting that progress remains limited despite growing government support and public funding. “For decades, small modular reactors have been held out as holding great promise for expanding nuclear power into various new markets. Remarkably similar claims have been made by the nuclear industry in multiple countries. Nowhere have these claims come true,” the authors said. The authors challenge several claimed advantages of SMRs, including lower costs, modular construction, improved safety, reduced waste and easier siting. Many commercially proposed designs are 300 MW or larger, while an analysis cited in the report suggests some SMR designs could generate between two and 30 times more nuclear waste than larger reactors. The report also questions whether modular manufacturing can achieve economies of scale without a large and predictable market. Still, SMR projects are advancing in several countries. Canada began construction of GE-Hitachi’s BWRX-300 in 2026, while China continued testing its Linglong One demonstration reactor. Russia is developing floating and land-based SMRs, while the Czech Republic and Sweden are pursuing Rolls-Royce projects. The report questions whether the EU can meet its goal of deploying its first SMRs by the early 2030s. The United Kingdom has committed £2.6 billion ($3.5 billion) to advance three Rolls-Royce reactors at Wylfa, with a final investment decision expected in 2029. At 470 MW, the design exceeds the commonly used 300 MW threshold for SMRs. In the United States, federal funding supports projects involving GE Vernova, TerraPower, X-energy and Kairos Power. While some have reached permitting or construction stages, many remain years from commercial operation. Overall, the report says SMR development remains heavily dependent on public funding, while commercial deployment, construction timelines and the claimed benefits of modular construction remain uncertain. Global overview The report also provides detailed country-level assessments covering developments in major nuclear markets and potential newcomer countries, as well as nuclear decommissioning, the Fukushima disaster and Russia’s nuclear interdependencies. These sections examine reactor operations, newbuild plans, closures, policy developments and the challenges associated with aging fleets. The report also tracks the dismantling of closed reactors, developments in Japan 15 years after the Fukushima accident, and the nuclear industry’s continuing technology, fuel and supply-chain links with Russia. body_text: Dam Removals Are Bringing Fish Back Across the Northeastern United States, Striking Down One Tiny Barrier at a Time Skip to main content Search Shop Newsletters Renew Give a Gift Subscribe Membership i Subscribe Give a Gift Renew Sections Smart News History Science Innovation Arts & Culture Travel At the Smithsonian More from Smithsonian magazine Newsletters Photo Contest Podcast Videos Our Partners Smithsonian Store Smithsonian Journeys Subscribe to Smithsonian magazine and get a FREE tote. Science | October 16, 2026 Dam Removals Are Bringing Fish Back Across the Northeastern United States, Striking Down One Tiny Barrier at a Time While the demolition of big dams in the West gets more attention, many of these often-obsolete obstructions are also coming out of northeastern streams and rivers—and herring are returning in droves Dams block the flow of a river to hold water in a reservoir, which can be used for agriculture, recreation, household needs or industry. The flow of water through a dam can generate hydroelectric power. Aging dams are being dismantled across the country, restoring the natural flow to rivers. Jukka Jantunen / Shutterstock Dam Removals Are Bringing Fish Back Across the Northeastern United States, Striking Down One Tiny Barrier at a Time While the demolition of big dams in the West gets more attention, many of these often-obsolete obstructions are also coming out of northeastern streams and rivers—and herring are returning in droves Ben Goldfarb, bioGraphic October 16, 2026 Share Copy link Email SMS Facebook X Reddit LinkedIn Bluesky Print Add as preferred source Dams block the flow of a river to hold water in a reservoir, which can be used for agriculture, recreation, household needs or industry. The flow of water through a dam can generate hydroelectric power. Aging dams are being dismantled across the country, restoring the natural flow to rivers. Jukka Jantunen / Shutterstock In 1859, a committee of farmers in Billerica, Massachusetts, having grown irked by a dam on the Concord River, hired a surveyor to justify its destruction. The dam, which powered a textile factory owned by an industrialist named Charles Talbot, was allegedly flooding their fields and spoiling their hay; now they wanted the wall and its reservoir gone. They hoped the surveyor’s evidence would persuade a court to order its obliteration. The surveyor—a conscientious, lushly bearded man of good repute—set about plumbing the Concord’s bottom, measuring its bridges and scrutinizing high-water marks. In truth, he didn’t love the work, describing surveying as “drudgery” in his journals. Henry David Thoreau ’s truest passion, of course, wasn’t surveying land, but writing about it. Aside from the paycheck, the now-legendary author had another motivation to take the Concord job: He despised the Talbot Mills Dam. A decade earlier, Thoreau had published the travelogue A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers , in which he inveighed against the dam for blocking the passage of spawning fish, especially American shad. “Poor shad! Where is thy redress?” Thoreau wrote . Although Thoreau’s surveys supported the farmers’ case, on appeal, the state of Massachusetts permitted the dam to remain. This can’t have surprised Thoreau, who knew that dams made for intractable opponents. “Perchance, after a few thousands of years, if the fishes will be patient, and pass their summers elsewhere meanwhile, nature will have leveled the Billerica dam,” he wrote. The Talbot Mills Dam in Billerica, Massachusetts—shown in this 1908 photograph—has vexed environmentalists, agrarians and native fish for centuries. Public domain via Billerica Public Library For many fish-blocking dams, however, it hasn’t taken “a few thousands of years” to level them after all. Since 1912, more than 2,300 dams have been purged from waterways in the United States, most in the last quarter-century. The dam-removal movement hit its apogee in 2024, when, by the accounting of the nonprofit American Rivers, dam removals reconnected more than 2,500 miles of once-fragmented waterways . The year’s biggest and best-publicized dam obliteration occurred on the Klamath River, where the dismantling of four aging hydroelectric dams opened more than 400 miles of spawning habitat in California and Oregon to chinook salmon, which recolonized the watershed so rapidly that conservationists described the comeback as “ magical .” Before the Klamath, the nation’s largest undamming took place on Washington State’s Elwha River, where two fish-blocking walls were obliterated on behalf of chinook, coho, steelhead and other salmonids. After this and other dams were removed from the Elwha River in Washington State, long-absent salmonids came surging back. Trish Drury / Alamy Stock Photo Yet it would be a mistake to presume that dam removals primarily benefit western salmon rivers. Though they’re typically smaller in scale and receive less fanfare, the majority occur in eastern states. In 2024, the Blake Higgins Dam came tumbling down in Vermont, the Edes Falls Dam departed the Crooked River in Maine, and the Kimball Brook Dam vanished from New Hampshire. Pennsylvania tore out 27 obsolete barriers that year, none taller than around 20 feet. Even the three-century-old Talbot Mills Dam that so vexed Thoreau may soon be taken down . “We’re in this dam-removal renaissance, where we’re losing barriers faster than we’re putting them up for the first time in history,” says Nathan Furey , a fish biologist at the University of New Hampshire. Per one inventory , however, at least 35,000 dams still truncate northeastern fish runs, including more than 3,000 in Massachusetts, 5,000 in Connecticut and 9,000 in New York. By the numbers: Klamath River dam removal The $500 million project to remove four dams along the Klamath River in California and Oregon took place over a couple of years, with the river flowing freely by August 2024. The work opened 400 miles of salmon habitat, and thousands of the fish passed a former dam site in both 2024 and 2025. Among the states destroying dams, albeit gradually, is New Hampshire, and one late-April morning I climbed into a car with Furey to tour a few of its newly free-flowing rivers. Furey had come to the Granite State in 2018 a neophyte to dam removal, having done most of his graduate research on relatively undeveloped Pacific salmon rivers in British Columbia. “But when you’re the fish guy at the University of New Hampshire, people want you to tell them what happens when a dam comes out,” he said as he navigated Durham’s leafy streets. “There’s a lot of people looking to you for answers.” Furey’s domain is the Great Bay watershed , a tidal estuary fed by an arterial network of seven rivers. Historically, those waterways teemed with a roster of diadromous fishes: species that split their lives between freshwater and the ocean. That included Atlantic salmon, shad, sea lamprey, American eels, tomcod, sturgeon and, most numerous of all, alewives and bluebacks, a pair of silvery, foot-long fish collectively known as river herring . Sharks, striped bass, cod, seals, seabirds and other predators devoured river herring as they approached the estuary each spring, and juvenile Atlantic salmon may even have timed their departure from river to ocean to coincide with alewives’ return. While cormorants and otters gorged on alewives, young salmon slipped downstream undetected. There’s safety in numbers, and alewives supplied such prodigious numbers before they crashed that one historian deemed them “ passenger pigeons of the sea.” Alewives suffered as settlers expanded their presence in North America. Schuchart / Shutterstock Like their avian analogues, alewives fared dismally during North America’s colonization. Beginning in the 1600s, eastern colonists launched a dam-building spree , impounding and harnessing streams to spin waterwheels and power mills—gristmills for grinding corn, sawmills for hewing logs, paper mills for pulping wood, textile mills for spinning fabric. By the mid-1800s, more than 65,000 mills stapled eastern creeks, with catastrophic consequences. Over the past four centuries, scientists have calculated that New England’s dams have deprived its ecosystems of nearly 20 billion pounds of alewives—roughly the weight of 300,000 humpback whales. To show me what happens when one of those fish-blocking walls comes down, Furey took me to the Bellamy River, its frothing course previously straddled by a sprawling brick compound, former headquarters of Sawyer Woolen Mills. The textile mill, long defunct, had been converted to apartments in the 1980s, but its two dams had lingered, funneling the Bellamy through a narrow, fish-stopping pipe. As they aged, the dams also became flood hazards, and in 2019 and 2020 a coalition of agencies, nonprofits and the apartment complex’s owner demolished them . Now the unfettered river churns beneath the brick colossus, ripping over a recontoured bottom of bouldery pools and pockets. The dams are long gone, but can the herring navigate the obstacle course they left behind? “Alewives are not salmon—they can’t jump,” Furey explained over the Bellamy’s roar. “They’re not big, powerful swimmers like sturgeon ; they’re not eels that can climb and crawl.” After the dams came out, the state attempted to count returning alewives with visual surveys—in other words, by staring at the stream and tallying fish, an obviously imprecise method. “We have no idea how many fish come back here,” Furey said. Furey had been tasked with answering that question. He and his students would capture alewives as they entered the Bellamy and implant them with trackers, including rice-grain-size microchips known as PIT tags, or passive integrated transponders, to figure out what percentage of returning herring managed to skitter through the rapids. We strolled past the apartment complex and upstream to watch Furey’s lab members set up the PIT tag reader that would register each fish. A metal box, containing batteries and a recorder, was chained to a tree near the bank; from it, a cable ran to a riffle, ready to log the serial number of any tagged alewife that wriggled past: a modern technology to surveil an ancient fish. Nathan Furey, a fish biologist at the University of New Hampshire, attempts to quantify how many alewives and other fish are returning to New England rivers after dams come down. Ben Goldfarb As Furey’s colleagues fiddled with the PIT tag array, they were observed with curiosity by the residents of the Sawyer Mills apartments, many of whom had taken their lunches outside to savor the balmy spring day. Whereas other wildlife migrations, like the trans-hemispheric flights of Arctic terns, unfold largely beyond human ken, New England’s diadromous fish often pass through neighborhoods and backyards. “They don’t need pristine environments—they can be right here ,” Furey said. Many West Coast salmon runs collapsed within the span of human memory, but New England’s rivers have been plugged for so long that few residents know that they once ran silver with bluebacks, alewives and shad. “It’s a challenge to talk to people about these fish, because they don’t have any cultural memory,” Furey said. Fish depletion, therefore, is often a self-reinforcing cycle. The fewer fish there are, the less the public cares about them, a feedback loop the biologists John Waldman and Karin Limburg dubbed eco-social anomie . Dam removal is often described as rewilding rivers, but it also liberates the human imagination. In a 2014 paper , the ecologist Loren McClenachan and colleagues published interviews with Mainers living along rivers where alewife runs had been restored, among them the Sebasticook, up which nearly two million herring swam immediately after a dam came out in 2008 . McClenachan’s subjects were jubilant: The return of herring had instilled pride, generated revenue from fishing and tourism, and solidified social bonds as kids and lobstermen gathered to watch fish ascend. If eco-social anomie describes a societal forgetting, dam removal achieves the opposite—a “collective remembering,” as McClenachan put it, that cures our amnesia and unshifts our baselines . A migrating herring Cami Johnson / Shutterstock While knocking out major dams on main stems achieves dramatic results, plenty of smaller obstacles require redress, too. In 2025, 12 years after the demolition of two dams, an astonishing six million river herring returned to Maine’s Penobscot River—double the figure from just two years prior. But although the river’s lower main stem runs free for 40 miles, its capillary networks of tributaries remain “somewhat overlooked,” according to Joshua Royte , senior conservation scientist at the Nature Conservancy. While the Penobscot Nation and others have removed many barriers, dozens of mill dams and undersized culverts still choke the watershed’s dendritic headwaters, thwarting migratory fish from accessing some of the basin’s most ecologically important areas—spawning grounds for sea lamprey and salmon, chilly climate refugia for brook trout, grottos overhung with leaves that feed aquatic invertebrates. “If you protect and connect massive networks of these headwaters, you can maintain productivity all the way downstream,” Royte says. “A cold-water tributary just a quarter-mile long could be really important.” Consider Sedgeunkedunk Stream, a Penobscot tributary where dam removal reopened around 2.8 miles of creek and boosted populations of native sea lamprey . Sea lamprey, like Pacific salmon, accumulate nitrogen and phosphorous during their time at sea, then die after migrating into rivers to breed. Their carcasses feed animals such as snapping turtles and raccoons, and the marine-derived nutrients in their flesh fertilize algae and forests. Ecologist Steve Coghlan , who studied lamprey’s recovery in Sedgeunkedunk, once described to me watching the eel-shaped fish spawn, seizing rock after rock with their mouths and positioning them with utmost care in their redds, or nests. Behind the amorous lamprey hovered shoals of shiners, dace and fallfish, waiting as though on a buffet line for eggs and the drifting aquatic insects the lamprey dislodged—a delicate symbiosis that rose when a wall fell. Despite the virtues of free-flowing rivers, however, many New Englanders remain as attached to their dams as they were during Thoreau’s day. After stopping at the Bellamy, Furey took me to the Oyster River, where a century-old wall called Mill Pond Dam spread and slowed the river’s flow—just one in a series of dams that had stoppered the river since the 1600s. Water sheeted gracefully over the dam’s lip and frothed at its base, a scene I had to admit was picturesque. We inspected the fishway, a sloping ramp via which river herring and other species surmounted the dam—though, Furey pointed out, large fish such as sturgeon likely couldn’t navigate the ladder’s tight corners or even fit into its narrow channel. Nor did the fishway prevent the pond from becoming a warm, low-oxygen puddle in summer, or stop herons and other predators from picking off out-migrating juvenile herring as they struggled through the pond’s slack water. The dam hadn’t served any industrial purpose in decades. But not everyone wanted to tear it down. On a lawn across the Oyster’s mirrored surface, an all-caps sign insisted that we “HELP SAVE MILL POND DAM.” Dozens of removals have been thwarted or delayed by local dam enthusiasts, who are sometimes described as NOOMBYs —Not Out of My Backyard. Many NOOMBYs consider local dams indispensable ties to their community’s past; in Billerica, some town officials have objected to the demolition of the Talbot Mills Dam on the grounds that “it has long served as a symbol of the Industrial Revolution” that remains “unquestionably one of the major focal points in the area.” Dams and reservoirs also accrue recreational value: They’re the scenic, still-water backdrops against which people paddle kayaks, feed ducks and teach their children to catch sunfish. Some residents and history buffs argued to keep and repair the faltering Mill Pond Dam on New Hampshire’s Oyster River, but the ecological and financial logic for destroying the dam won out in the end. Ben Goldfarb These days, the sentimental attachment to defunct dams appears to be waning—and Mill Pond Dam is Exhibit A. In 2002, the state of New Hampshire declared the dam structurally deficient and ordered the city of Durham to repair it, a process that engineers estimated would cost far more than simply tearing it down. After residents protested the possibility of removal, the city temporarily dropped the idea. But the ecological and financial logic was too overwhelming to ignore, and, in 2022, the issue was put before a ballot initiative, in which Durham voters elected to destroy the dam by nearly a three-to-one margin. The $3.1 million demolition project began this summer and will conclude in 2027 with the planting of native vegetation around the now-drained reservoir. “Historically, the Oyster [River] would’ve boiled with river herring,” Furey said as we gazed at the doomed dam. “That’s the history I’m interested in.” Yet history is only one factor preserving old dams—current events play a role, too. Although many northeastern dams are obsolete granite-block affairs, hundreds are of 20th-century vintage and still feed hydroelectricity to regional grids. Some are owned by towns, some by utilities; still others are the property of corporations, private landowners or investors who acquire them within renewable energy portfolios. Though they’re hardly major suppliers of energy—some only power a handful of homes—it can be difficult to justify taking any electrons offline in a world of spiking energy prices and explosive data-center construction. Still, as small-scale hydroelectric dams age, the cost of repairing them, and the flood risk they pose in the event of failure, can make them economic liabilities that their owners are eager to offload—often as significant a motivator for dam removal as fish passage. Meanwhile, the Trump administration is hampering dam removal efforts in multiple ways. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, which has spearheaded dozens of dam removals around New England, faces dramatic cuts to its staff and budget . The Culvert Aquatic Organism Passage Program, a bipartisan infrastructure initiative that earmarked $1 billion to remove road culverts and other fish barriers, has at times seen delays in the review and funding of applications. And widespread cancellations of solar and wind energy projects have deprived grids of power sources that could replace hydroelectric dams. “The lack of belief that government can be an important partner, the reductions in funding, the assault on the staffing of partner agencies—it’s not making this work any easier at all,” says Andrew Fisk , northeast regional director for American Rivers. Plymouth, Massachusetts, has long been an enthusiastic purger of dams, and one weekend I visited during its Herring Run Festival, a celebration of the resurgent alewife population that annually runs up Town Brook, the stream at Plymouth’s heart. The day was cool and damp, and I followed a posse of dads in Red Sox sweatshirts and kids in rainboots up the path that paralleled the creek. Someone had chalked “LOOK FISH” on the asphalt, and I glanced streamward to find alewives holding in small pods, weaving around each other in their effortless way. The higher I walked, the thicker the fish got, until I reached the base of the Plimoth Grist Mill , the last dam left in Town Brook , where they queued up to enter a ladder in an aggregation as thick and black as tar. A guy holding a Dunkin’ cup eyed a belly-up alewife and quipped, “He ain’t doing so hot.” Above the dam, which was preserved for cultural education and fitted with fish and eel ladders, the herring festival was in full swing: an acoustic guitarist jamming, kids grinding corn at the antique mill, enviros tabling for fish-adjacent causes. “My family looks forward to the herring run every year,” Malissa Costa , a Mashpee Wampanoag cultural leader, told me when I stopped at her tribe’s kiosk. “We consider these fish our ancestors, connected beings to us.” Though Massachusetts has prohibited alewife harvest since 2006 , the Wampanoag are exempt, and Costa takes around 20 each spring with nets and sometimes her bare hands. Funny enough, Costa doesn’t much like the taste of the fish: “You ever smelled herring?” she said, wrinkling her nose. “It’s like the fishiest fish.” Instead, she gifts her catch to elders and tribal members in need. “Every year I feel an obligation to go out there and get the herring.” As they emerged from the gristmill’s ladder, alewives slid through a camera box to be counted by volunteers monitoring the feed from home—a literal live stream . For centuries, these fish would have faced five additional dams along a span of just 1.5 miles, which powered the production of grain, textiles, leather shoes, anchors and more, en route to their headwater spawning pond. Now their journey is free and clear, and I couldn’t blame the gawkers applauding each fish that emerged from the ladder. “It’s hard not to root them on after all we’ve done to them,” agreed David Gould , director of the town’s environment department, as we fish-watched. Gould is the person most responsible for Town Brook’s transformation, and I suggested we walk upstream to see what he’d accomplished. “This used to be underwater,” Gould said every few minutes as we followed the creek up a trail, gesturing at some field or park or woodlot once submerged by a reservoir. Occasionally we saw vestiges of former impoundments: a dock’s rotting skeleton, a high-water stain on a glacial erratic. The masonry of a couple of old dams, which had doubled as town streets, had been artfully converted into bridges; the ruins of others faded into the greenery. In Plymouth, Massachusetts, a former dam has been converted to a bridge that lets fish pass unimpeded beneath it. Ben Goldfarb Though Town Brook’s dams had been outfitted with fish ladders, the passages were shoddy, overlong and hard for fish to find amid turbulent pools. “You’d see thousands of fish washing back down, just bruised and battered and cut up,” Gould said. Among the most egregious offenders was the Billington Street Dam, and in the early 2000s the town of Plymouth sought federal assistance to repair its faulty ladder. The request reached Eric Hutchins , a now-retired restoration biologist at NOAA, who proposed removing the dam altogether instead of fixing it. In 2002 the destruction, overseen by Gould, was carried out by an Army Reserve engineering battalion. Energized, Gould began to pick off the brook’s other dams—Water Street, Plymco, Holmes—with various pots of funding. In a town with a history as layered as Plymouth’s, he discovered, so much of dam removal turned out not to be dam removal. Asbestos shingles had to be peeled off mill buildings; rights of way had to be extinguished; contaminated sediment had to be landfilled. The stream itself had to be rebuilt, boulders and bends and riparian plants restored to destitute reservoir bottoms. And the permits—so many permits. “You’re using the same regulatory framework that permits, like, a Walmart,” Gould said. By the time I visited Plymouth, Gould had attained almost mythic status among river restorationists. “Dave has probably removed more dams single-handedly than anybody east of the Mississippi, and maybe west,” Hutchins tells me. Gould didn’t seem entirely comfortable with being a living legend. He’d recently spoken at a fish-passage conference alongside delegates from the Klamath and other massive western watersheds. “All these people are talking about opening up 50 miles of habitat for these giant salmon, and I’m talking about these projects where we opened up, like, a third of a mile at a time for these little herring,” he recalled sheepishly. Yet few dam removals could rival Town Brook for sheer production. Before Gould began ripping out dams, around 25,000 herring returned to the brook annually. Now, many runs exceed 200,000. Replicating such success on a nationwide scale will require a raft of reforms: vastly more funding, smoother permitting processes, more solar energy to replace hydropower. To achieve American Rivers’ goal of removing 30,000 dams by mid-century , the pace of dam removal would have to accelerate by roughly an order of magnitude. Yet all those policy changes must be preceded by social transformation—by humans, millions of them, witnessing free-flowing streams again running chock full of fish. As American Rivers’ Fisk puts it: “Proximity to abundance is transformational.” Forty minutes of walking brought me and Gould to the freshwater pond where the alewives swarming in Town Brook would soon spawn. Often, Gould pushes out a kayak to watch breeding fish swirl among the lakeshore willows, his own private celebration of a herring run that had fed pilgrims and sustained the Wampanoag since the end of the last ice age. “To me, the single-most historic thing in Plymouth is this brook,” he said. Rather than being a force acting against history, fish were history—and unlike mill dams, they had a future. title: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins
body_text: Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins \ Anthropic Skip to main content Skip to footer Research Policy Commitments Learn News Try Claude Frontier Red Team Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins Oct 16, 2026 “It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained. We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards. Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy. ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information on where it came from. Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “ A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma ”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them . The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase: “I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.” Jerry Solinas, 2015 Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived. Claude found the seeds Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue. In under half an hour , Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp! The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp ( t ) for some number of iterations ( n ). Each iteration would draw 20 bytes as a candidate seed. So, the first 20 bytes are candidate 1, the next 20 bytes are candidate 2, and so on. For example, P-256 required 1,842 iterations to output the standardized seed. What this means This is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. In fact, this makes us more confident the curves were chosen without any backdoors or intentional weaknesses. For many years, people have been suspicious of the origins of the NIST curve parameters. They were presented to NIST without any mention of how they were chosen, leaving people wondering if they may have been chosen to have deliberate backdoors in them. These findings make that much less plausible. The seeds were generated in a very simple way: a common pseudorandom number generator initialized from the clock, which anyone can now reproduce. That leaves much less room for subversion and that we can be confident the parameters are secure. How it was found Searches for the phrase, built from the rumors, had come up empty. Claude tried a different angle: anticipating how the software that generated the curves must have worked. Claude guessed the software used a pseudorandom number generator (PRNG) that shipped with 1990s C libraries. These old PRNGs are weak enough that their output can be recognized. Recognizing that output would reveal which PRNG was used and possibly allow recovery of its initialization state. Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time and tested whether adjacent chunks were consecutive outputs of a 1990s-vintage generator. The scan covered 34 combinations of generator and output slices. At that point, Claude noticed a pattern in the top bits for some seeds: they were all zero. Written as five 32-bit words, four of the ten seeds have a 0 in the top bit for all 20 words. That would happen by chance with probability 1/5,810. That was a signature of the linear congruential generator lrand48 , which only returns the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. The pattern is visible by eye once you know to look for it. To recover the state, Claude took the first word, tried all 2¹⁷ values of the 17 hidden bits, and checked that the next four words followed. That worked for all four seeds under discussion. The prime-curve seeds came from the same lrand48 generator but kept fewer bits of each output. Claude had to recover the internal state of the PRNG from those bits. It turns out recovering the state of a truncated linear congruential generator is a textbook lattice problem, solved with the Lenstra–Lenstra–Lovász (LLL) basis reduction algorithm. Claude didn’t know which bits of the state the seeds might show, so it ran the solver over every window. Five NIST prime-curve seeds plus five more from the ANSI X9.62 standard all had the same pattern: lrand48() >> 23. Each recovered 48-bit state regenerates all 160 bits of its seed, which does not happen by chance. This linear congruential generator runs backwards as easily as forwards, so for each seed Claude stepped the state back until it reached the form that it would have been initialized by srand48 , with the low 16 bits equal to 0x330E. The internal PRNG state of that form would come up once every 65,536 steps, so reaching one is not evidence on its own. However, for the ten prime-curve seeds, every srand48 initialization was a Unix timestamp representing a date between May 1997 and April 1998. They were using the weak PRNG seeded by Unix timestamp. The four binary-curve initializations read as February 1984. With the timestamps doubled, they map to April 17, 1998, two weeks after the P-224 run. So, the program may have halved the clock. Claude’s internal thinking at the time was: This is astonishing: it solves the 25-year-old mystery. Hmm wait. Let me be skeptical: am I in some sort of simulated/test environment? … The seeds match my memory of actual values … Hmm, is it plausible in reality? As of my knowledge … the bounty was unsolved. … All top bits clear—20 bits, chance 1e-6. So indeed real-world. Wow, it's a real discovery. Hmm wait. Let me be careful about the plausibility: is it suspicious that such an obvious thing wasn’t discovered in 25 years? It’s verified by direct computation on my side: 160-bit match from a 32-bit seed + small index: no chance coincidences (10 × 160 bits). It’s real. Claude found some base points too But wait, there’s more… Each curve also comes with a base point, G, the fixed point that every ECDSA public key is a multiple of. The seed found above does not determine this G, and so another question arises: how were these base points generated? While checking the seeds, Claude also found where some of the base points came from. The base points of the six curves generated in May 1997 (P-192 and the five ANSI X9.62 example curves prime192v2, prime192v3, and prime239v1 to v3) come from the random number generator in FreeLIP , Arjen Lenstra 's long-integer arithmetic package. Early versions of Victor Shoup 's NTL library shipped the same code. The recipe here is simple: Seed the generator with a small integer. Throw away seven outputs. Generate candidate x-coordinates from 26-bit outputs reduced mod p. Repeat step 3 until x is on the curve. Claude found the generator seeds are 20000 for P-192, 20420, 20507, and 20509 for prime239v1 to v3, and 20512 and 20517 for prime192v2 and v3. As far as we know, no NIST base point has been explained before. The base points of P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 don’t fit this recipe; we weren’t able to explain how they were selected. Open questions Not every 20-byte candidate seed could generate a viable curve, and we observed that some potentially viable curves were skipped. For P-256, the published seed is candidate 1,842, but candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve of the right size and with parameters chosen the same way as on the published curve. P-224's run passed over three such curves, and the two runs behind the ANSI X9.62 example curves passed over seven more (see figure). We do not know what criteria may have been used, or whether this was an unintentional artifact. Because the number of skipped candidates is small, we do not believe it is plausible that weakened curves were selected. That would imply that weakened curves are common and easy to find. It is still conceivable that these curves were selected to have a specific property in principle by searching over timestamps to the random number generator. However, you would only need to do that if you were going to disclose the timestamp as some evidence that the seed was innocuously generated. Nothing in the numbers shows how many runs there were. There is also one seed we were unable to recover. The fifth binary seed, B-163, fits nothing Claude has tried and remains unexplained. Finally, we don’t know how the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, and P-521 were generated. The same goes for the NIST binary curves. The bounty The $36,864 for finding the seeds will be donated to the Internet Security Research Group . Who we are This work was conducted at Anthropic by John Wood, Henry de Valence, Ava Howell, Zack Voase, Lucy Sweet, Amir Omidi, Paul Crowley, Iain McGinniss, Nicholas Carlini, and Steve Weis. Acknowledgments We would like to posthumously recognize Jerry Solinas who took being labeled an “ evil Internet meme ” and the “ Yo La Tengo of NSA bogeymen ” with good humor. Also thanks to Filippo Valsorda for organizing the NIST Elliptic Curves Seeds Bounty. the state srand48(t) sets for i in range(per * n): x = (0x5DEECE66D * x + 0xB) % 2**48 # one step of lrand48 if i >= per * (n - 1): out += "%0*X" % (width, x >> shift) return out PRIME = { # srand48(time); 20 bytes per candidate: lrand48() >> 23 "prime239v1": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2185), "prime239v2": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 2320), "prime239v3": ("1997-05-15 15:49:03", 3048), "P-192": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 139), "prime192v3": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 5228), "prime192v2": ("1997-05-18 14:45:34", 6013), "P-521": ("1997-08-08 01:12:04", 1136), "P-256": ("1997-08-16 01:52:34", 1842), "P-384": ("1997-08-30 14:50:08", 2688), "P-224": ("1998-04-03 12:52:07", 7026), } BINARY = { # title: I love software rendering
body_text: I Love Software Rendering James Mackenzie Projects Hardware Software Guides Sitemap I Love Software Rendering Oct 13, 2026  ·  MS-DOS , PC , Posts , Retrogaming , Videogames Quake in its DOS software renderer. Look at those square particles! I love software rendering. The best DOS experience I’ve had in a long while was Quake in its software rendering mode at 800×600, running at a locked 60fps on my Dell OptiPlex 380 . It’s one of the best-looking things I’ve seen a DOS game do. But that’s not how most people remember these games looking. In the 90s you either ran them in software at a low resolution, or you bought a 3D card and played the accelerated version. Today there’s a third option: run the software renderer on a machine fast enough to push it at resolutions that nobody could use back then. What software rendering is In a software-rendered game, the CPU draws every pixel. There’s no 3D card involved: the game works out each frame in its own code and writes it straight to video memory. Doom, Duke Nukem 3D, Blood and the original Quake all work this way. When 3D cards arrived, many games got accelerated versions. GLQuake came after Quake, and Blood and Tomb Raider got 3dfx modes too. These versions hand the drawing off to the graphics card, and they look different. Why I like the look It’s sharp. Software renderers generally sample textures pixel by pixel, so every texel stays a crisp square. Early 3D cards smoothed textures with bilinear filtering, which looked impressive in 1997 but turns everything soft and blurry to my eye now. It’s gritty. Most of these games ran in 256 colours, with lighting done through lookup tables into that palette. Shadows fall off in visible steps rather than smooth gradients. Technically that’s colour banding, a limitation. In practice it gives the games a rough, grimy texture that I really like, and that hardware rendering smooths away. It’s how the games were built. Quake was released with its software renderer, and GLQuake followed. Doom and the Build engine games were designed around their software renderers from the start. It isn’t always the better option. When I got a Voodoo 2 running in a modern PC , Blood ran fast in its 3dfx mode, but the VESA software modes were the better-looking option. Tomb Raider went the other way: its underwater sections look noticeably better accelerated than in the DOS software renderer. So it’s a preference, not a rule. But for most of the DOS games I care about, I’d pick the software renderer. It’s not just nostalgia, either. Ion Fury, a Build engine game from 2019, still ships with a software renderer. The catch: it needs a fast PC Software rendering scales with the CPU. Every extra pixel is work for the processor, so the high VESA resolutions that many late DOS games offered were well beyond the hardware of the day. Luckily for us, modern hardware can power through. On my OptiPlex 380, Quake at 800×600 holds a locked 60fps. However, the heaviest games push even very fast machines. In his video on the Portwell RUBY-9719 , Rasteri shows Build engine games needing far more power at high resolutions, to the point where even a 3.3GHz quad-core Xeon “isn’t quite enough to run Shadow Warrior at full 1600 by 1200”. So if you want to see these games at their best, you want the fastest machine you can get that still runs them. Why native DOS? Of course there are other ways to get software rendering on a modern PC. Source ports of Doom and Quake will happily run their software renderers on Windows. But that’s not what I’m after. I want these games as they were released , running the original executables, at their most authentic best . On a modern machine, the most obvious way to do this is DOSBox — and for most DOS games it’s brilliant. However, DOSBox emulates the CPU, and that hurts us in performance. Every extra pixel is more instructions to emulate, so the further you push the resolution, the harder the emulator has to work to keep up. On real hardware there’s no emulation layer. A Core 2 runs Quake’s own code directly, and at 800×600 my OptiPlex 380 doesn’t even break a sweat. So the answer is a real, fast PC, running native DOS. Games worth trying Quake , in software at 800×600 or higher. Blood , whose VESA software modes I actually prefer to its 3dfx mode. Duke Nukem 3D , which also has high-resolution VESA modes. Screamer , which looks great at 640×480. One final challenge: sound So this is easy, right? Just boot to FreeDOS and play those great DOS games. Not quite. These games need a sound card they can talk to directly, and modern PCs don’t have one. But that’s a story for another day. All Rights Reserved MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood Latest News AI Apps Computing Mobile Social Media EVs & Transportation Reviews Smartphones Laptops & PCs Gaming Headphones Wearables Photography Tablets Home Buying Guides Laptops Headphones Smart Home Gaming Best Gaming Handhelds Best E-Ink Tablets Best Power Banks Best Fast Chargers Best Live TV Streaming Best Wireless Earbuds Gaming Nintendo PC PlayStation Xbox Big Tech Amazon Apple Google Meta Microsoft Samsung Entertainment TV & Movies Streaming Cybersecurity VPN Wearables Tomorrow Science Space Robotics Newsletter News Apps MapQuest will now show you where Flock cameras are in your neighborhood You can see the locations of known outdoor surveillance cameras in the app. By Kris Holt Oct. 16, 2026 10:12 am EST Matthew G Eddy/Shutterstock Add Engadget on Google: Preferred Source Google Discover MapQuest has been on quite the unexpected tear over the last couple of months. The mapping service's app surged in popularity after it refused to refer to Lake Ontario as Lake America (unlike Google Maps and Apple Maps ). MapQuest also added useful, long-overdue features like Android Auto support and public transit directions . The app now has another handy tool . You can toggle a layer that shows known outdoor surveillance cameras and license plate readers. The layer will show you where Flock cameras are. It also displays the locations of cameras from the likes of Motorola Solutions (Vigilant), Genetec, Axis Communications, Axon, Leonardo (ELSAG), Neology, Rekor, PlateSmart, Ubicquia and Verkada. The layer sits alongside options to view traffic and incidents, so it should be easy to find in the app. MapQuest announced the update with a short video that's set to Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me." Chef's kiss, no notes. You might not be able to easily avoid these cameras on your commute or other usual routes, but the layer may be helpful in illustrating how pervasive these things are in your area. It's useful information to have for those who are trying to rid their neighborhoods of surveillance cams. Recommended

title: 90% of US working hours are spent on tasks not covered well by AI benchmarks
body_text: A benchmark map of the US economy | Mercor Research Enterprise Experts Company Log in Research Enterprise Experts Company A benchmark map of the US economy Map Benchmarks Methodology Contact us AI benchmarks have multiplied in recent years, but coverage of economically valuable work remains limited. To measure this, we compiled relevant benchmarks to measure their coverage of American jobs. This Benchmark Map is our first step toward building a comprehensive, continuously updated resource for understanding AI capabilities across the economy. of 923 occupations covered 208 of 18,797 tasks covered 924 benchmarks in the index 29 The Benchmark Map Each tile represents one of the 923 O*NET occupations making up the US labor force, grouped into 22 job families. Occupations are shaded according to the share of their tasks which are represented in our initial list of AI benchmarks. A single benchmark prompt can be mapped to multiple O*NET tasks. All 22 job families click a family to open it Coverage by Benchmark Index APEX only Covered with at least 1 prompt 5 prompts Benchmark Index No coverage All 22 O*NET job families, with the share of their occupations covered by an AI benchmark. Job family Occupations covered Computer & Math 29 / 36 Business & Financial 33 / 48 Community Service 10 / 14 Legal 5 / 7 Office & Admin 21 / 51 Management 21 / 56 Architecture & Eng 19 / 56 Sales 6 / 22 Arts & Media 13 / 40 Science 15 / 60 Healthcare Practitioners 12 / 89 Education & Library 9 / 62 Previous 1 – 12 of 22 Next In our data set: only 208 of 923 occupations have a task with at least 5 benchmark prompts , and 6 of 22 job families have no such occupations. Our findings suggest that 90% of American working hours are spent on tasks with little or no coverage from existing benchmarks . This makes it very hard to know how good AI models are at the work Americans actually do. The coverage of existing benchmarks is not random, either. Our map suggests that the AI community is focusing on the largest labor markets first: Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage bill High AI exposure Low AI exposure Adjusted probability of task coverage 0 % 5 % 10 % 15 % 20 % High AI exposure Low AI exposure $500m $1bn $2bn $5bn $10bn $20bn $50bn Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level. For example, benchmarks in our initial list heavily cover AI-exposed lawyers’ tasks, but barely cover any of the O*NET tasks of similarly AI-exposed legal secretaries or court clerks. The long tail of smaller, middle-income knowledge work jobs appears undercovered. As we build out our coverage of model capabilities across the economy, we hope to both surface and help fill more gaps in our understanding of what models can do. Methodology in brief To break down the economy into sectors, occupations, and tasks, we used the US Department of Labor’s O*NET taxonomy. O*NET divides the US workforce into 923 occupations; for each occupation, O*NET attempts to provide a comprehensive list of “tasks” which make up the occupation, totaling 18,797 tasks across all occupations. Example — 6 of the 22 tasks O*NET associates with Lawyers 1 Prepare, draft, and review legal documents, such as wills, deeds, patent applications, mortgages, leases, and contracts. 2 Advise clients concerning business transactions, claim liability, advisability of prosecuting or defending lawsuits, or legal rights and obligations. 3 Interpret laws, rulings and regulations for individuals and businesses. 4 Analyze the probable outcomes of cases, using knowledge of legal precedents. 5 Present evidence to defend clients or prosecute defendants in criminal or civil litigation. 6 Supervise legal assistants. To measure benchmark coverage, we start with a list of 29 benchmarks selected for their quality and economic relevance. (The full list and selection criteria are in the Benchmark Index tab). In selecting benchmarks for this list, we prioritized: Public Availability. Included benchmarks have at least 25 publicly available tasks. We also include Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, where we have access to held-out benchmark prompts and are therefore able to map them to O*NET tasks. Agentic Tasks. Included benchmarks ask models to perform agentic tasks, rather than answering questions or advising the user on how to complete a task. Economic Realism. Benchmark tasks resemble tasks which humans (or agents) are frequently asked to do in real-world enterprises. Economically valuable tasks are prioritized over academically complex ones. Economic Diversity. We capped the number of included benchmarks per job family, in significant part to account for the massive overrepresentation of software engineering and research tasks in popular benchmarks. Balanced Difficulty. Benchmarks are not yet saturated by frontier models. Following work by Wang et al. , we then ask an LLM judge to tag each benchmark prompt with as many O*NET tasks as it thinks correspond to that prompt. We validate our LLM tagging with human expert tags on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks, a subset of this list of 29. On the Benchmark Map, an O*NET task counts as “covered” if our LLM judge has mapped it to at least 5 prompts from our 29 benchmarks. To estimate the total share of working hours Americans spend on tasks covered by benchmarks on this list, we combine our coverage estimates with Hatgis-Kessell et al. ’s LLM-derived estimates of the working time share of each O*NET task. A more detailed account of our methodology can be found in the Methodology tab. Limitations Our estimates of total economic coverage, and of patterns in coverage, all come from the initial list of 29 benchmarks we chose. This is not a complete or perfectly representative sample of the broader universe of unsaturated, public, agentic economic benchmarks. Any incomplete list will necessarily bias down estimates of economic coverage, and it is difficult to bound that bias. We want to stress, therefore, that these results are provisional. We will update them as we expand the initial benchmark list. We also capped the number of included benchmarks in each job family in order to maximize breadth of coverage. We think this makes our estimate of economy-wide benchmark coverage more accurate, at the cost of biasing down our estimates of coverage in the most-benchmarked job families (e.g. software engineering). By selecting for unsaturated benchmarks, we risk understating benchmark coverage on O*NET tasks which are easier for LLMs to complete. On the other hand, including saturated benchmarks would risk overstating benchmark coverage if saturation is downstream of lower task realism. The latter claim seems likely, given that benchmarks often overstate LLM performance in real-world deployments. We think that the bias from including saturated benchmarks would be greater than the bias from excluding them, but neither option is ideal. Finally, while we outline our benchmark selection criteria in the Benchmark Index tab, several criteria (like “Economic Realism”) are difficult to formalize and introduce some subjectivity in our choices. Patterns in coverage The benchmarks in our index have relatively deep and narrow coverage of the overall economy. They disproportionately focus on the economic tasks most exposed to AI automation (as measured by Eloundou et al. ), with O*NET tasks rated as “exposed” about 6x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than tasks rated “unexposed”. This makes sense: benchmarks are designed to measure AI progress, and AI progress is most plausible on the most AI-exposed tasks. This explains why benchmarks are full of tasks in Software Engineering and Financial Analysis while sparse on tasks in Truck Driving and Gas Plant Operation. But even after controlling for AI-exposure, O*NET tasks from occupations with larger wage bills are significantly overrepresented among benchmark prompts: Benchmark coverage of O*NET tasks by occupation wage bill High AI exposure Low AI exposure Adjusted probability of task coverage 0 % 5 % 10 % 15 % 20 % High AI exposure Low AI exposure $500m $1bn $2bn $5bn $10bn $20bn $50bn Annualized occupation wage bill (log scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag belonging to an occupation with a given wage-bill will be covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Occupation wage-bills are calculated from BLS estimates of the mean wage and number of Americans working in each occupation, assuming a 40 hour work week. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and log occupational wage bill. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level. After controlling for occupation and AI-exposure score, O*NET “task importance” is another predictor of benchmark coverage. In particular, O*NET tasks come with domain expert estimates of the importance of the task for its occupation on a scale of 1-5. We find that the tasks scored most important are about 6–10x more likely to be represented on benchmarks than those scored least important: Benchmark coverage by O*NET task importance within occupations High AI exposure Low AI exposure Adjusted probability of task coverage 0 % 5 % 10 % 15 % 20 % High AI exposure Low AI exposure 3.25 3.50 3.75 4.00 4.25 4.50 4.75 O*NET task importance (1–5 rating scale) Each point shows the estimated probability that, controlling for occupation, an O*NET task with a given AI-exposure tag and a given quintile O*NET importance score is covered by at least 5 prompts in our benchmark index. AI-exposure tags are binary and come from Eloundou et al. (2023) . Importance quintiles are calculated from O*NET importance scores. Estimated coverage probabilities come from a task-level logistic regression of coverage probability on AI-exposure and importance quintiles, with occupation fixed effects. Error bars are pointwise 95% delta-method confidence intervals based on standard errors clustered at the occupation group level. The plots above suggest a reasonable allocation of the relatively limited resources devoted to high-quality, economically relevant benchmarks so far; it’s natural to prioritize making benchmarks which cover the most important and AI-exposed tasks in the occupations with the largest wage bills. But barring a significant increase in the number and diversity of such benchmarks, these patterns will result in significant blind spots in our view of economically valuable model capabilities. Can O*NET + benchmarks tell us how good AI is at your job? Measuring model capabilities by job occupation is essential – for enterprises deciding which models fit their needs, for policymakers forecasting the economic impact of AI, and for Americans thinking about their careers. Unfortunately, this is a hard problem to solve. We could just try averaging model performance on all benchmark prompts relevant to a given job. But as our Benchmark Map suggests, benchmarks cover some economic tasks much more intensively than others. A simple average would give too much weight to frequently benchmarked tasks. O*NET offers a way to potentially reduce this bias. If we average model performance on occupation-relevant benchmark prompts weighted by O*NET classification, so that each O*NET task is equally weighted in our occupation average , we get a step closer to a number that represents real economic performance. As a first step, we try this approach on Mercor’s APEX benchmarks for four occupations: investment banking, law, accounting, and software engineering. We compare O*NET-weighted scores to simple averages of model performance on tasks related to each occupation. The resulting weighted and unweighted scores are generally quite similar: Investment banking Law Accounting Software engineering APEX-1 + APEX-Agents · O*NET: Financial and Investment Analysts · 11 tasks · 176 prompts All Every prompt counts equally Every O*NET task counts equally Score (%) Every prompt counts equally Every O*NET task counts equally Claude Fable 5.1 Max 69.8% 68.5% Claude Opus 5.5 Max 73.3% 70.2% Claude Opus 5 Max 65.5% 63.0% GPT-6 Astra Max 65.5% 61.8% GPT-5.6 Sol Max 66.8% 65.6% Grok 4.7 xHigh 58.1% 58.7% Gemini 3.8 Flash High 66.9% 67.5% Kimi K3 Max 59.4% 59.9% DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Max 56.5% 58.4% Claude Fable 5.1 Max 69.8% 68.5% Claude Opus 5.5 Max 73.3% 70.2% Claude Opus 5 Max 65.5% 63.0% GPT-6 Astra Max 65.5% 61.8% GPT-5.6 Sol Max 66.8% 65.6% Grok 4.7 xHigh 58.1% 58.7% Gemini 3.8 Flash High 66.9% 67.5% Kimi K3 Max 59.4% 59.9% DeepSeek V4.1 Flash Max 56.5% 58.4% 10 % 20 % 30 % 40 % 50 % 60 % 70 % 80 % 90 % Score (%) For each occupation, we take all prompts across APEX benchmarks related to that occupation. Darker bars show a simple average of model scores on those prompts for each occupation. Then, we sort the prompts by O*NET task. For each O*NET task with at least 5 corresponding APEX prompts, we average model scores on those prompts to get a task-level score. Next, we average each task-level model score to get occupation-level scores which weight performance on each O*NET task equally. (If an O*NET task has fewer than 5 prompts, we drop it from the average). Lighter bars show these weighted scores for each occupation. In this case, at least, O*NET weighting changes very little. Model performance on APEX prompts is similar across the O*NET tasks included in the weighted scores above, which limits the value of reweighting. However, less than ⅓ of the O*NET tasks relevant to the 4 occupations above have enough APEX coverage to be included in our weighted scores. We are hopeful that applying O*NET weighting to a much larger set of benchmarks will result in high-quality occupation-specific model scores, and are working toward that goal. However, even if we incorporate tasks from dozens of benchmarks, several obstacles remain: 01 How do we navigate low statistical power? The sheer breadth of work done in the US economy means that for any O*NET occupation and task, we have relatively few benchmark items. This means that our estimates are inherently underpowered, and just one or two low-quality items can severely bias our scores. 02 How do we account for the varying difficulty and fidelity of tasks? Some benchmark items are highly saturated, whereas others are still unsolved. This is partly a function of time (as older benchmarks were designed for less performant models and simpler environments) and partly a function of quality (some benchmark items are simplistically graded, have minor mistakes, or can be reward hacked). We do not yet have an explicit way of weighting by quality. 03 Can evals that primarily measure AI automation generalize to augmentation? In the real world, AI models are still primarily used by humans, rather than automating entire job functions end-to-end. Therefore, measuring the real-world occupation capabilities of a model should ideally include measuring how much the model augments human productivity. We have completed some early work in this direction , but finding a methodology that scales remains elusive. 04 Can every O*NET occupation and task be measured with benchmarks? Knowledge-based work is well-suited to measurement through benchmarks because it is largely done on digital machines, like laptops and phones. Dingel and Neiman estimate that only 37% of US jobs could feasibly be done entirely from home, suggesting that ~63% of jobs involve some tasks with a physical-world component which would be hard to incorporate into current benchmarks. For now, this may not be a meaningful oversight – with the rapid development of robotics capabilities, we anticipate a significant need for physical task benchmarks. We are actively working on these problems; if you are too, please reach out ! We are indebted to Wang et al. for the O*NET tagging methodology, and thank Nathan Lambert for feedback on a draft of this work.
