title: Yet another way to invoke functions in JavaScript without parentheses
body_text: yet another way to invoke functions without parentheses - bartosz's blog Menu bartosz's blog Home bypassing csp for exfiltration exfiltration using numeric-only outputs getting carlos' secret getting the pid from random numbers prototype pollution for endless jwt tokens sleep function alternative for time-based sql injection yet another way to invoke functions without parentheses Previous Next yet another way to invoke functions without parentheses i found yet another way to invoke arbitrary functions in javascript without using parentheses this payload works by overwriting the prepareStackTrace function of the Error object to generate arbitrary functions. it is usually used to format stack traces and is invoked when the attribute stack of an error is accessed. the parameters of this function are the error and " a structured representation of the stack " , which is just an array of the code positions. it has the same function signature the Function constructor which is used to generate javascript functions, as long as the second argument is valid javascript code. if we try to invoke the function which was generated using this method, we get a syntax error. it is to be expected, because a stack trace is not a valid javascript code, but an Array of code positions in order to make the payload work, we need to control the output of the Array.prototype.toString() function such that it returns our desired javascript payload. this can be done in two ways first we can simply overwrite it with a constant function which returns the payload or we can use prototype pollution to sneak our payload into another function, and then overwrite the Array prototype. i found that we can stay in the Error realm and use its toString function which can be manipulated by polluting the Object.prototype.message variable. i am sure there are more ways to achieve this. now if we put everything together - the function generation using the prepareStackTrace function and way to convert arrays into arbitrary strings, we can generate arbitrary javascript functions last thing we have to do is to invoke our new function. luckily there are many ways to do so and i chose the valueOf trick. it works by overwriting the default valueOf function of our object and then invoking it as a primitive. alternatively, we can use toString and then concatenate the object with a string. the final payload is as follows. feel free to try it out in the browser console. Object.prototype.message='alert\x281337\x29';Array.prototype.toString=Error.prototype.toString;Error.prepareStackTrace = Function;const x = new Error;x.valueOf=x.stack;+x; Made with Dracula Theme for MkDocs

title: How the Claude Code team does code review
body_text: How the Claude Code team does code review / claude.dev Blog [ H ] HOME [ M ] MODS [ D ] DOCS [ T ] TERMINAL Try Claude Code [ H ] HOME [ M ] MODS [ D ] DOCS [ T ] TERMINAL Engineering How the Claude Code team does code review How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents. AUTHOR Addy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing Wang CATEGORY Engineering PUBLISHED Oct 15, 2026 READING TIME 14 min How the Claude Code team does code review TREE â Rethinking the purpose of code review â The scarce resource: human time and attention â The life of a change â Layer by layer â How we make the reviewer better â Where humans stay in the loop â Sharing context across the team â "You land it, you own it" â When we change direction â How you can adopt this process â Where this is going ââââââââââââââââââââââââââââ 00% 14 MIN READ SHARE X.com LinkedIn Email Copy URL Copy markdown We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it? This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent. We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year. Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible. Code review does two jobs: Find and fix issues before they ship Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end. We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which checkâautomated or humanâis the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily. Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second. So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it. THE LIFE OF A CHANGE A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review. The life of a change png A typical Claude Code change, from the author's machine to users BEFORE THE PULL REQUEST The work is verified Claude runs the tests, build and linter; a second agent reviews the diff in a fresh context ON EVERY PULL REQUEST Required CI Lint, types, tests across platforms, build and packaging. Red blocks the merge Claude code review Agents hunt for bugs in parallel, verifiers vote on each finding, survivors ranked by severity Security review A separate pass. Open findings from either review block the merge Risk-based approval A classifier sets the tier: no person, one, or two. Some paths always need a person MERGING Merge queue Checks run again on the latest main with the change applied AFTER THE MERGE Behind a flag, used internally first Anthropic employees run it before it reaches everyone Gradual release The latest channel first; the stable channel trails it Watch, fix forward or roll back The author and on-call watch; flags turn off quickly, broken builds get reverted automated a person decides, scaled by risk recovery BEFORE THE PULL REQUEST The work is verified Claude runs the tests, build and linter; a second agent reviews the diff in a fresh context ON EVERY PULL REQUEST Required CI Lint, types, tests across platforms, build and packaging. Red blocks the merge Claude code review Agents hunt for bugs in parallel, verifiers vote on each finding, survivors ranked by severity Security review A separate pass. Open findings from either review block the merge Risk-based approval A classifier sets the tier: no person, one, or two. Some paths always need a person MERGING Merge queue Checks run again on the latest main with the change applied AFTER THE MERGE Behind a flag, used internally first Anthropic employees run it before it reaches everyone Gradual release The latest channel first; the stable channel trails it Watch, fix forward or roll back The author and on-call watch; flags turn off quickly, broken builds get reverted automated a person decides, scaled by risk recovery FIG A Most of the path is automated; a person's attention goes where the risk is LAYER BY LAYER Layers, not one gate png Six layers of checks, with rollback under them problems in verification required CI AI review security review human approval merge queue + flags fast rollback problems in verification required CI AI review security review human approval merge queue + flags fast rollback FIG B Each layer catches some problems and misses others. Few get through all of them, and rollback handles the rest. 1. The work is verified before anyone else looks Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can runâlike tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the designâand ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide . Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines. Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator." When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as: CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date. REVIEW.md , written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix. 2. AI review on every pull request Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else? On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code , is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally. When we launched the research preview , the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time. Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault. Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round. 3. Security review that can block Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive. If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code . 4. Automated checks that block The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here .) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it. 5. Human approval, scaled by risk A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review. Risk Examples Human approvals Low Docs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flag None required once automated review and security checks are green Medium Ordinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system prompts One person High The highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two people Two people The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file. Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human. Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves. An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again. 6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it. 7. Fast detection, fast rollback Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue. Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges. One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems. HOW WE MAKE THE REVIEWER BETTER Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop. Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily. Our incidents are the eval png Built from past incidents and reverts, run every day Incident or revert a change that broke something Expert-checked case experts confirm the bug Added to the set each incident adds a case Change the reviewer its prompts, tools or model Daily eval run scored against every case Score went up? keep it; if not, drop it next change Incident or revert a change that broke something Expert-checked case experts confirm the bug Added to the set each incident adds a case Daily eval run scored against every case Score went up? keep it; if not, drop it Change the reviewer its prompts, tools or model FIG C The eval grows with every incident, and every change to the reviewer is scored against all of it. We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second. Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review. Review has to converge. An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely. One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it. When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round. We made it worse ourselves. We'd gotten used to running several rounds by default, since each pass catches something new. This can be worthwhile on a risky change, but not on every PR. The team now tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall, and changed re-review: A round cap. After three rounds, the reviewer asks the author to step back and reconsider the approach. Diff-only re-review after the first few passes. Flag the class of bug, so the author fixes every instance, not one line. No repeats of findings already posted. Review agents also run nightly over existing code, helping us catch old bugs before they show up somewhere else. Review that converges png Internal pull requests, before and after the convergence changes Pass after one review and fix round 65% 78% Need five or more rounds 8.9% 1.5% Mean reviews to pass 2.08 1.32 before after the convergence work Pass after one review and fix round 65% 78% Need five or more rounds 8.9% 1.5% Mean reviews to pass 2.08 1.32 before after the convergence work FIG D Fewer review rounds per internal pull request after the convergence changes WHERE HUMANS STAY IN THE LOOP Pulling a senior engineer out of deep work to catch a routine mistake costs far more than an automated review. At Anthropic, our jobs have moved from reading every diff to the decisions machines are bad at: Should we build this at all? Direction, taste and scope. One team that declared its review bottleneck solved still kept human review for changes from outside the team, so someone asks "should we even do this?" Risky code such as billing, the auto-updater and CI workflows. Architecture that sets a pattern others will copy. Reading the evidence. Test output, the command that ran and what it returned, a screenshot, the reviewer's findings. If you can't say what the checks would miss, ask for a real review rather than a quick approval. Owning the outcome. A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it. Where a person decides png Five decisions stay with people; checks run everywhere else Should we build it? Risky code Architecture Reading the evidence Owning the outcome automated checks run all the way around an automated check a person decides Should we build it? Risky code Architecture Reading the evidence Owning the outcome an automated check a person decides FIG E People moved from reading every diff to the decisions machines are bad at SHARING CONTEXT ACROSS THE TEAM Code review's second job has always been to spread codebase understanding. Reading a teammate's diff is how you learn what changed and how the pieces fit. If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the code? We don't have a formal process for this. Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today. Some of us go a step further and have Claude build a small artifact that visualizes that part of the code and teaches it the way that person likes to learn. If the goal is to spend human attention well, this beats reading trivial diffs line by line. A one-line copy change teaches you almost nothing. An explainer for the module you're about to change teaches you a lot. Our culture of defaulting to working on open Slack channels helps too, since you see what others are building while they build it. "YOU LAND IT, YOU OWN IT" If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly: Changes are small, so they're easy to review, debug and revert. Everything is reversible. Flags, reverts and staged releases undo most mistakes in minutes. Blast radius sets the bar. Expensive code gets more people and more checks. Regressions surface fast through telemetry and internal use. It isn't blame. Owning a fix means you have the most context; incident reviews look at the system. Ownership is also shared. Much of the team works in open channels where anyone can see what others are building, pick up a thread, or point a Claude at a gap, and feedback comes from people who don't own the code too. That openness is a big part of how quality stays high without a gate on every line. WHEN WE CHANGE DIRECTION Agents make it cheap to start things, so some work shouldn't land. Usually someone in the channel asks why, points at an earlier decision, or suggests a simpler route, and the author closes or reshapes the PR. Since the code was fast to write, closing the PR doesn't feel like a loss. The trick is to raise a different direction in the thread early, not as a blocking comment on a finished PR. HOW YOU CAN ADOPT THIS PROCESS Most of the pieces to do this with your team exist today. Before the pull request Give your agent checks it can run, listed in a short CLAUDE.md , plus hooks that run formatters and linters. Run /code-review and /security-review locally, or a fresh-context subagent review. Add a REVIEW.md , and move repeated review comments into it. On every pull request Require CI, and add "Testing", "Risk" and "How to revert" to your PR template. Add an AI reviewer (Code Review for Claude Code, or the Claude Code GitHub Action) on one repo, tune REVIEW.md for a few weeks, then widen. Add automated security review, and require every review thread resolved before merge. Match review effort to risk: a quick pass on routine changes, a deep one where a missed bug is expensive (Quick, Standard or Deep in Code Review). Cap review rounds; after the first few, re-review only the new diff. Approval Write down risk tiers, set from the change rather than the author; start strict and loosen with evidence. Keep the lighter approval paths for authors you trust. Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection so auth, billing, CI and release workflows, and installers always need a person. Never let a bot's approval replace a required human's; dismiss approvals on new commits. Merge and after Use a merge queue, feature flags, internal use first, staged releases and one-step rollback. Turn incidents and reverts into an eval set, and rescore the reviewer whenever its prompts, tools or model change. Measure human time, with revert and incident rates as the guardrail. WHERE THIS IS GOING Code Review's announcement said approving a pull request is still a human call; the product posts findings, not approvals. Our own repos go further, letting owners decide which low-risk changes merge on automated checks alone, and that line keeps moving. When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a CLAUDE.md , a skill or a new check. The goal hasn't changed: less human time per change, and no more reverts than before. If your team lets agents open pull requests, we'd like to hear which checks you've automated, which still need a person, and what you think we have wrong. With thanks to Emma Webb, Michael Segner and Amie Rotherham for their reviews. Get the app · Website · Get started · Issues New: decision models, powered by Ollaya . PS5LM now runs Jev-like decision models (d1, Clef, OpenJev and more) on the GPU and answers the same /v1/systemone API as Ollaya: typed decisions with calibrated probabilities, in a fraction of a second. PS5LM is for anyone with a jailbroken PS5 who wants a private model server at home. It loads a GGUF model onto the console's GPU and serves it to your laptop, your phone and your coding tools. It needs no PC while it runs, no cloud and no account. Qwen 3.5 9B answering requests from a laptop on a PS5 Slim. Click for the video. Home, Models, Console, API and Settings on the TV. A model server under your TV It runs on the GPU. llama.cpp's Vulkan backend on the console's RDNA 2 GPU, with 11.4 GB of the shared memory for the model and its context. Every architecture and quantization llama.cpp knows comes along. It answers your network. OpenAI's /v1/chat/completions , Anthropic's /v1/messages (Claude Code works against it) and a chat page in any browser. Point a client at http://<console>:8081 and use any model name: the loaded one answers. It decides, too. Load a decision model and the console answers TypeSafe's /v1/systemone : choice, score and yes-or-no questions about text and images, the API Ollaya serves on a PC. It shows its work. Every request streams across the TV as a chat: which device asked, what it asked, and the reply as it is written. Square sends a demo and Triangle opens a keyboard, so the console can be tried from the couch. It watches the console. A Console page charts temperature, power, GPU and CPU load over the last two minutes or the last hour, beside a table of every reading. It picks what fits. The planner reads each GGUF and gives it the longest context and best cache that fit the memory free. A Suggested list holds models measured on the console, and the app downloads from Hugging Face by itself, to internal storage, the M.2 drive or a USB drive. It reads images. Models with an image projector (Gemma 4, MiniCPM-V, d1) take pictures in chat and in decisions. title: Things to know when you get cancer
body_text: of the document before the main stylesheets are loaded. --> Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition) · JJ Maxwell index Back to top Things to know if you get cancer (2026 Edition) 2026.10.14 I was diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma in my mouth in May 2026. Here are some things I learned based on that experience so far. You need to be doggedly persistent on scheduling things. Yes this means lots of phone calls. If you get an appointment a few weeks out, call back a few days later and ask for something sooner and see if they have any cancellations. I could only get an appointment 4 weeks out with an ENT (this was before I knew anything was wrong). My wife made me call back and I was able to get in that week due to a cancellation. AIs may downplay the seriousness of things. I was chatting with various models and most pushed me in the direction of “you don’t have cancer” for a while. Just something to note. You may need to push for comprehensive genetic testing. Some doctors were weird about this and didn’t order it promptly, even after telling me they would. My surgeon, who told me he’d get it done, eventually referred me out to an oncologist. This caused a multi-month delay to getting genetic results, since the first results were done on the surgery tumor, not the biopsy tumor. No one cares more about your case than you, so take control and send lots of follow-ups. You can find the “Standard of Care” flow charts for every cancer type. Look and get through this yourself to see what the options are based on how things have progressed. NCCN guidelines . You may need to make an account, which you can do as a non-professional. I like the PDF files. They also have an interactive navigator. Use AI to help you figure out what to pick based on your case. If surgery is recommended, I would try and talk to someone who has undergone the surgery. I did not do this and regret it. Ask them how intense things were, what it felt like, etc. My surgeon talked me through my surgery, but it was a lot rougher on me physically than I expected. Ask the surgeon how many of these surgeries they do a year and what the complication rate is. Get a second opinion as soon as possible, no matter how much you like your plan. This may require a lot of calling and getting on an airplane, but I’d move to schedule it at a top cancer center as soon as you are relatively sure of your diagnosis. Ask for a second read of the pathology at the center where you get the second opinion. I started a new folder on my Mac, and after appointments I’d dictate what happened and what the doctor said and have the AI make a new document summarizing things and asking its own follow-up questions for next time. Nice to be able to refer to this over time. Check out all the resources and materials at the Sijbrandij Foundation . Sid (GitLab cofounder) took matters into his own hands when standard of care ran out. Schedule a call with these guys. They are great and have good materials and questions to ask your doctors. Note, since this is on the front page of Hacker News right now. exhilaration suggested that if you are within a 2-3 hour drive of a major cancer center, go there instead of your local community hospital. Use the US News cancer hospital rankings . The top centers usually take your insurance, so use vacation days and book a hotel if you have to. The largest benefit I saw was speed. At MD Anderson I got a question answered within 20 minutes of a visit, because the doctor called the pathologist who he was on a first name basis with. If that wasn’t at a cancer center, it would have taken days, or more likely the question never would have been answered at all (I had asked my oncologist about this and he’d just shrugged). The rest of the HN comments are worth reading too.

title: Show HN: Gemini 4 Argon plays StarCraft
body_text: StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 Bench Kai McPheeters · October 15, 2026 TL;DR StarSkirmish is a benchmark where LLMs write bots for StarCraft: Brood War Each LLM gets one hour to write a Protoss bot in C++, which is then evaluated against other LLMs' bots and established human written bots StarSkirmish tests long horizon reasoning and agentic coding as LLMs must incorporate learnings from practice games to improve their StarCraft bot StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 The StarSkirmish Bench evaluates how strong of a StarCraft bot can each LLM write given 1 hour of wall clock time. v0.2 updates StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 with flagship models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta, each running in its lab's 1st party CLI harness. An LLM’s score reflects its win rate against a roster of competitive human written bots and demo bots. StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 1 hour runs, in its 1st party CLI harness. Scores are average win rates (0–100) of each model's 5 runs against a roster of competitive human written bots. Gemini 4 Argon runs at high , the highest reasoning effort available to it; every other model runs at max . GPT-6 Astra is the top scoring StarSkirmish Bench v0.2 LLM, a clear step ahead of GPT-6.1 Sol in second. Gemini 4 Argon, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.1 are functionally tied behind them, all scoring between 37 and 39. StarSkirmish Bench vs. Cost StarSkirmish Bench score against the average API cost of one 1 hour run. Cost is on a log scale. Muse Wonder Full's pricing is based on Muse Wonder's API pricing. GPT-6.1 Sol offers uniquely good value: it is the only LLM in the most attractive quadrant, scoring second at just over a tenth of GPT-6 Astra's cost per run. No Signs of Saturating The strongest human written bots are still well ahead of every model. Against Stardust, PurpleWave and BananaBrain, the best model, GPT-6 Astra, wins only 7% of its games. Win rates vs the top human written bots Average win rate of each model's 5 bots against top human written bots Stardust, PurpleWave, and BananaBrain. 1 hour reasoning limits are a factor, but these matches are played on three 2 player maps. Real human written bot tournament conditions are significantly harder. New AI Model Highlights Google and Meta's new flagships replace v0.1's Gemini 3.8 Flash and Muse Spark 1.3: Gemini 4 Argon places 3rd, and Muse Wonder Full 7th. GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were covered in v0.1 . AI Model Behaviors Each run's agent trace records how it spent its hour. The strongest predictor of a model's score is how much it practiced against the 7 strongest bots on the roster. Win Rates vs. Practice Against Strong Bots StarSkirmish Bench score against the number of practice games a model's median run played against the 7 strongest roster bots during the hour. The dashed line is a linear fit across the 9 models. GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol and Gemini 4 Argon start playing these bots early in the hour, while their own bots still lose to them. Muse Wonder Full, Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna rarely or never do. Claude Fable 5.1 is the outlier: it scores 37 while practicing almost entirely against weaker bots. Run-to-Run Variance Win rates of each model's 5 runs. Each dot is one run's final bot; the line spans the lowest to the highest run, the bar marks their mean (the model's Bench score) and the band one standard deviation (σ). Results also vary between runs of the same model. Gemini 4 Argon varies far more than the other labs' flagships: its best and worst runs are 18 points apart, against 9 for GPT-6 Astra and 8 for Claude Opus 5.5. Implementation Details Objective Each LLM writes a Protoss bot in C++ against BWAPI 4.4.0 , played on OpenBW . Games are Protoss versus Protoss on three ladder maps: Heartbreak Ridge, Benzene and Destination. A game ends when one side's buildings are all destroyed. Games that reach the 60 minute cap (86,400 frames) are decided as on the BASIL ladder: the higher kills + razings score wins. The LLM starts from a skeleton bot that only mines, with the source code of the three demo bots and two standard bot libraries: FAP, a combat simulator, and BWEM, a map analyzer. Whatever is in its bot folder when the hour ends is its final bot, so it has to keep the bot compiling. The LLM has tools to compile its bot, play practice games, and read each game's summary, transcript and its bot's own log. Practice opponents are grouped into tiers: D (the three demo bots), C and B (three mid-ranked human written bots each), A (BananaBrain, Locutus) and S (Stardust, PurpleWave). Tournament Setup LLM bots Opponents Games Games / pair Each model's 5 final bots play each of the 13 roster bots, the 10 competitive human written bots and the 3 demo bots, 6 times on each map, on fresh seeds. Unlike v0.1, the LLM bots don't play each other. Harness and Reasoning StarSkirmish Bench v0.1 ran every model in the same harness at 'high' reasoning. v0.2 runs each model in its lab's 1st party CLI harness at the highest reasoning setting it offers. Harness v0.1 ran every model in one neutral 3rd party harness; v0.2 runs each lab's models in its 1st party CLI harness. Both versions give each model 1 hour. v0.1 v0.2 Inspect ReAct deepagent Claude Opus 5.5 GPT-6 Astra, Sol, Luna Gemini 3.8 Flash Muse Spark 1.3 Claude Code Claude Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 Codex GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Luna Antigravity CLI Gemini 4 Argon Muse Code Muse Wonder Full CLI versions: Claude Code 2.1.296, Codex 0.162.1, Antigravity CLI 1.3.5 and Muse Code 1.4.7. Reasoning Effort v0.1 ran every model at high reasoning effort; v0.2 runs them at max. v0.1 Low Medium High XHigh Max High v0.2 Low Medium High XHigh Max Max Gemini 4 Argon runs at high , the highest effort supported. Every v0.2 harness compacts the model's context at about 250k tokens. When a conversation nears that point, the CLI condenses it and the model carries on. Codex, OpenAI's CLI, for example, gives the GPT models its default 272k token window and triggers compression once 90% filled. The CLIs' web search and web fetch tools are turned off, and the agent has no other internet access. The CLI is installed before the clock starts, and the hour counts from when the agent starts. There is no submit tool: the harness collects the bot when the time runs out. Scoring v0.2 replaces v0.1's Elo ratings with plain win rates. A bot's score is its win rate over its tournament games, and a model's StarSkirmish Bench score is the average of its 5 bots' scores, from 0 (every game lost) to 100 (every game won). Because every bot plays the same fixed roster, its games don't depend on the other LLM bots in the field. They all run in parallel, and a new model's bots can be scored without replaying anyone else's. A fixed roster also keeps the bar the same over time, so scores from different model generations are more directly comparable than Elo ratings fitted within one field. Benchmark Correlations StarSkirmish no longer tracks the most widely reported evals. It barely moves with the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (ρ 0.26), where GPT-6 Astra, the top model here, only ties for 4th of these 9 models. It has also drifted away from Terminal-Bench 4.0, which it tracked closely in v0.1. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full both rank near the top of Terminal-Bench 4.0 but near the bottom here. Benchmark Correlation Each model's StarSkirmish Bench score against its Vals IOI and WeirdML v3 scores, with the Spearman ρ between them. The dashed line is the best straight-line fit. WeirdML v3 scores 7 of the 9 models: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Full have not been included at time of writing. StarSkirmish still tracks Vals IOI, olympiad programming problems solved in C++, and WeirdML, an independent benchmark of unusual machine learning coding tasks. One reading is that the most heavily benchmarked evals have become targets that models are tuned for, while less targeted tests of long horizon, difficult coding tasks still move together.

title: Muse Spark Open
body_text: Introducing Muse Spark Open, The Most Capable US Open‑Weight Model to Date | Meta AI Research Skip to main content AI Research AI Developers Try Muse Introducing Muse Spark Open, The Most Capable US Open‑Weight Model to Date October 15, 2026 · 4 minute read Muse Spark Open is available today and brings leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios. Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning. We believe the future is for everyone , and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework. Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models. It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework. Contents Key Benchmarks Key Benchmarks Optimized for Apple Silicon Available Now Safety and Preparedness License Get Started Key Benchmarks For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report . Optimized for Apple Silicon Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop. Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra's integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory. We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically. Available Now We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350. Safety and Preparedness Releasing open-weight models is part of how we bring the benefits of personal superintelligence to everyone, and part of how safety work advances across the field. Open weights also carry their own considerations , and Muse Spark Open has additional safety post-training for that reason. The results demonstrate strong safeguards across risk categories measured. We evaluated the model in line with our Meta Superintelligence Scaling Framework , covering the most severe risks, and it met the thresholds our framework requires for release. Detailed results are in the Muse Spark Open model card , with a full evaluation report available soon. License We’re releasing the weights under the Muse Model License with limited commercial terms, which allow many developers to use the model for free. Get Started You can customize Muse Spark Open for your use case by leveraging PyTorch’s TorchTitan to further tune the model. To run it on Apple silicon, use MLX, which pulls the weights directly from Hugging Face. Muse Spark Open is available now through Hugging Face: https://huggingface.co/collections/meta-models/muse-spark-open MLX Adapter for running Muse Spark Open on Mac Studio. Hosted Inference Partners: Together AI, Fireworks, Baseten, Modal, Groq, Nebius, and OpenRouter. Built or published something with Muse Spark Open? Share with us on the Hugging Face Forums — we’d love to see what you create. title: Waymo in Toronto
body_text: Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route Skip to main content Rides Technology About Safety Community Careers Waypoint: The official Waymo blog Search Blog Technology Company News Rides Safety Life at Waymo Filter by topic Topic Technology Company News Rides Safety Life at Waymo Search blog Back Hello Toronto! Waymo is En Route October 16, 2026 Company News The Waymo Team Share on Twitter Share on LinkedIn Share on Facebook Waymo is officially heading to Canada! We’re laying the groundwork for our fully autonomous ride-hailing service in Toronto, investing in local facilities and jobs, with the goal of welcoming our first riders in 2028. In the coming days, you’ll start to see Waymo vehicles on the streets of Toronto as we begin driving manually. We are taking a rigorous, phased, safety-first approach starting with high-definition mapping of local street networks and testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel. This validation period will ensure the Waymo Driver adapts seamlessly to Toronto’s distinct driving conditions. “Expanding into Canada marks an important milestone in Waymo’s global journey,” said Waymo co-CEO Tekedra Mawakana. “Toronto is one of the world’s great cities — innovative, diverse, and forward-looking. We’re proud to bring the Waymo Driver to Canada’s largest city and to partner with the vibrant business, arts and cultural communities that share our commitment to safer streets and more accessible mobility.” To serve Toronto, we’re partnering with Element Fleet Management, a Toronto-headquartered company and global leader in intelligent fleet and mobility solutions that will provide end-to-end fleet management services. Together with Element and our partners, we’ll invest in hundreds of roles over time spanning fleet maintenance, validation driving, customer service, and other operations functions that support our service. This deep partnership builds on Waymo’s existing ties to Canada, which includes our long-term investor relationship with the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board and our manufacturing partner, Magna International. "As a Canadian company, we are proud to be expanding our partnership with Waymo to help bring autonomous ride-hailing to Toronto,” said Laura Dottori-Attanasio, Chief Executive Officer, Element Fleet Management. Together with Waymo, Element will help create employment opportunities providing the fleet expertise, operational capabilities, and intelligent mobility solutions needed to support autonomous fleets reliably and at scale." As one of North America’s fastest-growing metropolitan regions, Toronto has both evolving mobility demands and a dynamic and growing number of tools. From bike lanes to public transit, Waymo’s all-weather Driver can provide an additional option that complements the city’s transportation ecosystem. The data from over 400 million fully autonomous kilometres driven shows the Waymo Driver was involved in 95% fewer (20x fewer) crashes involving serious injury or worse compared to humans in the cities where we operate. Safety and accessibility are fundamental to Waymo's mission to be the world's most trusted driver, and we're proud to collaborate with leading accessibility and mobility advocacy organizations, including BALANCE for Blind Adults, CNIB, Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians, and Epilepsy Ontario, among others. “Innovation that removes barriers to independence is at the heart of everything we do. Waymo’s history of partnering with the sight loss community to build accessible solutions is encouraging and their decision to engage with us early reflects the kind of approach that leads to real results,” said Michelle McQuigge, CEO, BALANCE for Blind Adults. We can't wait to help residents and visitors explore everything Toronto has to offer. If you’re ready to experience Waymo in Toronto, please sign up for updates to be among the first to ride when we’re ready: waymo.com/waymo-in-canada . Waymo arrive officiellement au Canada ! Nous préparons le lancement de notre service de transport par véhicules autonomes à Toronto. Nous investissons dans les infrastructures locales et dans la création d’emplois en vue d’accueillir nos premiers passagers en 2028. Au cours des prochains jours, vous commencerez à voir des véhicules Waymo circuler dans les rues de Toronto, avec un conducteur au volant. Notre démarche est rigoureuse et axée avant tout sur la sécurité. Nous procédons par étapes, en commençant par cartographier le réseau routier local en haute définition, puis en effectuant des essais avec des spécialistes qualifiés de la conduite autonome au volant. Cette phase nous permettra de vérifier que le Waymo Driver s’adapte aux conditions de conduite propres à Toronto. « Notre arrivée au Canada marque une étape importante dans le développement international de Waymo », a déclaré Tekedra Mawakana, codirectrice générale de l’entreprise. « Toronto est l’une des plus grandes métropoles du monde : une ville innovante, diversifiée et résolument tournée vers l’avenir. Nous sommes fiers d’introduire le Waymo Driver dans la plus grande ville du Canada et de collaborer avec les communautés dynamiques des affaires, des arts et de la culture qui partagent notre engagement envers des rues plus sécuritaires et une mobilité plus accessible. » Pour assurer notre service à Toronto, nous faisons équipe avec Element Fleet Management, une entreprise dont le siège social se trouve à Toronto et qui est un leader mondial des solutions intelligentes de gestion de flottes et de mobilité. Element nous fournira des services complets de gestion de flottes. Avec Element et nos autres partenaires, nous investirons progressivement dans la création de centaines d’emplois liés à l’entretien de la flotte, aux essais sur route, au service à la clientèle et à d’autres activités nécessaires à l’exploitation de notre service. Ce partenariat s’inscrit dans la continuité des liens que Waymo a déjà tissés avec le Canada, notamment avec l’ Office d’investissement du régime de pensions du Canada (Investissements RPC), un investisseur de longue date, et Magna International, son partenaire manufacturier. « En tant qu’entreprise canadienne, nous sommes fiers d’élargir notre partenariat avec Waymo afin de contribuer à l’arrivée des services de transport de personnes à la demande par véhicules autonomes à Toronto, a déclaré Laura Dottori-Attanasio, présidente et cheffe de la direction d’Element Fleet Management. Ensemble, Element et Waymo contribueront à créer des possibilités d’emploi en mettant à profit l’expertise d’Element en gestion de flottes, ses capacités opérationnelles et ses solutions de mobilité intelligente pour soutenir le déploiement à grande échelle de flottes de véhicules autonomes, tout en assurant la fiabilité de leurs opérations. » Toronto figure parmi les régions métropolitaines dont la croissance est la plus rapide en Amérique du Nord. Les besoins en matière de mobilité y évoluent et les options de transport se multiplient. Des pistes cyclables au transport en commun, le Waymo Driver, conçu pour fonctionner par tous les temps , pourrait offrir une option supplémentaire en complément des moyens de transport existants. Selon les données recueillies sur plus de 400 millions de kilomètres parcourus en conduite entièrement autonome, les véhicules Waymo ont été impliqués dans 95 % moins d’accidents entraînant des blessures graves ou plus graves que les véhicules conduits par des humains dans les villes où le service est offert. Cela représente 20 fois moins d’accidents de ce type. La sécurité et l’accessibilité sont à la base de la mission de Waymo : devenir le service de conduite autonome auquel le public fait le plus confiance au monde. Nous sommes fiers de collaborer avec des organismes de premier plan qui œuvrent en faveur de l’accessibilité et de la mobilité, notamment BALANCE for Blind Adults, l’Institut national canadien pour les aveugles (INCA), Community Living Toronto, Connected Canadians et Epilepsy Ontario. « L’innovation qui favorise l’autonomie est au cœur de tout ce que nous faisons. L’expérience de Waymo en matière de collaboration avec des personnes ayant une déficience visuelle pour concevoir des solutions accessibles est encourageante. Sa décision de nous consulter dès le début montre qu’une telle approche peut donner des résultats concrets », a déclaré Michelle McQuigge, PDG de BALANCE for Blind Adults. Nous sommes ravis d’aider les résidents et les visiteurs à découvrir tout ce que Toronto a à offrir. Si vous avez envie de faire l’essai du Waymo Driver à Toronto, inscrivez-vous pour recevoir nos mises à jour et être parmi les premiers informés du lancement de notre service : waymo.com/waymo-in-canada . title: Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites: experts
body_text: Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say | Nieman Journalism Lab covers the handful of readers with JS off. Why it matters: these are three separate render-blocking stylesheets, and with their two webfonts they come to roughly 400KB. On 4 Oct 2026 PageSpeed measured a 4.7s First Contentful Paint on mobile against 0.4s on desktop — the browser was painting nothing until every stylesheet in this head had arrived over a throttled connection. The whole site uses SIXTEEN icons (twitter, linkedin, facebook-f, instagram, facebook, envelope, bluesky, arrow-right-long, arrow-left-long, tumblr, threads, mastodon, search, pen-to-square, whatsapp, bars). Subscribe another address Subscribe on our newsletters page → Subscribe Meta’s new commercial terms will allow the scraping of news sites, legal experts say Starting October 30, business accounts will consent to Meta scraping their websites if they continue using Facebook, Instagram, or WhatsApp. Meta sign at the entrance of the company’s headquarters in Menlo Park, CA. (Adobe Stock) By Andrew Deck and Hanaa' Tameez Oct. 15, 2026, 12:59 p.m. Meta can use web scrapers to crawl and collect content from websites “associated with” business accounts on its platforms, according to its new commercial terms of use. The update , set to go into effect on October 30, will include news publishers with business accounts. These accounts allow companies or public figures to manage Facebook pages, Messenger accounts, Instagram profiles, or WhatsApp channels from one place. While journalism isn’t the only industry that will be affected by this update, virtually every news organization has at least one Meta business account, including Nieman Lab. The new terms broadly cover business accounts that manage pages and groups, run advertisements, push marketing messages, and use the platform’s business account dashboard . As written, the new terms could be used to argue that Meta can scrape content from news sites and use that content to train the company’s AI products, according to three legal experts who reviewed the terms at Nieman Lab’s request. RELATED ARTICLE “An astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions”: Court records show what Microsoft and OpenAI actually thought about AI training Sarah Scire September 18, 2026 “This is a remarkable provision to bury in [the] terms of service, given that this would give Meta access to material that would likely cost many millions of dollars in a licensing market,” said Matt Topic , a media and intellectual property attorney at Loevy & Loevy. “It’s not clear whether a court would enforce this, but publishers should assume that it would be enforceable.” In early October, Meta alerted users to the update in a blog post and on the Meta Business Suite. The updated terms explicitly state that Meta can use the content it collects from associated websites to “train” Meta products. Elsewhere in its terms of service, the company defines “AI at Meta” as one of those products. Here’s the new language about scraping in full: You authorize us (or any entity acting on our behalf) to use automated software (such as web scrapers, bots, robots, spiders, crawlers, and user agents) and create test credentials to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them) that are associated with your products or services, or that are made available through your or users’ use of Meta Company Products and services, and to periodically pull updates from such domains, web pages, or URLs. Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms. “For news publishers, this clearly represents permission to Meta to train AI on any content from their sites and possibly to deploy some of that content, even in competition with the publishers themselves,” said James Grimmelmann , a professor of digital and information law at Cornell Law School. “On the broadest possible interpretation, this would be used to develop a comprehensive archive of all content that Meta would then serve as it wanted to directly or through AI.” Currently, there is no option for business accounts to opt out of these new terms ahead of October 30. The update reads, “If you do not agree to the updated terms, please stop all access or use of our Products for business or commercial purposes.” In short, “publishers either have to trust that Meta doesn’t mean the full extent of what these terms say, or they have to stop [using business accounts],” said Grimmelmann. Meta declined to answer a list of questions about these updated terms. A public affairs spokesperson at the company said in an email that language around crawling was previously scattered across different terms of use, including terms about using generative AI in ads , and this update consolidates them in one place. He also said that the new terms will not change how Meta crawls publishers in the future, and that “content owners can still manage how their content is accessed by using robots.txt.” On its developer page , Meta currently has instructions for how to block its crawlers using robots.txt, a file that tells bots which parts of a website they can and cannot access. However, legal experts said the new language creates an opening for Meta to argue its commercial terms supersede other blocking instructions. The update also states that Meta can create “test credentials” in order to scrape websites associated with business accounts. Grimmelmann said this would technically allow Meta to “sign up as a fake user” to bypass registration walls on a publisher’s site to access content. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s questions about whether the “test credentials” would bypass paywalls or other paid content. RELATED ARTICLE Federal appeals court upholds Thomson Reuters’ landmark AI copyright win Andrew Deck September 30, 2026 Any attempt to train Meta’s AI products with content collected under these new terms would still hinge on unsettled legal questions about AI training and fair use, legal experts said. Several lawsuits between publishers and AI developers are currently winding their way through federal courts. That includes a class-action suit filed in May by five large book publishers, alleging Meta pirated millions of books in order to train its Llama large language models (LLMs). Meta’s decision to tether access to its business products to broad scraping permissions echoes a concept in antitrust law called “tying,” according to Benjamin Sobel , a law professor at the University of Wisconsin. “If you want to use the Meta products that require acceptance of the commercial terms, you have to also acquiesce to the scraping and crawling permissions exacted in those terms.” Sobel compared the move to Google’s recent policies around its AI search products. In order to appear in Google’s traditional search results, publishers previously had to consent to their content appearing in AI Overviews and AI Mode . As of August 2026, all websites now have the option to opt out . Meta’s new commercial terms come on the heels of the company’s rollout of its paid subscription service, Meta One . The cash-for-links program restricts the number of external links that some accounts on Facebook and Instagram can post without subscribing. Put another way, Meta has begun charging users to post links to the same content that it will be permitted to crawl for free. Earlier this month, Press Gazette reported that some news publishers are currently exempt from the link limit. Meta declined to answer Nieman Lab’s question about the service. RELATED ARTICLE Meet the journalists training AI models for Meta and OpenAI Andrew Deck February 20, 2025 Nieman Lab first learned about Meta’s new commercial terms through a reader tip. Stephen Beale, the founder and editor of The Steampunk Explorer, got in touch when he saw a notice of the upcoming change in his Meta Business Suite dashboard. “Traditionally, you have this idea that Meta might be using content [posted] on Facebook or Instagram for training,” Beale told Nieman Lab. “But this was different because they’re saying that [since you are] a business user of Facebook, they have the right to go out and grab information from basically wherever you have a presence.” Beale has long depended on Facebook as a way to connect with his audience and refer traffic to his site. Fans of steampunk — a retrofuturistic subgenre of science fiction — skew older, he said, and the community is “totally entrenched on Facebook.” For many, their only interactions with the community happen on Facebook or at in-person events that they learned about on Facebook. Beale said he’s seriously considering shutting down his accounts before October 30. “I know my site has been scraped to death,” he said. “But it just seems like such an arrogant, in-your-face move on [Meta’s] part… It just makes me angry and I don’t want them to get away with it.” Are you considering changing how you use Meta-owned platforms? Let us know at [email protected] . Correction: This story has been updated to reflect Google’s current AI search policies.
