title: Apple ML Research: Muse Spark Open with MLX on Mac Studio
body_text: Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio - Apple Machine Learning Research Machine Learning Research Open Menu Close Menu Overview Research Highlights Publications Events Work with us content type Featured highlight Local and Distributed Large LLM Inference with MLX and RDMA on Mac Studio October 15, 2026 MLX on Mac with Apple silicon lets AI researchers and developers experiment locally with the latest models and methods in a private environment. The open-source array framework leverages the unified memory architecture of Apple silicon, enabling anyone to run new inference and fine-tuning methods on their own hardware and explore other AI techniques. In a previous post , we highlighted the advantages of the M5 architecture and its GPU Neural Accelerators. In this post, we show how to run the latest frontier-class model â Muse Spark Open, with nearly a trillion parameters â right from your desk, using the latest version of MLX, released today. On a cluster of four Mac Studios, Muse Spark Open generates over 36 tokens per second (see Figure 1 ), well above average human reading speed. Beginning on a single Mac Studio (up to 512GB of unified memory), then scaling out across multiple Macs with the RDMA over Thunderbolt driver, below we share an overview of the range of models you can now run on Mac Studio. Muse Spark Open Decode Speed Context size of 8,192 tokens Figure 1: Muse Spark Open decode speed in tokens per second, on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, at a context size of 8,192 tokens. Higher is better. We report performance for three parallelization schemes: pipeline parallelization over two Mac Studio computers (2 M5 Pipeline), and tensor parallelization over two (2 M5 Tensor) and four Mac Studio (4 M5 Tensor) computers. Running Large Language Models with MLX We benchmark several popular open-weight LLMs on Mac Studio , using the MLX LM package, as described in our prior post . We compare two generations of Mac Studio: the recently released M5 Ultra and the previous generation, M3 Ultra. The M5 generation features the GPU Neural Accelerator, which supports dedicated matrix multiplication operations, essential for many machine learning workloads. We evaluate three frontier-class models ( Table 1 ) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts â and thus parameters â active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively). Model Total Parameters Active Parameters Native Precision Evaluation Precision Muse Spark Open 816B 42B BF16 NVFP4 Mistral Medium 3.5 128B 128B FP8 FP8 Qwen 3.8 27B 27B BF16 BF16 Table 1: Language models used in this post. Models ship in various precision formats; we evaluate Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 in their native precision, and Muse Spark Open in 4-bit (NVFP4) precision. Our evaluation measures three metrics across a range of context sizes: time to first token (TTFT, in seconds), generation throughput (in tokens/second), and peak power usage (in watts). All the performance numbers in this post were obtained with mlx_lm.benchmark . For example, running Qwen 3.8 with 8,192 tokens of context and generating 128 tokens is performed with the command line: mlx_lm.benchmark --model Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 A popular use of local LLMs on Mac Studio is running agentic experiences in a private environment, including agentic coding applications that often need large contexts. We therefore report performance at both 8,192 and 65,536 context sizes. Raw TTFT and decode throughput are reported in Table 2 and Table 3 , respectively. Inference Performance on a Single Mac Studio Qwen 3.8 27B and Mistral Medium 3.5 128B fit comfortably on a single Mac Studio with 512GB, taking up to 68GB and 158GB of RAM in the large context size (65,536 tokens) setup. In Figure 2 , we compare their inference performance on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, both on M3 Ultra and M5 Ultra. Time to first token (TTFT) is essentially compute bound, and that is where the Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU shine: the specialized hardware support for fast matrix-multiplication of the GPU Neural Accelerator directly translates into significant speedups for TTFT, up to 4.6Ã faster compared to an M3 Ultra (see Figure 2 ). That makes the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra the desktop of choice when it comes to handling tasks involving very large contexts. Generation speed (in tokens per second) is memory-bandwidth bound. The M5 Ultra chip delivers 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth, up from 819 GB/s for the M3 Ultra. Here again, that translates directly into generation speed (see Figure 3 ), with the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra reporting 1.6Ã faster tokens/s. TTFT Speedup Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0Ã) Figure 2: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. The M5 Ultra GPU Neural Accelerator shines on compute-bound workloads. Decode Speedup Single Mac Studio, M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline (1.0Ã) Figure 3: Decode speedup on M5 Ultra over an M3 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Decode is memory-bandwidth bound, and the M5 Ultraâs 1.2 TB/s of unified memory bandwidth (vs 819 GB/s on the M3 Ultra) is a key advantage. The Mac Studio is also energy-efficient for LLM inference (see Figure 4 ): peak power consumption is about 200W for the Mac Studio with M3 Ultra, and 300W for the Mac Studio with M5 Ultra â a fraction of the power used by a common toaster. More importantly, that modest amount of power consumption means a Mac Studio can be deployed for AI work in any home or office environment. Peak Power Consumption Context size of 65,536 tokens Figure 4: Peak power consumption (in watts) during Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5 inference, at a context size of 65,536 tokens, on Mac Studio with M3 Ultra and with M5 Ultra. While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers. Pipelining Inference Across Two Mac Studio Computers Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the modelâs inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the modelâs layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5 ) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes. Splitting Large Models Across Multiple Computers Figure 5: MLX supports two approaches to splitting large models across multiple computers. With pipeline parallelization, a model is split across depth, while with tensor parallelization, a model is split across width. MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation . These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives ( jaccl , pronounced âjackalâ) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. Once the hosts are set up, MLX provides mlx.launch , a helper command to launch jobs across multiple nodes: mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.benchmark --model mistralai/Mistral-Medium-3.5-128B -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 --prefill-step-size 8192 --pipeline In this command, --backend jaccl specifies the RDMA Thunderbolt driver backend. The --env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 flag enables an experimental MLX feature for fast CPU-GPU synchronization, reducing communication overhead between the CPU (which initiates the Thunderbolt communication) and the GPU (which does the compute). In general, decode inference speed with pipeline parallelization (see Figure 7 ) is very similar to that of a single machine, since the layers are still evaluated sequentially. Communication overhead is also very low, as only the intermediate outputs between the two sets of layers need to be exchanged. It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill â up to ~1.8Ã faster (see Figure 6 ). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192 ) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk k k k , the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk k + 1 k+1 k + 1 , so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization. TTFT Speedup Two Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0Ã) Figure 6: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Splitting the context (here into 8,192-token chunks) lets MLX overlap computation across the two machines â hence the speedup at 65,536 but not 8,192. Decode Speedup Two Mac Studios with pipeline parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0Ã) Figure 7: Decode speedup of two M5 Ultras with pipeline parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Pipeline parallelization leaves decode speed essentially unchanged. Tensor Parallelization for Faster Inference Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5 ) distributes the LLMâs width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl , is critical for this approach to yield any speedup. With MLXâs high-level mlx.launch helper, it is easy to switch to tensor parallelization. The Mac Studio computers are connected in a Thunderbolt mesh, with each pair of machines linked peer-to-peer by two Thunderbolt cables. Assuming the hosts are set up, we simply launch the benchmark across multiple machines with: mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.benchmark --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 -p 8192 -g 128 -b 1 Figure 8 and Figure 9 show the speedups obtained with two or four Mac Studio computers with M5 Ultra, relative to a single-machine baseline (or, for Muse Spark Open, the pipeline parallelization baseline). Notably, dense architectures scale better across multiple computers. With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the expertsâ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5. The two-cable mesh also pays off during prefill, where the extra link bandwidth is felt. For Muse Spark Open on four M5 Ultras at a 65,536-token context, two cables per link cut TTFT from about 50.5s (one cable) to 40.6s â the two-cable value reported in Table 2 , the one-cable run being an additional experiment. TTFT Speedup Two or four Mac Studios with tensor parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0Ã; Muse Spark Open: two-machine pipeline) 2 machines 4 machines Figure 8: Time to first token (TTFT) speedup of two or four M5 Ultras with tensor parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Muse Spark Open does not fit on a single machine, so its baseline is the two M5 Ultra pipeline configuration. Decode Speedup Two or four Mac Studios with tensor parallelization, over a single M5 Ultra baseline (1.0Ã; Muse Spark Open: two-machine pipeline) 2 machines 4 machines Figure 9: Decode speedup of two or four M5 Ultras with tensor parallelization over a single M5 Ultra baseline, for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Muse Spark Open does not fit on a single machine, so its baseline is the two M5 Ultra pipeline configuration. Time to First Token (seconds) Lower is better 8,192 tokens 65,536 tokens Model M3 Ultra M5 Ultra 2 M5 Pipeline 2 M5 Tensor 4 M5 Tensor Muse Spark Open â â 8.4 8.2 4.8 Mistral Medium 3.5 95.9 24.6 24.5 14.4 7.5 Qwen 3.8 18.2 4.1 4.1 3.1 1.7 Table 2: Time to first token (TTFT) in seconds for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Lower is better. We report a single M3 Ultra, a single M5 Ultra, two M5 Ultras (pipeline and tensor parallelization), and four M5 Ultras (tensor parallelization). Decode Speed (tokens per second) Higher is better 8,192 tokens 65,536 tokens Model M3 Ultra M5 Ultra 2 M5 Pipeline 2 M5 Tensor 4 M5 Tensor Muse Spark Open â â 15.74 24.99 36.73 Mistral Medium 3.5 4.95 7.70 7.70 13.69 23.37 Qwen 3.8 12.46 19.69 19.44 33.27 50.89 Table 3: Decode speed in tokens per second for Qwen 3.8, Mistral Medium 3.5, and Muse Spark Open, at context sizes of 8,192 and 65,536 tokens. Higher is better. We report a single M3 Ultra, a single M5 Ultra, two M5 Ultras (pipeline and tensor parallelization), and four M5 Ultras (tensor parallelization). Decode speed was measured over 128 generated tokens following the context. Local Agentic AI on Mac Recently, agentic AI on Mac has gained considerable traction, with agentic coding tools seeing widespread adoption among developers. With MLX, powering these tools locally is as simple as launching a server with the mlx_lm.server tool. For example, a server running Muse Spark Open on port 8080 is started with: mlx.launch --hostfile hostfile.json --backend jaccl -- env MLX_METAL_FAST_SYNCH=1 -- \ mlx_lm.server --model meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 --port 8080 As with mlx_lm.benchmark , the mlx_lm.server helper can be prefixed with mlx.launch to parallelize computation across multiple Mac Studios. From there, agentic AI can be enabled with tools like OpenCode , which can be easily configured to use that local LLM server: { "$schema" : "https://opencode.ai/config.json" , "model" : "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4" , "provider" : { "mlx" : { "npm" : "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible" , "name" : "Local MLX" , "options" : { "baseURL" : "http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1" } , "models" : { "meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4" : { "name" : "Muse Spark Open 816B (MLX)" } } } } } Many other local agentic AI experiences can be enabled through a similar approach. Conclusion Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon â Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 â that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6Ã the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio. Sill shows a window from your Mac, or the whole desktop, on your iPhone or iPad. You use it there with touch, a trackpad, a keyboard or Apple Pencil. Sill for Mac captures the window, encodes it as HEVC video and sends it to the Sill app on your device. Your taps, clicks, scrolls and keys go back to your Mac. Your Mac and your device connect on the same network, over a USB cable, with Direct Wireless Connection when they share no network, or through your own VPN, such as Tailscale, with Remote Access. There is no account and no server in between. getsill.app · Download for Mac · Support · Privacy · Terms Sill for Mac is a free, notarized download from getsill.app ; with Homebrew , brew install --cask saffsanity/sill/sill installs the same download from Sill's own tap . Sill for iPhone and iPad is free on the App Store , and you can also build it from source (below). Screenshots These are the iPad screenshots from the App Store; on iPhone and iPhone Duo, Sill has layouts of its own. Requirements A Mac with Apple silicon, on macOS 14 or later. An iPhone or iPad with iOS 17 or iPadOS 17 or later. On your Mac, Sill asks for Screen Recording, to show your windows, and Accessibility, to click, scroll and type for you and to move and size the window it shows. On macOS 15 or later, also allow Local Network. On your iPhone or iPad, Sill asks for Local Network, to find your Mac, and for the camera when you scan your Mac's pairing code (you can type the code instead). Your Mac and your device on the same network, joined by a USB cable, or near each other with Direct Wireless Connection on. Away from home, your own VPN, such as Tailscale, with Remote Access on. How it works Sill for Mac lives in the menu bar. When your device picks a window, or the whole desktop, Sill captures it with ScreenCaptureKit and encodes it as HEVC with VideoToolbox, on the hardware video encoder in your Mac (or, while that is busy, in software). It captures nothing while no device is connected. The picture goes over an encrypted connection (TLS 1.3) straight to the Sill app on your iPhone or iPad, which decodes and shows it. When the encoder or the link falls behind, Sill drops frames rather than queue them, so the picture stays current. Your input goes back the same way: taps and clicks, scrolls with momentum, the on-screen trackpad, keys and typed text, and Apple Pencil as the pointer. Sill for Mac turns it into mouse and keyboard events, which needs Accessibility. A keyboard attached to your device types on your Mac as soon as the picture shows, Esc included, and a trackpad or a mouse scrolls the window under its pointer. Three fingers swipe and pinch as on a Mac's trackpad: Mission Control, App Exposé, the Spaces, Apps and Show Desktop, through the keyboard shortcuts your Mac has for them. On iPhone , held upright, the picture is on top with buttons, keys and a trackpad below. Larger Picture, in the settings panel, gives a window's picture the room of the window thumbnails, down to where the keyboard comes up; the Desktop keeps the usual layout. A window keeps its own shape until you set its text size with Aa, or turn on the virtual display; then your Mac makes it fill the taller picture. The clipboard goes both ways while Share Clipboard is on, in both apps: text you copy on your Mac is ready to paste on your device, and Paste in Sill sends what you copied on your device to your Mac's clipboard, where you press ⌘V. Sill never reads your device's clipboard by itself, and copies a password manager marks as concealed stay on your Mac. On iPhone Duo , Sill follows the hinge: open it flat and your Mac fills the inner display; half open, the picture is above the fold with a trackpad and keys below; closed, Sill runs on the cover display. Nothing you touch sits on the fold. The menus of the app you use reach your device too: in the iPad's own menu bar on iPadOS 26 or later, and behind the Menus button in Sill's bar. Sill for Mac reads each menu from the app as you open it and chooses the item you pick, through Accessibility. When someone moves the mouse at your Mac, your device shows the pointer where it is. Nearby , your device finds your Mac with Bonjour on your local network. Over a USB cable, your Mac shows as Wired and the connection uses the cable. With no shared network, Direct Wireless Connection (off by default) connects over peer-to-peer Wi-Fi, the way AirDrop does. Pairing : you pair each iPhone or iPad with your Mac once. Tap your Mac on the device, and your Mac shows a code: scan it, or type its 12 digits. Over a USB cable the device pairs by itself. From then on each end knows the other's key, and every connection, nearby or away, is pinned to those keys. In Sill's Settings on your Mac, Devices lists the devices you paired, and you can remove any of them there. Away from home , Remote Access (off by default) lets the devices you paired reach your Mac through your own VPN or a port you forward on your router; a device learns how the next time it connects at home with Remote Access on. A device away from home gets a quality of its own, Low at Standard resolution until you pick another there or in Sill's settings, so a slow connection never starts at your home quality; your home quality comes back as soon as a device at home connects. When your device comes home and your network lists your Mac, the session moves to your network by itself. When the link can't keep up , Sill for Mac notices that it is holding frames back and tells your device, which says so over the picture and, in its Settings, offers a quality the link can carry. Text size : Aa on your device resizes the window you stream on your Mac, through Accessibility, so its text shows at the size you pick, and keeps it at that size while it streams. The window goes back to its own size and place when Sill stops showing it: you pick another window or the Desktop, your last device disconnects, or you quit Sill. If you moved it on your Mac meanwhile, it keeps its new place. The virtual display (off by default) moves a window you stream onto a display of its own on your Mac, so it keeps updating when other windows cover it. It uses a private macOS API, which is one reason Sill for Mac comes from the website and not from the Mac App Store. Good to know: Sill shows one window, or the whole desktop, at a time, and it does not play sound from your Mac. The clipboard carries text only, up to 256 KB at a time, and only between apps that both have it. Your Mac needs to be awake, with Sill open. Sill may not be able to wake it. After a restart Sill opens only once someone logs in, with Launch at Login on. Only the iPhones and iPads you paired can connect, unless you turn off Require pairing in Settings › Devices; then any device on your network can, still encrypted. Pairing at home came with Sill for Mac 0.4.0 and Sill for iPhone and iPad 0.5 (2), and each needs the other: the iPhone and iPad app shows an older Sill for Mac as "Update Sill", and an older iPhone and iPad app can't connect to Sill for Mac 0.4.0 or later at home. Since 0.5.1 the two apps share one version number for each release. With Sill for Mac 0.3.1 or earlier, connections on your local network, over the cable and over Direct Wireless Connection are not encrypted, and anything that reaches your Mac there can connect without pairing: update it. Tips Sill is free, with no ads, no tracking and no subscription. If it is useful to you, a tip through GitHub Sponsors helps pay for the developer account. A tip unlocks nothing: every feature is free. Building from source You need a Mac with Xcode (Sill is built with Xcode 27; the iPhone and iPad app needs Xcode 27.1 or later, for the iPhone Duo's hinge and fold), selected as the active developer directory, with its license accepted. Sill for Mac, from the repository's folder: Scripts/make-app.sh --install --open This builds Sill.app with SwiftPM, signs it with your Apple Development identity, replaces /Applications/Sill.app and opens it. If that was the Sill for Mac you downloaded, grant Screen Recording and Accessibility again and pair each device again: the download keeps its key and paired devices in the data-protection keychain, which only a Developer ID build with the project's provisioning profile reads, and a build of your own keeps them in your login keychain. Without --install it only builds .build/Sill.app . With no Apple Development identity it signs ad hoc, and then Screen Recording and Accessibility have to be granted again after every build. For work on the host itself, swift run -c release SillHost runs the same host on the command line, with one difference: unless you add --pairing , its home door is plain and open, with no pairing and no encryption, and any device on your network can connect to it, so run it only while developing. The App Store's Sill for iPhone and iPad never dials such a door ("Update Sill"); a Debug build from this repository can ( docs/DEVELOPMENT.md , Pairing at home). With --synthetic it streams a test pattern with no Screen Recording needed. The iPhone and iPad app: Open iOSClient/Sill.xcodeproj . In the Sill target's Signing & Capabilities, pick your team, and change the bundle identifier me.saffer.sill to one of your own. Run it on an iPhone or iPad on the same network as your Mac, and tap your Mac. The first time, a Sill for Mac built from this repository asks you to pair: scan the code it shows, or connect the device with a USB cable. docs/DEVELOPMENT.md has the rest: every command-line flag, the test tools and the simulator harness, permissions and how to reset them, Remote Access, troubleshooting and releases. Contributing Issues are welcome: bug reports, questions and ideas. For a pull request, keep to the conventions and decisions in CLAUDE.md : Swift and Apple frameworks only, no third-party dependencies, nothing that needs a server, and latency before picture quality. Open an issue before starting anything large. Before a pull request, Tests/checks/run-all.sh runs the same pure checks as CI, in about five minutes and with no device. Contributions are accepted under the project's license. Please report a security problem privately, as SECURITY.md says, not in a public issue. License Sill is licensed under the Apache License 2.0 . The ARRL Solar Report Just Ahead in Radiosport Upcoming ARRL Conventions and Major Events Florida Hams Provide Communications Support During Hurricane Isaias Amateur radio operators from Florida’s Santa Rosa, Nassau, Lake, Pinellas, and Leon Counties played an important role in supporting emergency communications efforts during and following Hurricane Isaias, helping ensure that critical communication capabilities remained available throughout the storm. In Santa Rosa County, volunteer amateur radio operators staffed the Emergency Operations Center (EOC) and the evacuation shelter at the Milton Community Center. These volunteers provided a communications link between the shelter and the EOC, relaying situational updates and maintaining readiness to support emergency communications should traditional systems become unavailable. Amateur radio operators across the state also supported auxiliary communications efforts, providing additional capabilities to maintain contact with the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee if conventional communication networks experienced disruptions. "While traditional communications systems have become significantly more reliable over the years, amateur radio continues to serve as a dependable auxiliary communications resource," said Arc Thames, W4CPD, Santa Rosa County Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) and Amateur Radio Emergency Service (ARES) Program Manager. "When disaster strikes, our volunteers are trained, prepared, and ready to step in wherever we're needed. It's another layer of resiliency that helps protect our communities." Thames also serves as the ARRL Northern Florida Section Emergency Coordinator and the Amateur Radio Liaison to the Florida Division of Emergency Management, supporting the coordination of amateur radio and auxiliary communications resources statewide. "During tropical weather events impacting Florida, our Auxiliary Communications team provides volunteer operators to monitor amateur radio communications at the State Emergency Operations Center in Tallahassee," Thames explained. "This ensures that if someone is unable to reach emergency officials through traditional means, we have another way to receive and relay critical information. We always hope we're not needed, but we're glad to be there just in case when all else fails." — Thanks to ARRL Northern Florida SEC Arc Thames, W4CPD, for the above The Santa Rosa County, Florida, emergency operations center was a hub of activity during the response to Hurricane Isaias. [Photo courtesy Arc Thames, W4CPD] eBay Restricts Listings of Radio Equipment, but Exempts Ham-Band-Only Gear Online marketplace eBay has imposed new restrictions on listings of radio transmitting equipment in response to new FCC rules that took effect this week, but responded to ARRL that its new policy will not apply to gear that operates exclusively on amateur radio frequencies . The FCC’s rules are intended to use its equipment authorization program to protect against “national security threats to the communications supply chain” and cover a wide variety of products. In its Third Report and Order issued on July 23, 2026, the Commission makes clear that online marketplaces share in the legal responsibility to assure that unauthorized RF devices are not offered for sale on their platforms. The rules took effect on October 13. Moving forward, equipment subject to FCC authorization must have its FCC ID number submitted to the marketplace and posted with its listing. There are exemptions for posts already online, “small sellers,” and used equipment, but initial messages to sellers from eBay suggested that an FCC ID would be required in order to post a listing for any equipment that transmits RF energy. In response to a request from ARRL for a clarification relating to amateur radio equipment that does not require FCC authorization, an eBay spokesperson provided the following statement: eBay allows the sale of devices capable of operating only on frequencies that the FCC has allocated for use by Amateur Radio Service licensees. As these devices do not require FCC equipment authorization, FCC IDs will not be required for these listings as an amateur licensee may use his or her license to operate such radios. However, two-way VHF/UHF radio equipment capable of operating outside of the amateur frequency bands cannot be imported, advertised, sold, or operated within the United States, including on eBay, without an FCC equipment certification. If eBay inadvertently takes action against listings for devices that don't require FCC IDs and are otherwise authorized, the affected seller should inform eBay and we will assess whether to remove restrictions from the listing. It should be emphasized that the FCC did not change its underlying equipment authorization rules. Amateur radio equipment, except for commercial HF amplifiers, continues to not require FCC authorization. Radio Club of America Announces Awards and Fellows for 2026 The Radio Club of America has brought together both wireless industry professionals and amateur radio operators for more than 100 years. Each year, it bestows prestigious awards and elevates several members to RCA Fellows. This year, as always, many of those on the list are hams. The award recipients include Dr. Charles C. Counselman, III, W1HIS, who developed technology for making highly accurate GPS positioning widely available; Jay Adrick, K8CJY, who helped develop digital television and serves as Board President of the National Voice of America Museum of Broadcasting; inventor Charles Kirmuss, WØCBK, who developed digital video and audio recording systems for public safety; Carole Perry Young Professional Award winner and electrical engineer Audrey McElroy, KM4BUN, a longtime proponent of youth in amateur radio; Dr. Ajay Poddar, AC2KG, an internationally-recognized leader in radio science and engineering; Dr. Henry Richter, W6VZA (SK), who developed the communications system for Explorer 1, the first US Earth satellite; and Anthony Rizi, NR1Z, a military and cybersecurity professional and college professor who is also active in ARISS, the Amateur Radio on the International Space Station program. This year’s class of RCA Fellows include amateurs Rachel Jones, KO4HLC; Geoffrey Mendenhall, W8GNM; Nick Pennance, N1CKP, and Dominic “Nick” Tusa, K5EF. The award winners and new Fellows will be formally recognized at RCA’s 2026 Technical Symposium and Awards Banquet in New York City on November 21. Visit the club’s website for a complete list of awardees and their biographies . PoPping In to 44Net Connect Back in the earliest days of the internet, a whole block of IP (internet protocol) addresses — beginning with 44 — was set aside for amateur radio use. Most of that block of addresses is still there and is managed by ARDC, Amateur Radio Digital Communications. In December of 2025, ARDC launched 44Net Connect, a service intended to make it easy for hams to begin using 44Net addresses for such things as experimenting with digital modes, improving repeater infrastructure, setting up a home lab, and more. In the ensuing months, more than 2000 users have signed up and ARDC is now expanding access by doubling its number of “points of presence,” or “PoPs” around the world, adding new ones in Chicago, Los Angeles, and Sydney, Australia (current ones are in Frankfurt, Toronto, and Dallas). A PoP is a physical access point that connects different networks. “The additional PoPs will expand network capacity and bring nodes closer to users in different parts of the world,” explained Rebecca Key, KO4KVG, ARDC’s Communications Manager. “This can shorten the distance data travels, reducing latency, and improving the overall experience.” “44Net Connect gives licensed hams a simpler way to get a static 44Net IP address without a complicated setup,” adds Key. “We’re seeing it used for everything from personal tinkering to club projects, education, and EmComm.” You can find more information about 44Net Connect, including how to get started, in ARDC’s introductory blog post . Nominations are open for the 2027 CWOps Award for Advancing the Art of CW . The purpose of the award is to recognize individuals, groups, and organizations that have made the greatest contribution(s) toward advancing the art or practice of radio communications by Morse code. Candidates for the award may be one or more of the following: Authors of publications related to CW; CW recruiters, trainers, mentors, coaches and instructors; public advocates of CW; organizers of CW activities; designers and inventors who advance the art or practice of CW, and other contributors to the art or practice of CW. Six new amateur radio satellites built by three different AMSAT organizations were launched into orbit on October 1, riding aboard SpaceX’s Transporter-18 rideshare mission . The AMSAT News Service reports that the group includes three PocketQubes from AMSAT-DL in Germany, two satellites from AMSAT-EA in Spain, and another PocketQube from AMSAT Nepal. The spacecraft traveled aboard OSSIE-D, the first orbital transfer vehicle developed by Spanish space transportation company UARX Space. Following separation from the Falcon 9 upper stage, OSSIE-D began deploying its collection of small satellites, giving the worldwide AMSAT community a particularly strong presence on the mission. The AMSAT-DL “PocketQubes” are satellites measuring just 5 centimeters on each side, intended to promote amateur radio and space technology through open-source communications, telemetry, and other experiments. AMSAT-EA’s two satellites offer voice communication capabilities. HADES-E2 carries a repeater with a 145.925 MHz uplink and 436.888 MHz downlink, while HADES-L features a 10-meter uplink, on 29.472 MHz USB, with an FM downlink on 436.665 MHz. AMSAT Nepal’s SanoSat-2, also a 5-centimeter PocketQube, carries a camera capable of transmitting images as SSDV packets using GFSK modulation, allowing amateurs to receive and reconstruct imagery from orbit. SanoSat-2 can also operate as a digital store-and-forward repeater through which amateur operators can upload messages for later transmission. ARRL member and Amateur Extra Class operator Brian Daly, WB7OML, has been reappointed to both the FCC's Communications Security, Reliability and Interoperability Council (CSRIC) and the Technological Advisory Council (TAC) . He has also been selected to continue serving as Co-Lead of the TAC Emerging Wireless Broadband Working Group, which is examining technologies and policies that will influence the future of wireless broadband communications. Daly is an AT&T Fellow and Radio Club of America Fellow. The appointments place him among a select group of experts advising the FCC on issues ranging from communications security and network resilience to emerging wireless technologies and future spectrum needs. Daly says his continued service reflects the longstanding tradition of amateur radio operators contributing technical expertise, innovation, and public service at the highest levels of communications policy and technology development. According to NOAA’s Space Weather Prediction Center (SWPC), the increase in activity is being fueled primarily by sunspot Region 4551, which is described as the largest and most complex of six sunspot regions currently visible on the surface of the Sun. Mostly quiet geomagnetic conditions are expected as well, with some disturbances possible late next week. The Australian Space Weather Forecasting Centre predicts mostly normal HF propagation conditions worldwide. The W3LPL Propagation Forecast from the Daily DX is predicting significantly improved DX conditions on 10 and 12 meters for as many as the next 10 days, with excellent conditions on 17, 15, and 20 meters as well. DX openings on 30 meters should begin in late afternoon each day, followed by 40 meters around an hour before sunset, and 80 meters just after sunset. title: Neural networks are clean
body_text: Neural Networks Are Already Clean Skip to essay An informal research essay and working hypothesis about neural networks More Goodfire research Neural Networks Are Already Clean The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought. Nick Cammarata · Goodfire A working hypothesis · 65-minute read · Text version · Prior work ↓ With contributions from Curt Tigges ( language neuron research ) and Tarun Gogineni (editing) 1 Revisiting canonical evidence Canonical polysemantic circuits and superposition 2 Exploring vision models Studying how neurons change as models grow 崎 −saki Miyazaki Nausicaä 3 Exploring language models Looking inside native neurons and their circuits 4 Zooming out From one neuron to the whole network The Short Version I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks. After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. This means we can study networks directly, instead of first untangling them. Neural networks are already clean. There are at least two ways to approach mechanistic interpretability. The first is rapid normal science on the network itself: look at a network’s neurons and circuits, study how they relate, watch data flow through them, and run experiments at agentic scale to test explanations. The second starts from a list of hypothesized features and tries to extract them all, designing increasingly sophisticated reconstruction objectives and usually ignoring the original. The field began with the first approach and fell back to the second because neural networks seemed to be tangled knots. We had canonical examples of polysemantic neurons, the broad name for a neuron that appears to have multiple unrelated jobs or that looks impossible to understand. The most famous one, in an image model, responded to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. And the last layer of the early field’s model organism, InceptionV1, seemed so full of arbitrary mixtures it wasn’t clear how to study it: almost none of the neurons were easily interpretable. The leading explanation for polysemanticity was superposition. This proposed a new learning principle: when a neural network runs out of neurons, it stops grouping related things together and instead begins folding unrelated things together, simply because they don’t interfere. The result is a kind of knot: the network could have folded in many almost equally good ways, so which things a neuron groups together tells you almost nothing. You have to unfold the knot before you can study anything. In practice that means training a second model – a decomposition such as a sparse autoencoder – to approximate the network as it would look unfolded and studying that instead. If the network really is knotted, there may be no alternative. One main result is that superposition was the wrong explanation for InceptionV1. Architectural problems made later layers overflow. Weak interpretability tools amplified these problems, making the late layers seem incoherent. Since then, architectural changes designed to help deep layers learn better have had the unintended effect of making them more interpretable. When we first studied InceptionV1, we found almost no interpretable neurons in its last layer. But with these ordinary improvements, and no change to model size or training data, 99-100% of neurons in that last layer are easily interpretable and the model is broadly legible the whole way through. It’s the first non-trivial neural network I feel I mostly understand; you can browse it here . I trained versions of it across a 300× range in size, and it’s broadly legible at every scale. With less room, the network doesn’t fold unrelated things together; its neurons just cover coarser-grained concepts, like one car neuron covering many kinds of car. With more room, that neuron differentiates into many specific cars. So the problem wasn’t the presence of a second learning principle, it was just an ordinary learning failure of the first one, and it’s easy to fix. The canonical vision examples of polysemanticity and superposition were errors too. In 2019, Chris Olah and I found the circuit that was originally introduced as the superposition phenomenon in Zoom In [4] Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓ . It showed a car feature appearing to spread into a set of unrelated dog neurons. It was the only one we showed, and the only one I ever saw. We read it as the network placing the car in a high-dimensional hiding place, for downstream neurons to read back out. But nothing reads that combination. It wasn’t hiding anything; it was ordinary generalization and composition. To my knowledge, no one has published a second circuit with the right shape. Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood 1 A note on this number: the share of neurons with one job varies depending on how you set the threshold for counting weak activations, depth, density of sub-circuits, and what you view as “one thing”. How far to go into weak activations is a big factor here. There’s a section describing weak activations below. It tends to increase how many “related things” there are, more than whether the neuron is a judgement of something legible. For instance, the Trump neuron’s weak activations bring in MAGA hats and people related to him. The Titanic neuron’s weak activations bring in stories of more general voyages, or steam engines and other technologies of the era. There’s also the question of whether to care about activation percentiles, or fraction of the strongest activations. In general I think what the neuron learns should be trusted, its natural sparsity and activation ranges and so on. Which I used to mostly not believe! I’m somewhat against trying to standardize things across all neurons. Percentiles are more common today, I think because they’re easier to think about. It goes the other way too. For instance, when you look at the Titanic neuron’s “unrelated jobs,” it’s often detecting that “boat” comes next. The tool missed this because it only looked backward when judging context. When we look at these “unrelated jobs” in depth, it’s almost always this kind of thing. It’s easy to build an imperfect tool. Overall, I don’t think coming to a single score is actually that important. But when it was taken out, early reviewers felt unanchored without even a rough number. In the sets I’ve looked at more closely, considering strong activations, it’s closer to 97% non-arbitrary mixtures, but these are relatively small samples. Overall distilling everything into one “cleanliness” score should be taken as a broad pointer to the regime a neural network is in, rather than something precise to either optimize directly or hold too tightly. A lot of this essay is for being less dimensionality reduced, treating each neuron and circuit differently, according to their motifs, depth, role etc. Despite this, a rough number can be useful. . Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. These percentages compress a high-dimensional picture into a few numbers, and the precise number depends on where you set thresholds for what counts as “one thing” – like whether you lump together closely related idioms in two languages. I don’t think much in interpretability hangs on that question. What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place. Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. This idea first appeared in a forgotten subsection of a paper I worked on called Multimodal Neurons [3] Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks Goh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ (2021). At the time, I hadn’t watched neurons grow over training. Now it’s easier, and it holds up everywhere I’ve seen. Even the original InceptionV1 wasn’t knotted. When I retrain its original architecture, which still produces messy deep layers, and follow the least legible neurons I can find, they turn out to be overgrowing locally into reasonable, adjacent territory. So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. That leaves one learning principle after all. It’s still generalization, but it turns out generalization is fractal. That’s far less concerning: there’s something to learn from the way things were grouped, and nothing to learn from two items in superposition. And since the generalization itself is fractal, our explanations can be too: start with a basic explanation, then zoom in when you want to understand more. In that sense, almost the entire network is interpretable if we look closely enough, especially if we look at how it grew over training. Why was the gap so large? I think several ordinary problems compounded. The explainer models of 2023 couldn’t run the loop of conjecture and test; the tools and metrics were weak, rewarding explanations that could simulate activations rather than ones that were right, which often come apart; no one knew what language neuron motifs to expect, and people broadly looked for the wrong kinds of things; and most studies used small or simplified models. In a sense, those models really had run out of room, which made superposition the natural explanation. But a network short on room doesn’t switch learning principles; its neurons just get broader, as in the small vision models. Broad neurons are usually easy to break down once you know what to look for. Without that knowledge, and with primitive tools, they look like arbitrary mixtures. Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. At first, you’re looking at a single neuron. If you can’t understand it, little else helps: circuits and attribution graphs only explain a neuron in terms of other neurons you don’t understand yet. This can make getting started hard. Once the map starts to fill in, though, it goes surprisingly well. If you don’t understand exactly what a neuron does, you can study what it connects to, the ecosystem around it, and – in a mixture-of-experts model – what its expert specializes in. As with a puzzle coming together, every piece comes with many clues, and they’re well structured and easy to run experiments against. That’s why nearly empty and mostly filled in aren’t surprising places to be; they’re the natural anchors. Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. Imagine finding this one with no knowledge of language neuron motifs and no circuits to lean on, because few neighboring neurons are explained yet. Most humans and agents expect neurons to detect nouns by firing on them, which they mostly don’t. Look at where this one fires most strongly, and you see a pile of seemingly unrelated commas. Now imagine the map is mostly filled in. You know many neurons detect subtle feelings or social contexts, and that they often fire not on the words that carry the feeling but on punctuation, like commas, where the model summarizes what a sentence meant, or on the word just before the feeling matters for predicting what comes next. So you read the surrounding sentences instead, and check its steering effects (what the model writes when you turn the neuron up), which line up closely. You look upstream at how it’s built and downstream at what it does, and both line up. You check its negative pole, what pushes it strongly negative, and find a subtle variant of the same cue, or the moment the social context ends. You can run specific tests, like checking which store brands it responds to. Any of these could break the explanation, yet they keep pointing to the same place. And understanding this neuron sharpens the broader motif: after thousands of subtle-feeling and social-context detectors, you start to know what to expect from the next one, which is part of why the map fills in faster as it goes. It works on the tools too. When you can see 2% of a network, you can’t tell where your tools are broken; when you can see most of it, the unexplained remainder points straight at them. That’s how some coworkers and I found a double-negative regime in SwiGLU neurons that, as far as we know, no one had noticed, and that a decomposition mixing many neurons together would likely have hidden. The bad news about modern neural networks is that they're enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place. In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. First, it’s hard to know how to think like a neural network until you’ve studied it closely. For instance, “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. Second, targeting a small set of mechanisms is like working on one row of an otherwise empty crossword. It’s doable, and might work, but without the crossings it’s hard to know whether you’re right. It may be easier to solve the whole thing – or at least the broader parts of the network these mechanisms connect to. When I ran this process on modern convolutional networks, it basically worked. Agents can map out neurons and circuits, build explorable microscopes and explore them, test explanations thoroughly, and track hundreds of thousands of attribution graphs. There was never a point where rapid normal science broke down. I now feel I basically understand these models, at least enough to know where I’d start asking any question I had; eventually, the crossword just got filled in. So far it has worked in language models too, up to trillions of parameters. Those aren’t close to solved due to sheer size, but I’m optimistic about scaling the process. All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps. Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them. With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect. Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit. Highly speculative: this might be most of what we need, and interpretability might be far more tractable, possibly in the near term, than we’ve assumed. That’s been the pattern for deep learning in general: the simple thing at absurd scale beats the clever one. Rich Sutton called it the bitter lesson [22] The Bitter Lesson Sutton, R., 2019. Incomplete Ideas. References ↓ . Maybe there’s a bitter lesson for interpretability too: scaling ordinary investigation beats engineering a clever new decomposition. A technical companion paper will offer a more detailed account of language model neuron experiments, such as what we’ve found about the different regimes of modern non-linearities and what kinds of circuit motifs show up at different depths. This essay glances at many places and conjectures about where it all might be pointing. Cars and Animals The most famous polysemantic neuron is 4e:55 of InceptionV1, which looked like an arbitrary mixture of cats and cars. It’s been brought up as evidence that neurons might not be the right unit of study in several of the field’s most widely read papers, from Feature Visualization [1] Feature Visualization Olah, C., Mordvintsev, A. and Schubert, L., 2017. Distill. References ↓ in 2017 to Zoom In [4] Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓ . In Zoom In , which I co-authored, we said outright that it “isn’t responding to some commonality of cars and cat faces”. 2 In Multimodal Neurons we came very close. We asked whether the neuron might be responding to some shared feature, “perhaps cat eyes and car lights look similar,” then decided from the feature visualization’s whiskers and chrome that it was “genuinely OR(cat, car).” We were right to look for a shared shape, but I think we underestimated how far generalization reaches. The shared feature was the V. I think the whiskers misled us because generalization happens inside high-level patterns. The V neuron really does take in cat circuitry, and feature visualization’s job is to raise the activation, so once it finds the cat route it adds everything that route brings. The whiskers come along for the ride, even if the neuron doesn’t “want” them. Downstream, the car readers do get a little cat signal through the V neuron, but it barely reaches the output: one cat detector firing does little on its own, since many work together, so the network never needs a negative weight to cancel it. To see the shared pattern, you have to visualize what the neuron’s inputs have in common, not the neuron on its own. After months of seeing clean neurons, I wondered if we’d misinterpreted some early prominent examples of polysemanticity and superposition. The canonical polysemantic neuron seemed like the obvious place to check, so I opened up the cat and car image grid I’d seen hundreds of times before and did something I’d never done: I spent a few seconds wondering what one thing this might be. Almost instantly it was obvious: it’s not a cat and car neuron, it’s a V-shape neuron. I looked at its circuit connections: V-shaped flames, V-shaped water jets from a fireboat, V-shaped fox faces. I looked at its negative pole: an O, round where the V is pointed. The circuit appeared to show a car going into a bunch of unrelated dogs, as if the dogs were a kind of high-dimensional storage place where the car could be recovered later as needed. But that’s not what the car was doing. Cars and dogs were being brought together because of shared pose. InceptionV1 has more than a hundred of these generalized pose neurons, each one its own clean detector of a pose shared across cars, dogs and other objects, and to my knowledge no one had noticed them. Later layers keep building on them, all the way to the end of the model. The car was not being stored in an obscure place, and nothing directly reads out the combination. It’s the opposite: it’s continuing to differentiate into car specialists and finer poses. Part of the reason was not knowing about generalized pose neurons, and part of the reason is that the technique we use to render icons of images — feature visualization — ends up being reward hacked in deeper layers. The intent is to find an image that maximizes the neuron, but the way that’s done is through gradient descent, and it takes the easiest path, which in InceptionV1 often means dogs. There are lots of dogs in InceptionV1’s training data and a lot of dog neurons, and the early optimization falls into them and never recovers. If you even lightly bias it toward the natural paths the top images take, most of them are cars, and some are both dogs and cars, because of shared pose. Visualized through the car, two are car neurons and two share a pose between cars and dogs. It can be tempting to discount this generalization, under the assumption that the dogs and cars are only together because there’s not enough space. Maybe it “really wanted” separate dog-pose and car-pose neurons, and a bigger model with more space would have separated them. It’s true that bigger models tend to have more narrow neurons, but when networks scale up, they can do it in counterintuitive ways. Our smallest model only has a rough version, with cars and dogs together but not by pose. Both human and automated interpreters seem strongly biased toward describing neurons as detectors for groups of nouns, like cats and cars, rather than for a shared pattern, like a V. Sometimes a neuron really does respond to a group of nouns. In my experience, though, it’s more often a shared pattern, and the neuron is better understood as a verb than a noun. Its job isn’t to name what’s in the input but to draw a distinction downstream neurons can use: it separates two subtle patterns at its positive and negative poles (a V versus an O) and pushes the flow of activations toward different neurons accordingly. I can often unblock my understanding of a neuron by asking: if I couldn’t use groups of nouns at all, how would I describe this neuron to someone else? Usually the shared pattern pops out right away, and it’s easy to test on more groups of nouns (for the V: shinkansens, pool tables). I suspect this is the largest source of misattributed polysemanticity in mid-layer neurons. Many explanations I’ve seen that call a neuron polysemantic look to me like a single pattern described as a list of nouns. We should treat a neuron that means two or three things as one neuron with a few grouped meanings. The grouping probably wasn’t a problem for the network: the meanings sit together because, from the network’s point of view, they’re similar. That makes the grouping a clue to how the network thinks, and following it can turn up generalizations we didn’t know about, as cats and cars did here. Often the extra meanings also melt away on closer inspection, turning out to be minor and rarely active. Finally, some apparent meanings are just our tools being bad, and this essay has several examples: the double-negative regime of SwiGLU, an unread saliency knob that makes the residual stream hard to visualize, and the reward hacking in feature visualization we just saw. Keeping the original neuron whole keeps these errors visible, so the error correction can continue. If we’d used optimization to get a cleaner list, we might have lost many of these hints. A History of Microscope Errors The story of interpretability, as I see it, has largely been one of finding out that what was under the microscope was better than we thought. The microscope just wasn’t tuned right, and what needed tuning was often pretty subtle. Modern neural network interpretability arguably started with feature visualization, which renders a synthetic image of what a neuron responds to most: the famous psychedelic pictures. For a while they didn’t look very good. You could reasonably conclude the neurons had learned something, just nothing very clean. It turned out the method was missing transformation robustness. Once researchers added it, the same neurons came out crisp. But that only gets you so far into the model. Near the end, feature visualization starts to break down again, for two reasons: the reward hacking we saw with the car circuit, and regularizations that weren’t quite right. Fixing it didn’t require anything fancy. A few subtle tweaks to reasonable settings, and now we can see much deeper into the network. As far as I can remember, no one, including me, suggested it might be the general explanation, for instance for what was wrong with InceptionV1’s last layer. Superposition Recursive generalization isn’t a particularly bold explanation, it’s arguably just what we should expect out of ordinary generalization. But there’s also a much bolder explanation that has been proposed for polysemanticity, a new learning principle. The main learning principle we see everywhere is generalization. With generalization, things are put together because of a shared pattern that it’s useful to have in one place, so it can be built on. With superposition, unrelated things are placed together because they don’t interfere. These have opposite predictions: generalization should be local, superposition should be non-local, since it would want very different things to be near each other. Generalization would want a floppy ear dog neuron, which can be thought of as lots of slightly different floppy ears at different angles and kinds together. Superposition would want a floppy ear dog + Latin poetry neuron. Along with superposition, Zoom In [4] Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓ introduced the idea of features as the fundamental unit of neural networks. Depending on where you look, superposition then means either “more features than dimensions,” which even a fully monosemantic network would satisfy, because its neurons compose, or a learning principle like the one above, applied sometimes to what neurons learn and sometimes to where features go. 4 For instance, InceptionV1’s layer 4b has basically monosemantic neurons for car parts like windows, car bodies, and wheels, which the next layer assembles into a car neuron, 4c:447. In the feature view, it’s reasonable to say the “car feature” isn’t just in 4c:447, but also in the combination of 4b neurons that builds it. So there are two car features in adjacent layers, sharing almost exactly the same mechanics. In the “more features than dimensions” view, the first is in superposition and the second may not be. In the sense of the informal note Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition , the first is distributed, but by composition, and the second isn’t distributed at all. This is part of why I find hypothesized features hard to think with, and why I usually prefer specific mechanisms, like neurons, and specific pieces of data. So “superposition” is itself in superposition between several common uses. We focus on the learning principle applied to the mechanisms like neurons, because whether it forms holds such a disproportionate share of the good or bad news for interpretability. It’s also fairly easy to test: recursive generalization and superposition predict nearly opposite things, and you can watch a neuron grow and see which one happens. When I say superposition in this essay, I’m referring to this version, and we’ll address the question of “more features than dimensions”, which I basically don’t think is bad news, later. Superposition of the Gaps Polysemanticity is often more a claim about the observer than the neuron. It says there’s no good explanation yet. There’s a few reasons that could be: Bad tools: our lens or microscope isn’t good enough Bad explanations: created from those tools Bad learning: the network learned poorly due to bad architecture, training data, or something else Recursive generalization: while generalizing, the neuron branched off in a few related directions Superposition: a change in learning principle where the network packs unrelated things into the same neurons because they rarely collide. For years I was a staunch superposition believer. I started studying language model neurons not out of any interest in neurons or superposition, but because I was interested in whether agents had research taste! I wanted to see if they’d ask good questions as they tested explanations, and started with neurons only as a baseline. I expected them to run into intractable feature fragments in superposition. That would produce a new baseline for how clean neurons really are, then the agents could continue with some cleaner learned basis. But it never came, because the neurons kept coming, resolving to a simple explanation that made surprising predictions that held. In a frontier language model, I found a neuron that mostly fired on “pr”, but also on a bunch of Base64 URL strings as well as some Bengali. I thought this must finally be an arbitrary mixture. Across hundreds of cases like these, nothing shook my belief in superposition. It just kept moving. If the strong activations came back clean, superposition would move to the weak ones, or to combinations of neurons, or to the neurons I hadn’t looked at yet. Or maybe across layers themselves. But eventually I wondered what was going on. Unless this was some dramatic extended case of selection bias, something wasn’t matching the early model organisms. So I went back, the original evidence fell, and that led to this essay. I now think I was making superposition the null hypothesis when it should have been the last hypothesis, since it’s the most radical and the least testable. It just looks like things that don’t make sense. But that’s also what bad tools look like (feature visualization reward hacking), or recursive generalization you haven’t followed yet (“iy” neuron), or a bad architecture (5b of InceptionV1), or generalization you haven’t understood yet (cat and car). References ↓ paper said as much in 2022: “In the mechanistic interpretability community, superposition is often treated as the default hypothesis simply because it seems intuitively more compelling than other explanations, but there is little evidence.” 5 In the next sentence, the paper says its own results are moderate evidence for superposition. That evidence is circumstantial, in the paper’s own word: SoLU suppresses activations spread across many neurons, an extra LayerNorm restores performance, and after the LayerNorm a neuron’s weak activations looked less related to its main job, which the paper reads as features being smuggled through small activations. We read it as evidence about distributed representation in an architecture built to suppress it, rather than about neurons packing unrelated things together, which is the sense we care about. Telling the two apart in weak activations is hard even with today’s tools, since meaning shifts in every direction at once as activations weaken, and it was harder still in 2022, for all of us. The paper also notes that its discussion of superposition has been superseded by Toy Models of Superposition, which we address in the appendix. We bring it up not as a criticism of either paper, but because it’s the only place we know of where someone said plainly how little real-world evidence there was, and we think people still often assume there’s more than there is. To my knowledge, no one has found a superposition circuit in a real network since my original one, which was an error. I don’t see anything like it in real models, despite expecting to, and I think the bar for claiming it should be high, since it’s such a radical explanation and would be big news, terrible news, for how we should study neural networks. Of course, this risks the opposite error, an explanation of the gaps: assuming every neuron must have a sensible story. Two things make it less worrying. First, each of the other causes can be tested. A better tool either resolves the neuron or it doesn’t; retraining with a better architecture shows whether learning was the problem; and recursive generalization can be watched as it grows, in small steps. Superposition’s only symptom is that something doesn’t make sense. Second, real explanations tend to be narrow and easily testable. Once you suspect a neuron is a Colorado neuron, steer it and see what it says. If a neuron fires for some narrow TV trope, the set of things that could count as that explanation is tiny, while “something that doesn’t make sense” covers everything outside it. Also, we don’t have to force an explanation we don’t have. If a neuron might do a couple unrelated things and you’re not sure, it’s fine to say so. I think recursive generalization should be high on the list of things to suspect, and it’s easy to check if you have training checkpoints. I now think superposition should be far down the list. Exploring Image Models Small image models may seem obsolete, but I think they matter a lot to this question because we can see them so clearly. They're also where much of the original worry came from: there we saw what looked like high-resolution chaos, not low-resolution ambiguity. Language models are massive, we don't have tools like feature visualization which make our life easier, attention mixes different kinds of mechanisms together, and many of their motifs are surprising. As I showed above, even vision motifs can be counter-intuitive, and language is worse. Each one of these deficiencies can make a monosemantic neuron look polysemantic. If you're looking at a blurry image trying to figure out if it's a dog or a cat, the blur makes it harder, but it doesn't favor either answer. If you're looking at a blurry image and trying to decide if the image itself is blurry or if you're just looking badly, every flaw in your eyesight gets counted as blur in the image. If we want to study how neurons change with scale, compression pressure, activation strength, and depth, it's better to start where we can see clearly. I trained three ConvNeXt models spanning roughly 300× in size: a small one with 92k parameters, a medium one with 7.06M (the same size as InceptionV1), and a large one with 28.6M. We’ll look at those, and also InceptionV1, to try to understand what neurons do in different situations, and try to find places packing may form. How I Think About Neurons I used to think of neurons as human-shaped nouns: one is a car, another is a curve. Now I think of them more as control flow. A neuron is less about what it sees than about what it does to the flow coming in, and often its job is to gate a region of the network. Seen this way, monosemanticity is almost the wrong question. A better one is what a neuron lets through and what it keeps out. Pixels come in, and the network begins grouping and distinguishing things. Cars and dogs might be grouped together because they share a pose. Further along there are specific car detectors – for taxis, ambulances and the like – and they don’t want dogs. So a neuron in front of them acts as a gate: it responds positively to cars and negatively to dogs, and its negative side keeps the dogs out. The dogs go on to their own area, which doesn’t have to worry about cars. Later neurons build on this, specializing further: an ambulance neuron might have a taxi on its negative pole, and a taxi an ambulance. In a larger model, these distinctions can become finer still, separating one view of a taxi from another. Smaller models may stop at coarser distinctions, with something closer to a general “car” neuron. pose car detectors dogs pose car detectors dogs Replay Cars and dogs share a pose early on; a gate in front of the car detectors lets cars through and turns dogs away with its negative side. The negative side of neurons matters almost as much as positives for understanding them, even in ReLU networks where the negative side is cut off. A neuron is built from votes: each input weight votes for its positive side or its negative side, and the votes add up before the nonlinearity. The negative side never gets gradient on its own, but the individual votes do whenever the neuron is on, so it’s shaped by learning too. The negative side’s meaning depends on context: when a neuron in the sports car’s path separates it from snakes and dogs, it isn’t calling cars and dogs opposites, just gating out things that were usefully grouped earlier. The negative side tells us what distinction matters at this point in the circuit, which also makes it a quick check on whether a grouping is real: the V neuron’s negative side is an O. What Dictionaries Learn If combinations of neurons were hiding things, a dictionary (eg an SAE) should find building blocks the neurons lack. So I trained several on these layers and went looking, myself and with agents. I didn’t find any. Mostly, the two looked like what they mechanistically are: the neurons like building blocks, the SAE units like those blocks grouped by context. It was clearest with spiders. The SAE units were spiders in different settings; the neurons were leg patterns and webs. They didn’t disagree much. SAEs did help with “what’s in this image?” They helped most in the smallest model, whose neurons are coarse. At medium size I slightly preferred them; at large, I think I prefer the neurons. But I care more about understanding the network than about any one image, and I never saw the SAE grasp something fundamental the neurons didn’t. If a model at a particular size failed to understand baseball players, so did its SAE. When the model finally understood a baseball player, it was on a neuron. What did the SAE find that didn’t already have a clear neuron counterpart? On the last layer, 88% of its activity is near-copies of single neurons, and the rest is faint: removing every dictionary direction that matches no neuron leaves accuracy unchanged, and the few answers it flips were already near-ties. Additionally, if you search the rotations of a layer for the one where a handful of units carry the most activity, starting from a random one, you land back on the neurons, in every block. Among the few features strong enough to look at, what the SAE added was loose groupings built from existing neurons, like animals at the water’s surface or pale, lumpy food. Nothing we found there looked like a fundamentally new building block.
