What the SAE added Typical features ‹ 1 of 16 › × Rare Things and Memorization A lot of the worry about hidden features comes from rare things. They seldom collide with anything, and they may not seem worth a neuron of their own. So we looked at rare things every way we could think of. Rare classes are often more consolidated: you need a lot of dog patterns for ImageNet, but only one Triceratops neuron. When I removed weak activations in the last stage, no class stood out. The adversarial examples we traced used normal semantic circuit routes. I looked at the images whose representations in the last layers are furthest from any other image. They end up being entertaining, weird images that the model misreads with ordinary neurons: a hummingbird seen as ice cream, a giant banana seen as a vault, and a guy in a fallen wheelbarrow seen as a lawn mower. I also trained an ImageNet model to map random noise to random labels, and even that was partly semantic: it partially leaned on wool textures and the texture of distant trees, which are high-frequency, a bit like high frequency noise. I didn’t fully audit the model, but thought it was interesting that it used them at all. Across all experiments in language and vision, memorization tends to want to sit as close to the output as possible, since all it has to do is look the answer up, and the late layers did most of the work. What we see instead is an off-ramp between two routes the network already has. Do Weak Activations Matter? When people ask whether weak activations matter, I think there are several questions mixed together, and they have different answers. Are they generalization or superposition? Unsurprisingly, I think it’s generalization. Imagine you’re a packed, unrelated feature trying not to collide with what’s in a main neuron. Weak activations are vastly denser, so you’d be colliding with orders of magnitude more things, for little upside. strong half 0 half of max max 100 million tokens through one Qwen3-32B neuron. Almost all sit near zero; about 160 reach the strong half. But maybe you hide in the weak activations of many neurons at once. What we see is that you can ablate almost all the weak activations of the network for almost no cost. The places where removing them costs the most are some of the easiest to understand. In language models, they include the last layer, which is largely used to suppress single tokens, for what we call a “say or just think” motif. In vision models, it’s the early layers, which function like dials: the difference between slightly bright and medium bright matters, but for a later detector, like king penguin, low or very low evidence doesn’t. So critical common things can’t be in the weak activations, since we can remove them. We can also look at what we lose when we cut weak activations. Across several kinds of studies, it’s usually fine distinctions between things the neural network is already confused about. And the faint activations that tip them come from the semantically related neurons you’d expect. I used to think in percentiles, since they’re easy to think in and standardize across neurons. But I’ve come to think a neuron’s raw shape is telling us something. Some neurons hold their meaning far down the range; others drop off a cliff, like the Christmas neuron above at about 5% of its max. Some fire a few times a book, others a few times a page. Percentiles flatten that, and it’s often what tells you whether you’re looking at a dial, where the middle matters, or a detector, where it mostly doesn’t. Percentiles also mess with intuition. The 99th percentile sounds high, but 1 token in 100 is about a quarter of a page, and a neuron for a niche feeling or social context – which are all over language models – shouldn’t come up four times a page. Thinking in pages helps: the 99.9th percentile is every two or three pages, the 99.99th every 25 or 30. Do you need them to label a neuron? Usually not. After looking at thousands of language model attribution graphs by hand, it’s hard to overstate how much neurons are analogizers. If you’re talking about voyaging on a boat, the model might judge that a bit Titanic-ish. I don’t think it’s usually helpful to think of a “naval voyage feature” spread across the weak activations of the Titanic neuron and others. Instead, there’s a Titanic-ish mechanism: whenever something is Titanic-ish, it fires, and its weights are votes for Titanic-ish things. So you look at the top activations, see that it’s Titanic-ish, and that label usually holds up through the rest of your audits. If you ever really care about a particular activation, you can follow its pathways, ablate the circuits, and keep zooming in to almost arbitrary resolution. My main takeaway: if a weak activation looks unrelated, don’t be too worried unless you’ve looked at it carefully. Of the probably hundreds I’ve followed by hand, almost all turned out to be related, coming through a reasonable circuit; it just wasn’t visually obvious until I traced it. Many were clever, like a Zen koan neuron that fires weakly on recursion in math: many koans turn on the same kind of self-reference, looking for the observer. Others were more distant and ugly, not always the connection I would have drawn, but you could usually follow how it got there. I suspect most, possibly almost all, are like this. Explanations That Can Lose There’s a risk of defining explanations too broadly, like a “multifunctional language neuron.” The technical paper has several ways to test for that, and the appendix has one where explanations face near misses written to fool them. One we found particularly useful is blind maximum. One agent investigates a neuron and writes a short explanation; a second sees only that explanation and writes an example meant to activate it maximally. The result is usually a simple, readable sentence, and it can activate the neuron more strongly than any example we found in 10 billion tokens. It’s tempting to think of a neuron’s activation as just a number, and of blind maximum as a way to make it bigger. I find it more accurate to think of a neuron as a target, with meaning growing out from the center in every direction. Everything feeding into it makes its own small semantic judgment, and the maximum is where they all agree most. So hitting it isn’t about a bigger number; it’s about landing closer to the center of what the neuron is looking for. Ten billion real tokens had their chance, and a sentence written from the explanation alone got closer. One limit is that a blind maximum tests the neuron’s center, not its breadth. If a neuron has several jobs, even related ones, a single blind maximum may only reach one. So we also cluster the attribution flowing into the neuron. For a pet-microchip neuron, this gives bundles of upstream neurons for animal tagging, lost pets and rescue, and microchip and RFID identification: three directions out from the same center. We then run a blind maximum for each bundle, ablating all the others, and compare it against the strongest corpus example under the same ablation. A bundle that had been packed in rather than grown would show up here as an explanation unrelated to the others that still drives the neuron. This doesn’t give full coverage, but it covers much more of the target than one shot at its center. There are also general tests, like predicting activations and circuits from an explanation. To be honest, I trust these only up to a point. “Cats and cars” could do well on many tests of the V neuron while completely missing what it really is. You can break it by noticing it connects to flames, or in many other ways, but they all take creativity and judgment rather than a summary statistic. Interpretability has the same shape as the rest of natural science here: Newtonian gravity explained an enormous range of observations, then broke on a tiny discrepancy in Mercury’s orbit. The best criticism is specific to the conjecture. References ↓ I thought small simplified models would be the best starting place for interpretability, since there’s fewer bells and whistles to think about, and small size means fewer things to study. But now I think it may be the opposite. The bells and whistles are there to help the neural network learn better, like the residual stream InceptionV1 never had, and by simplifying it’s easy to make neurons learn less well. And bigger models tend to have more narrow neurons, so it’s more easy to spot patterns and motifs. At least for GPT-2, I was often looking at multiple motifs together, neither of which I knew, which made things hard. By adopting the architectures and scale the field wanted anyway, we may have been slouching towards monosemanticity without knowing it. The Residual Stream The worry with the residual stream isn’t that there are more things we care about than dimensions. It’s a continuous version of packing: manifolds woven through each other, accepting some interference in exchange for room to store more. Ruling that out entirely may not be possible. But in practice it hasn’t been a bottleneck. We can read what neurons write to the residual stream and what they read from it, attribution graphs come out clean, and we don’t see the stream accumulating interference only to undo it later. In vision models, we could also check this by eye. For years I couldn’t visualize the residual stream of convolutional networks: every map came out as one big arc. It turned out the network was putting almost all of its activation mass into a single unread dimension, which it can change to scale all the other dimensions that are read through LayerNorm. Once we understood that, removing it was easy, and the maps made sense. The technical details of how it works, or even what it’s doing, are less important than the more general pattern throughout this essay: find what the architecture is doing and work with it, rather than fighting the network. It also pointed toward something the field ended up building anyway: attention. We don’t know whether language models need a similar fix. When we’ve visualized their residual streams, it has mostly just worked. Judging whether a whole map of text makes sense is much harder than glancing at a map of images, though, which is why we did most of this work in vision. A single global map may not be the best tool for language models anyway. Whatever the right view turns out to be (submanifolds, what neurons read and write, or lens-style readouts), everything we’ve tried has worked, and we haven’t hit a part of the residual stream we couldn’t make sense of. Loading the map… The residual stream at every layer of the ConvNeXt, drawn as one map. Each line follows one image location from the first layer (left) to the last stage (right), starting in the color of its patch. At the first layer the map is sorted by color. Locations that end up as animal faces start wherever the color of their fur puts them, and gather gradually. Red patches start together and go on to become different things. Hover or tap a row to see its patch at each stage. How the map is made The same image locations are followed through every layer, with the heavy coordinates set aside and each layer centred. The four stages have different widths and resolutions, so each stage’s space is rotated to line up with the next one’s, matching each location with the cell that contains it after downsampling. That rotation is fitted; it isn’t the network’s own downsampling. One UMAP is fit to every layer at once, with each state’s neighbors taken only from other locations, so a location moves when its neighbors change. Nothing in the method orders the layers: the map comes out ordered by depth, and we turned it so depth runs left to right. The animal faces, and the groups in the small maps, are clusters of the stream partway through the last stage, so their meeting at the end is by construction. The red patches are a cluster of the first layer, so their starting together is by construction. What each panel adds is the other end. Measured in the full stream rather than on the map, the faces’ nearest neighbors go from chance to mostly other faces, and the red patches’ go from mostly other red patches to close to chance. The highlighted rows were picked by eye to be easy to read, and the faint lines are a random sample of each group. Lines are smoothed along depth. The output of the last block is left out, since there the stream clumps by image and class. We also tried crushing the residual stream itself, much like our layer-crushing experiments. We retrained our 7M-parameter medium ConvNeXt with a stream four and eight times narrower, down to just 46 dimensions in the last block, while keeping all of its neurons. Accuracy fell from 72% to 60% and 39%, but compared with a normal-width model the crushed stream’s map looks quite similar, just a bit messier. Nothing looks cleverly interleaved. Neuron reads and writes tell the same story: things get noisier, but what leaks in is the same kind of thing. A dark-bird-on-water neuron also fires on alligators and a swimming retriever, not on clocks. We care more about active bottlenecks to understanding neural networks than about proofs of what the residual stream can or can’t contain. If interference isn’t showing up in the maps or in what neurons read and write, even when we take away the room, we think we’re in a pretty good spot. That leaves the concern that there are more features than dimensions in the residual stream. A stream can hold far more than it has dimensions just by placing things in the right directions, so this alone isn’t packing. It mostly matters if you want a big list of all the model’s features, and people often go to the stream for exactly that. As we discuss in Zooming Out, we don’t think a big list is the right end goal. But if you want one, the directions neurons write to and read from are a good place to start. So are continuous submanifolds, like those Block Sparse Featurizer [28] Uncovering Neural Geometry in Vision Models With Block-Sparse Featurizers Fel, T., Kowal, M., Jacobs, M., et al., 2026. So far all of these have worked well: they find sensible subspaces, and we can follow them across layers. We’ve looked at language models’ residual streams less, but what we’ve seen fits the same story. For understanding higher-level structure and motifs, nothing in the residual stream has blocked us so far. Attention We’ve made less progress on attention than on neurons, and it’s mostly outside the scope of this essay. To be honest, I’m not sure anyone understands attention well enough to confidently say that illegibility is a superposition in the sense we care about. Distinguishing it from all the other things it could be is hard, and a change in learning principle shouldn’t be near the top of the list of hypotheses for why new mechanisms are hard to understand. A lot of attention’s value seems to be in the easier parts. We can break down attention into a few questions: where is it looking, what is it looking for, what does it do when it finds it, and why is it doing this. Where it looks is relatively easy. It basically comes for free, and it already tells you a lot. In the preeclampsia graph it does two separate things. First it gathers the facts of the case onto “she,” where the model works out the medical question. Then the question’s wording decides what to actually say next. We can also understand what it’s looking for, and what it does when it finds it, in terms of neurons. We think this gives you a lot of the benefit of what attention is doing. For instance, take the comma after “headache.” in the preeclampsia example. Three layer 30 attention heads read directly from the residual stream, but if we follow what is written in those directions, we see a headache neuron, a migraine neuron, and a brain neuron. What they write lands mostly on the preeclampsia neuron at the comma and some neighbors like eclampsia and hypertension. Ablating these heads drops preeclampsia by a quarter. Stopping them from looking at pain and nothing changes. The chips under tokens are neurons that activate there. We can follow some of what attention is doing by watching the flow of neurons it affects. It also works the other way. Some neurons are much easier to see once you can see the attention around them, and some heads only make sense through their neurons. Understanding attention and neurons through each other. Three cases in Qwen3-32B where a neuron and a head only make sense together. Below each, more examples: highlighted is what the head reads, boxed is where the neuron fires. Hover a drawing for the test. Overall, we don’t think attention and neurons are so separable. Understanding where attention is putting information is quite helpful for understanding the neurons that then work with that information. Even simple things like motifs around where information tends to be placed, like the ends of numbers, or on commas, have been helpful. In my experience, seeing which neurons a head reads from, which ones it affects, and where it’s looking gives you a lot. One main thing it doesn’t give you is a global name for each attention head. It’d be nice to have them, but it hasn’t been a big bottleneck on exploring neurons or attribution graphs. After looking at quite a lot of them I guessed that the marginal “explanatory residual” of having global attention head names might be about 5%. Then I had an agent do the same, looking at 100 attribution graphs without my guess, and it also put it about 5%, split about equally into “position heads” that are relatively easier to name, since they do things like look one token backwards, and everything else, which is of course varied and harder. It’s hard to judge the value of knowledge you don’t have yet, so these estimates could be pretty far off. But so far even without global attention head labels I think we can go quite far in discovering high level structure and motifs with just local attention flow and global neuron explanations. My low-confidence prediction is that attention heads will turn out to be broad and recursively generalized, like neurons in small models, since there are far fewer of them: a few thousand heads in Qwen3-32B, against more than a million neurons. Zooming Out What I Mean by Clean Nothing here has been changed or recombined. Every district, circuit and neuron is the network’s own, as it learned them. When I say neural networks are already clean, I mean something deeper than neuron monosemanticity, although even by that standard, I think things look much better than the field expects. I mean that a network’s parts are built to be read, and built upon, by its downstream readers. In this sense, a neural network is almost a fractal of explanations, of coherent, useful groupings: at the macro scale, in its mechanisms, and at the micro scale, where recursive generalization shapes each one. That points to a goal for interpretability: become another reader. The more we read it the way its own readers do, the more interpretable I think it will look. We should be wary of reading it too much like a human, and concluding it’s messy just because it doesn’t fit our preconceived concepts. I think the reason things end up so organized is partially because it was faster to build that way. Once you have a car area of the neural network with car parts, it’s easier to add the marginal car there than to build a second car area somewhere else. I think this is closely related to ideas of circuit racing and gradient starvation. We normally consider interpretable and monosemantic to be nearly synonyms. I think this is partly because these ideas grew out of a model organism (InceptionV1) that was almost bimodal. Early layers were interpretable and monosemantic, late ones seemed like arbitrary mayhem. But what we see in language models is somewhere in the middle, with most neurons meaning mostly one thing, some meaning a few. How bad is that? There are two broad styles of interpretability. One we can call enumerative interpretability. The goal is to have a big list of features to audit, to make sure we haven’t missed some meaningful pattern. A big concern within this view is avoiding the curse of dimensionality, or a combinatorial explosion of items connected to other items, where each one means more than one thing. Another style we can call exploratory interpretability. It starts with questions. It can explore any part of the neural network, zooming in and out fluidly like Google Maps across attribution graphs, and mechanisms like neurons or attention heads. We pick up more questions along the way. The mechanisms like neurons are a good place to start, but it’s not about neurons being some final solution to everything – though I do think it’s closer to that than most people realize. This approach is far more resilient to polysemanticity. It is also broadly fine ignoring lots of the neural network, in the same way someone studying a city would ignore areas irrelevant to their analysis. I think exploratory approaches will be more fruitful. My sense is that the field is moving in this direction already, but I’m not sure it has been written down clearly. This view has a couple implications. Questions like “are there more features than dimensions?” are mostly irrelevant. We don’t have to define features, which is famously difficult. We can focus mostly on mechanisms like neurons and attention heads which are part of the model, data flowing through it, and then groups of both and motifs that recur across all of this. The big feature list was always a means to an end. There may be other paths that don’t require them. Motifs Over Monosemanticity If I could push a button and make every neuron perfectly monosemantic, or instead understand the circuit motifs behind a few questions I care about (the right way to ask about an agent’s psychology, how circuits connect to the persona selection model, how an agent thinks about its goals and the boundary between itself and others), I’d take the motifs in a minute. Imagine an interpretability researcher arriving from a hundred years in the future, who knows not just the answers to our questions but which questions we should have been asking. What would they tell us? I can’t know, but I’ve been in a small version of their position once. I now feel like I mostly understand a vision model, which makes me something like a future researcher to myself eight years ago. Here’s what I’d tell myself then. Pay attention to the giant pose circuit right in front of you. Think of negative poles as gates in a circuit, not a neuron’s opposite. Feature visualization reward hacks in late layers, so some of the mess there is the tool’s, not the network’s. The last layer is messy partly because of a bad architecture; that’s a sign, so don’t paper over it. And whenever you see polysemanticity, look harder. The noise that stands out usually points to an explanation you don’t have yet. Almost none of this is a list of features. Short of handing my past self this advice, the best thing I could give is the original neurons and circuits, with a note to look harder at them. This is why the difference between recursive generalization and superposition matters so much. Following the noise only works if the noise has something to teach. A grouping that grew from generalization does. A grouping of things packed together because they don’t belong together would teach almost nothing. So my best guess of the future researcher’s advice would look somewhat similar. They might hand us a set of motifs that look obvious to them but not to us. But short of that, they’d say keep looking at the original neural network. Don’t fracture it too much. Learn how to see it. It’s a bit like The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy, where the answer, 42, is known, and the search is for the question. The network is the answer, and interpretability is largely the search for the right question. It’s hard to find a better guide to that question than the network itself. That’s the deeper sense in which I mean the network is already clean. A City vs a Knot A bigger system isn’t necessarily harder to navigate. In a small town, asking for the financial district barely makes sense. Whatever exists is scattered: a bank on one street, an insurance office on another, maybe an accountant with a home office. In New York, you could find it on a map in a minute. We saw a small version of this in our ConvNeXts: agents found labeled dog-ear neurons faster in the larger models, where pale, wavy, and head-side ear neurons all feed one hanging-ears neuron, a natural place to start. Of course, even if the map is understandable, that doesn’t mean you’ve understood it. We still have to do the ordinary science of conjecture and criticism: guess what something is, try to break the guess, and keep what survives. The network is strange, but its strangeness repeats, so a guess that survives scrutiny often pays off many times over. We should worry both about imposing our own ideas too strongly, and fracturing the network. Imagine arriving in Tokyo knowing New York well. “Where’s the Brooklyn of Tokyo?” could be a useful starting question. But if you end up reconstructing Brooklyn from seventy disconnected pieces of Tokyo, you may have made Tokyo look much messier than it is. That’s a bit like what happened with 4e:55. Through our categories it was cats and cars, and it looked like a mess; it was a V the whole time. An SAE trained on the layer fractures it the same way, splitting the V into a car feature and a cat feature. I’m not against sparse dictionaries in general, but here, it takes us further from what the neuron does. Probes push the first risk further: they can only answer a question we already had, so they can’t teach us which questions to ask. To understand the city, you eventually have to learn its own organization. Higher-level structures like probes and sparse dictionaries can still be useful, but they belong at the end, not the start. Everything of this kind I’ve run breaks down into highly interpretable neurons, as do the changes training makes, including on-policy self-distillation. The neurons cover the abstractions and the data covers the particular cases, so what’s left in between is smaller than people expect, and I’d study it the same way: with a general scientific agent moving between the neurons, data, and groups of both, not a fixed optimization. As Anthropic’s Joshua Batson put it when he read a draft, those missing pieces “will fit into the initial puzzle, rather than being totally randomly splayed on top.” Solving interpretability may share something with achieving AGI: the goalposts move as you get closer. There’s always another weak activation to point to. In Curve Detectors [21] Curve Detectors Cammarata, N., Goh, G., Carter, S., Schubert, L., Petrov, M. and Olah, C., 2020. Distill. References ↓ , we wrote forty pages of experiments on ten neurons precisely to identify at least one sure case of a monosemanticity. Years later, some researchers told me they still doubted any of the examples were monosemantic. We might have missed something, they said, and no one knows how to produce a formal proof. By that standard, it’s overclaiming to say even a single monosemantic neuron exists. Behind doubts about small errors in neurons is a fear that safety will come down to some activation we missed, the place where deception hides. The risk I worry about is different: like being in a well-organized city and not knowing how to think about it, because we aren’t native to it. Every error discussed in this essay was something hiding in plain sight that we didn’t know how to read, or that our tools read incorrectly. None was a hidden activation we missed. Deception might hide from someone reading a model’s outputs, but it has no reason to hide from the model’s own circuitry. It needs to be accessible to its readers, and if we become a reader, it should be accessible to us too. My fear is that deception will be right there, in plain sight, and we won’t know how to read it. Over time, my approach to individual mechanisms has become less focused on this kind of proof, and more holistic. Instead of trying to nail every detail of one neuron, I look around it: what flows into it, what it feeds, how attention moves information to and from it, and what it looks like zoomed in and zoomed out. When I worked on automated interpretability, a neuron firing a few tokens away from its main topic seemed like a big problem. But over time it was clear that attention moves things to reliable places, which then have neurons that activate near the “appropriate token” rather than on it. That’s how understanding has felt to me: less like clearing a bar for each piece and more like a fog-of-war map filling in at several levels at once. Attribution graphs help explain neurons, neurons help explain attention, and attention explains neurons in turn. Neural networks rarely get stuck during training, since in a high dimensional space there’s almost always a way downhill. In my experience, clearing the fog of war works the same way. There’s always another experiment to run, another explanation to narrow, another attribution graph to check, another neuron to watch grow over training. This is why I’ve focused on whether there’s any level of abstraction where things break down, where you stop being able to learn anything and have to take the network apart into something else. I haven’t found one. And when each new motif clears fog in many places at once, perfecting a single neuron probably isn’t the best use of effort. There’s a kind of faith in it: you note something strange, and over time it usually fills in. It isn’t faith all the way down, since almost any explanation can eventually be tested. Just faith that something strange is a good pointer. The V in the car and cat neuron isn’t hard to see – it took me about five seconds, and most people I’ve shown the image grid to and say “what’s the shared pattern here” see it too – but it took believing that the neuron had found something real. For years I’ve heard this neuron come up in almost every discussion of polysemanticity. It was almost always described in reference to neural networks being almost invalid objects of direct natural science. That’s what I was saying too, until I looked more closely. It didn’t take a lot of faith, but it took a little. The little faith is important because the mistakes aren’t symmetric. If you assume a network is clean and you’re wrong, a messy neuron is a lead: you investigate it, and over time normal science sharpens your explanation. If you assume it’s packed, not worth studying directly, and you’re wrong, a messy neuron is the end, because you stop studying it. I made that second assumption for years, and it explained away the evidence that would have overturned it. I could have improved my tools, watched the mixtures keep dissolving, and built up a prior that the neurons could be trusted. Instead, I spent most of a decade figuring out how to look at a model rather than looking at it. For the medium ConvNeXt, the map is mostly filled in. Eight years ago, I would have called that a reasonable solution to interpretability for that model. I can investigate most questions I have about it. Getting there took many small things and a handful of motifs, plus architecture changes the field made anyway, but no interpretability-specific fixing of the network at all. My guess is that frontier networks are where those vision models were eight years ago: legible, but waiting on many small fixes. If we learn to see them properly, follow the noise, and test explanations through many lenses, I think we’ll get there too. We may not have years to do it. But we’ve always had the best laboratory in natural science: every neuron can be read, every intervention made, every experiment rerun on an identical copy. What we did not always have is many automated scientists to work in it, far faster and in far greater numbers than we can. Now we do. They may be able to do in months in frontier language models what took humans most of a decade for vision models. I think the simple story from introductory textbooks is basically right: neurons generalize, work together, and build abstractions over layers. Somewhere along the way we overcomplicated that picture, but looking harder brought it back. If the network isn’t a knot, untangling it can make it look like one. What a Solution Might Look Like We usually imagine ambitious interpretability as an incredibly hard problem, maybe too hard to solve in time to matter. What if it isn’t? The network is enormous, but it may already have done almost all the work of preparing itself to be understood, not for us, but for its own readers. If we can become another reader, it’s ready for us too. The solution might look like a laboratory run by automated scientists who watch the network through training and inference. Each step is simple – labeling neurons, finding motifs and testing them, following data through circuits – and the pieces already exist. Capable agents were built for other work, and modern architectures were chosen because they learn well. Both happen to serve interpretability. Pause Guided by a mechanistic constitution, agents propose and test explanations at many scales, each grounded in individual neurons, and keep, drop, or replace them with better ones. So maybe all we have to do is plug one into the other. Alignment is supposed to be hard too, and it may well be. But the usual arguments assume we can’t see inside models. We assume we get one training setup, and it has to be right in advance. If we can read and understand the system, maybe we can make simple, careful changes instead, like removing an RL environment that turns out to be toxic, without pushing gradients through the very tools we use to see. Each fix might be simple too. There might just be a lot of them. This is the history of deep learning. It may also be the history of understanding and aligning what it builds. Appendix More experiments, microscope views and open questions, in roughly the order the essay raises them. A Note on “Superposition” The word has meant several things. Before Zoom In [4] Zoom In: An Introduction to Circuits Olah, C., Cammarata, N., Schubert, L., Goh, G., Petrov, M. and Carter, S., 2020. Distill. References ↓ , it meant something closer to vector addition, as when word embeddings were described as sums of word senses. Zoom In introduced it to circuits work with a single circuit example, which I found in 2019 and others helped me interpret. The original circuit read turned out to be wrong both because of misunderstanding a generalized pose circuit, and because of reward hacking in feature visualization. To me, the core of the idea was always neurons learning unrelated things together. Toy Models of Superposition [7] Toy Models of Superposition Elhage, N., Hume, T., Olsson, C., et al., 2022. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ later defined superposition as representing more features than dimensions. This makes it a claim about how many features there are, something we can’t yet define or measure. About eight months after that, an informal note [11] Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition Olah, C., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ framed composition and superposition as competing strategies for how features are laid out across neurons, close to our framing but about representation rather than how mechanisms grow. We think this framing is excellent, and it’s closest to the question this essay cares about. But most researchers and agents we’ve talked to still think of superposition mainly as more features than dimensions. 6 For agents, this may come down to a strange accident. The note opens with a large figure embedded directly in the page as base64 image data. Many agents’ web readers hit their length limit inside it, before the argument begins. None of the agents we tried could read past it, as of this writing. No one could have anticipated this in 2023, but it may have shaped how automated researchers understand superposition. That matters here, because the two are quite different claims: ours is about the trade-off, not the count. Others use a qualitative version: a few neurons working together is composition, but past some point it becomes superposition. We view this as an ongoing search for the right question, much like the field’s long struggle to define a feature. Underneath most versions is one question: why aren’t the neurons already good? Why can’t we study the mechanisms directly? Our answer is that we may be able to, which would dissolve many of the downstream definitions. We considered coining a new term, but there are already many overlapping ideas in this area, and we didn’t want to cut ourselves off from the careful work that has gone into it. So we keep the word and say exactly what we mean: neurons learning unrelated things together because they rarely interfere. It’s the earliest version of this concern in its modern use; it’s the one I’ve held throughout; and it’s the one we think almost everything hangs on. Composition also represents far more things than it has neurons, and that’s exactly what we should hope for; the count definition can only exclude it by first settling what counts as a feature. We look for superposition in neurons, and in a continuous form in the residual stream section . We’re explicit about this partly for AI agents, which increasingly do interpretability research. In our experience, they bring their own default reading of the term. On Simulation Scores Simulation scores often end up measuring where attention puts information, which is a question about attention motifs rather than about the neuron. Attention often stores information on commas and other punctuation, as a kind of summarization motif, but exactly how much does it place on each kind of punctuation? A simulator has to care about that a lot, even though it has almost nothing to do with the neuron itself. Simulation also rewards fine details of weak activations that matter little for understanding what a neuron does. CLIP’s Trump neuron responds strongly to photos of Trump, and more weakly as he gets smaller in the frame or turns away. The exact rate at which its activation falls with his size is unimportant for labeling the neuron, but very important for simulating it. Finally, language models are poor at outputting precise activation values even when they understand what’s going on, and they usually aren’t trained for the task. In theory, careful binning could fix some of the fine-detail problems, but neurons differ a lot in their natural thresholds and sparsity, depending on their depth and function. So I’d rather rely on normal science than on any one metric. Simulation might eventually become one useful score among several, but later, once we understand networks well, and probably with simulators trained for the job. But I don’t think they’re a good place to start. Feature Visualization in Later Layers My original circuit interface showed optimized neuron visualizations and the weights between neurons. Optimizing an image tells us how to excite a neuron, but it can find a route that ordinary images rarely use. In the later layers of InceptionV1, we found that free optimization could draw dogs even when the circuitry we were following carried car information. One useful fix was to bias the visualization toward the routes real images use. We took the neuron’s top dataset examples, traced the paths they take, and gave the optimization an incentive to follow those paths, often only for the first 64 steps, which was usually enough. We tried this a bunch of ways and don’t have a canonical best one. Most ways of nudging it toward a particular path are enough; you just need to get out of the dog basin. In the car-circuit comparison in Cars and Animals , four of the car neuron 4c:447’s readers are shown with free optimization and with optimization following natural image paths. Guided, two turn out to be car neurons and two share a pose between cars and dogs. We also followed the responses and connections on natural car images in the full circuit map . Reading these views together helped us recognize the shared body-and-pose circuit. A view of one route is still only part of what a neuron does. Where Adversarial Examples Go Adversarial examples can take ordinary routes through the model. In one ConvNeXt example, an attack makes a triceratops skull register as a jaguar. Six skull-related neurons fall quiet, while inputs used by a real jaguar switch on at roughly a quarter of their usual strength. The attack recruits recognizable parts of the jaguar circuit. A separate InceptionV1 experiment makes this visible. With a larger perturbation budget and an attack that must survive jitter, scale, and rotation, the skull’s frill develops a cat’s face and spotted fur. Nine of ten neurons selected for their responses to real jaguars become much more active than on the clean skull. Only the image changes; the network’s weights stay fixed. Original skull Optimized toward “jaguar” InceptionV1 · perturbation budget 32/255. The attack draws patterns that recruit the model’s existing jaguar neurons. I read this as evidence for the circuit ecology picture: even a nonsensical objective can recruit machinery that already does something useful toward it. The proposed connection to learning is that established routes have a head start in capturing residual error. They already provide ways to change the answer, so optimization can build on them. Memorization and Composition We can look at how Qwen3.6-35B-A3B continues “Once upon a midnight” with “dreary”. Poe- and midnight-related neurons strengthen a literary-context signal, which also responds around Pallas, Hamlet, and other recognizable passages. The later layers read this context to choose the continuation. Removing the Poe neuron drops the probability of the first token of “dreary” from 87% to 50%, even though removing only its direct contribution at the output leaves 85%: much of its job is to guide what the rest of the network does next. The context is assembled before the word. Audits of Attribution Graphs Auditing an attribution graph is hard: neurons can be grouped and reused through motifs, such as shared pose, that their labels alone don’t reveal. We had agents review 100,000 attribution graphs, and I inspected thousands of graphs across images and language. Apparent anomalies usually turned out to be motifs I hadn’t recognized; I haven’t found a substantial group of neurons whose joint activity remained inexplicable. I would update strongly on even one convincing example, but for now I regard this as qualitative evidence—I don’t trust our current tools enough to turn it into a cleanliness score. Explanations That Could Lose The worry that you can explain anything is fair, but a good explanation is specific enough to lose. For 200 random neurons from our gallery, an agent read only each neuron’s explanation and wrote five new examples that should drive it and five near misses that shouldn’t, before we measured any of them. Among the 183 whose explanations describe their positive side, the new examples fired their neurons strongly 76% of the time; the near misses, 11%. Reading only a neuron’s explanation, an agent wrote five new examples that should drive it and five near misses that shouldn’t. Responses are a share of the neuron’s strongest example in the corpus; a strong response is 30% or more. Positive controls are one of many tools for criticizing an explanation of a neuron, and our forthcoming paper has many more prediction metrics and positive controls. But we’re mostly not trying to claim a perfect explanation of each neuron here. We’re interested in why things form together, and how many neurons are broadly legible. Near misses ask a different question: as a branch grows, can you draw the boundaries of where it grew? That’s interesting, but it isn’t the question superposition raises. A neuron in superposition that’s just X or Y would do fantastically on near misses, since they’re neither X nor Y. Superposition would want something unrelated, very far apart, not a small difference from a neighbor. So we also had the agent invent the most distant concept it could, the kind of thing a network could pack in without interference, and write five texts for it. While this isn’t exactly the same as what superposition would do (depending on the exact definition, or the expected phenomenology, since there are several of each), we think it’s pretty close to what the cat-and-car neuron was thought to have been doing: two totally different things together, grouped only because they’re so different. We think this is a reasonably coherent test for that phenomenology. Those texts fired their neurons strongly about 1% of the time, and 179 of the 183 neurons never fired on them at all. In mixture-of-experts models this kind of packing is arguably almost impossible anyway, since tokens that far apart aren’t even sent to the same expert (see the expert map ). Whether something is generalization or superposition has more to do with why its things are together in the first place than with whether you can tell it apart from a control. So what matters more here is looking qualitatively at the most important canonical examples, and getting a sense for what kinds of things neurons form and what their activation ranges look like. Edge Featurizers We’re particularly excited about edge motifs: recurring patterns of connections in attribution graphs. If neurons make distinctions, these motifs map how one distinction feeds another. Factoring 25,000 ImageNet attribution graphs gave us connected circuits of ordinary neurons, such as the teapot circuit below. These motifs also predicted where ablation would matter much better than comparable groupings of activations: removing their neurons caused more damage on the images that used them. That makes connections a promising level of abstraction—one we can zoom out from, while still following every part back to the original network. Why Networks Generalize There’s no one standard explanation for why neural networks generalize, but most accounts come down to shared patterns: show the network six dogs, and it finds what they have in common. The problem is that a network never sees a group. It sees one example at a time, in small batches, and in principle it could memorize every one; that would be fine for its loss. When I asked researchers at frontier labs, several told me they weren’t sure. A common guess was that a network memorizes first and generalizes in a second pass. Our answer is that it starts generalizing from the very first step. 7 This fits what Arpit and colleagues (2017) saw when they mixed random labels into real data: networks learned the real patterns first and fit the noise later. It’s also close to Satrajit Chatterjee’s coherent gradients (2020): updates from similar examples add up, so changes that help many examples at once grow fastest. In the circuit ecology picture, generalization and composition are the winning learning strategy because they’re the fastest: circuits race to capture the remaining error, and the ones that reuse what’s already there, and can be reused in turn, outcompete the rest. Generalization is what’s left from the victor. Ends up with what’s shared ? first later Describes the end, not the steps Memorize, then generalize first later Stores each dog, merges later Generalize from the first step first later Grows one feature, dog by dog Replay Three stories of why networks generalize. The usual ones describe where training ends up, or assume it memorizes first; we think a broad feature starts winning from the very first example. Here’s how we picture it. Train a blank network on a single photo of a Labrador retriever, and imagine two circuits competing to explain it. One looks for something exact: if pixel 322 is this color, say Labrador. The other looks for something broad, like green grass or tan fur. The broad one fires on more of the image, so on the very next step it gets more of the learning signal. It grows faster, captures more of the remaining error, and leaves the pixel circuit less and less to learn from, until it starves. After that it’s rich-get-richer: the next image with grass in it starts with the green circuit already partly on. Labrador error green pixel 322 A blank network sees one Labrador. Petri dishes are enormously useful, as long as they keep the process you’re trying to study. One of ours extends TensorFlow Playground so you can watch several tasks share hidden neurons. In one run, two neurons learned to respond along opposite diagonals, and the network combined them one way for a circle and another for four corners. We didn’t expect that solution; it was clever. The two last-layer neurons respond along opposite diagonals, and each task reads them with its own weights (blue positive, orange negative). This is the original playground run, retrained live in your browser. You could call the circle and the four corners two features packed across the same neurons. That’s true, but it misses what the model did: it found geometry it could reuse for both. Looking at the neurons made that visible, and that’s the test I want an explanation to pass: does it show the computation the model actually learned? The best-studied petri dish is Toy Models of Superposition. It’s careful work, the kind our field should aspire to, and we found no problems with its experiments. But it pictures a network as a fixed number of neurons and a set of predefined features, and asks how the features get fit in. That prices the cost of sharing a neuron, interference, but not the benefit, reuse. In its reconstruction task every feature is an end in itself, and nothing downstream builds on what two features share. In a real network, a representation matters only through what reads it, and there are no predefined features: everything is grown, and defined by what uses it. The reuse argument also says where I’d look for packing: memories that really are ends in themselves, related to nothing else. That’s the toy’s world, and there it does pack, just as the paper found. So I don’t think we disagree with the paper about the toy’s world. The question is which world real networks are in: how much structure their data has, relative to what the model has room to store. In real data almost nothing is related to nothing. The same goes for the long tail of facts in language: a rare person still has a country, a job and a name. Even a photo with a nonsense label has parts the network already knows, as with the umbrella we taught to be a bee. What’s left is input with no structure at all, like pure noise with random labels. Networks can learn even that, as Zhang and colleagues showed [25] Understanding Deep Learning Requires Rethinking Generalization Zhang, C., Bengio, S., Hardt, M., Recht, B. and Vinyals, O., 2017. ICLR. References ↓ , though it’s slower than learning real data, and even then our model borrowed a little from textures it already knew. Toy Models of Superposition’s main setup squeezes many independent features into a few dimensions and copies them back out, with no hidden neurons for anything to grow on. Its other experiments study correlated features and models with hidden neurons, but separately. When we put correlated inputs and hidden neurons in one model, related inputs grew onto the neurons. Making inputs fire more often pushed the toy toward what the paper calls “PCA-like” solutions, combining related inputs into shared representations. More on Circuit Ecology Our findings don’t depend on knowing why generalization and composition keep winning, but we have a guess: they win a race. A region of the network that already has useful parts and readers can learn the next related thing faster than anything starting fresh, so it takes the error signal before a competitor can grow. Offshoots look like the same race, a bit of error picked up by the neuron that was already closest. We think the same head start is where recursive generalization comes from. A neuron that fires on “iy” is already on for “diy,” so it’s first in line to pick up “do it yourself,” which means the same thing but has no “iy” in it. Recursive generalization is what a niche looks like at its edges. A new computation doesn’t necessarily need its own neuron. It can begin as a local extension or composition of existing machinery, like the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee”: switching routes may be the smallest developmental distance, so it could capture the error before a new, separate mechanism gets started. We suspect that consolidation into a distinct neuron becomes especially useful when other computations need to build on it. A car neuron provides a reusable judgment and a sheltered place for taxis, ambulances, and other specialists to develop. Part of it is buildability. An obscure combination of unrelated neurons may be a poor place for that development. It may have weak activation paths, conflicting gradients, and little useful machinery to inherit. Its competitor isn’t just a dedicated neuron; it’s ordinary composition within a region already suited to the task. We saw something like this when we tried to build a packed code into InceptionV1 by hand, modeled on what we once thought its car → dogs → car circuit was doing. We expected installing it to be easy and keeping it to be hard. Instead, small mismatches added enough interference that the code often never worked, and when it did, the network usually came to rely on it less, though some persisted. Part of the trouble is that neurons aren’t really for copying; they’re for computing distinctions. Seeing how hard packing was to form at all was part of what moved us toward a developmental answer. Gradient descent is a much better fine-tuner than we are, so this isn’t enough evidence on its own, but even gradient descent didn’t use packing in the circuit we were copying. Unresolved Responses One InceptionV1 neuron collects a pinched-center shape: bow ties, butterflies, swimsuit tops. But it also picks up things that go with them, men’s dress shoes with the bow ties and beach bags and flip-flops with the swimsuit tops, since they share neurons in earlier layers. A Note on Features and Definitions Part of my difficulty discussing superposition is that “feature” can mean something we care about, something the neural network has learned as a building block, or some mixture of the two. These are different claims. A useful human description isn’t necessarily a fundamental unit of the model. Looking at mechanisms, we already find many motifs that don’t translate neatly into anything we expected. If the network has more fundamental units, we shouldn’t assume their boundaries match ours either. Features have often made things harder for us to think about. Are cars and cats inside the V neuron two different features within another V feature? Or did cars and cats stop being features when we recognized the V? Without an account of what these units are, it’s hard to know whether we’ve discovered something about the network or changed how we describe it. In conversations, I’ve found people much less committed to a particular account of features than to superposition. But if features are useful descriptions rather than fundamental units, a claim about how many there are depends on which descriptions we choose. I’m now fairly skeptical of working in terms of features at all. That doesn’t settle whether arbitrary packing occurs, but it makes the feature-count framing difficult to use. Maybe features are right anyway. It makes sense to think of cities in terms of districts, and I’m all for thinking in terms of groups of mechanisms. But the word is tainted, because by now it means too many things: we can’t use it for a district of neurons without people hearing either fundamental features or dictionary entries. If this picture is right, I suspect we’ll need more specific, harder-to-vary words going forward. Monosemantic and polysemantic may not be quite the right words either. A kidney filters waste, balances salt and water, helps set blood pressure and tells the bone marrow to make red blood cells, and nobody asks whether it’s mono-organic. We ask what we understand about it, what’s still open, and how organized it is. There’s also a distinction between a claim about representation and a claim about organization.
