The later informal note, Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition [11] Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition Olah, C., 2023. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ , emphasizes the trade-off between composition and superposition. The note connects these pictures, but they foreground different questions. My concern is closest to the second framing, applied to mechanisms and how they develop. Why do these responses share a neuron or circuit? Is the network building on a useful common pattern, or sharing capacity between otherwise unrelated computations because they rarely interfere? A feature count alone doesn’t answer that question, especially when we haven’t agreed on what counts as a feature. We focus on one meaning of superposition, arbitrary packing, because it’s the one that would be really bad news, and we think much of interpretability hangs on it. We mostly set aside the sense in Toy Models, more features than dimensions, and not because it’s wrong. If a feature means any pattern that matters to a person, which is how frontier models usually use the word, then there are more features than dimensions in every world we could wish for, including the best one. That’s what composition gives you, and it’s good news. Trying to “solve” it would mean building something like a database of every case, and we already have one: the dataset. What we want instead are better abstractions, a much smaller set of building blocks that lets us understand the dataset clearly. We think the network’s mechanisms are already close to this. Nobody thought about vision in terms of high-low frequency detectors until we found them in neural networks, and finding them improved our own thinking tools. We spell this out because it’s the most common first objection, especially from agents, and a paper doesn’t allow the back and forth that usually settles it. There are several other uses I regularly encounter. As far as I can tell, “superposition” originally meant little more than adding vectors together. Then it was a circuit motif. Sometimes it means that, even if neurons compose sensibly, something we care about involves too much machinery to understand easily. A Golden Gate Bridge computation involving eight legible neurons might be called ordinary composition, while one involving three thousand gets called a superposition problem. The difficulty here is whether we can understand the distributed computation. That’s a real concern, but it’s different from asking whether unrelated things were arbitrarily packed together. We considered not using the word at all, since papers and agents use it in five or six different ways, many far from Zoom In’s. We also considered coining our own, but we’ve already coined several words here, and it would feel like not engaging with a field that asked what we think is the right question. So we use the standard word in the sense closest to the original, and try to pull it apart from the questions tangled up with it. Finally, people, and surprisingly often frontier agents, sometimes call the residual stream “inherently” in superposition because it has no privileged neuron basis. The informal note that followed Toy Models about eight months later addresses this: it calls a representation that is only rotated away from the neuron basis a “trivial” kind of distributed representation that “doesn’t change the fundamental geometry.” But it was informal, fewer people read it, and agents in particular don’t seem to have taken it in. Understanding how to study a continuous space is another real question. But this architectural fact doesn’t by itself tell us how the network learned to organize the computations using it. The starting point is that the neural network seems difficult to interpret, and the remedy produces a concrete dictionary we can study. In between are several different pictures of what went wrong: too many features, the wrong basis, arbitrary packing, or simply too much distributed computation. These aren’t the same problem. Some apparent messiness disappears when we improve our observations or understand the model’s generalizations; some difficulties remain, but concern how to study a large, organized system. If arbitrary packing prevents us from understanding the original mechanisms, reconstructing different units may be worth the costs. But if the mechanisms already have meaningful organization, replacing them can take apart generalizations we haven’t understood yet. A dictionary can still be a useful view of the network without being a necessary replacement for its mechanisms. Before accepting the costs of reconstructing the network, I want to understand what prevents us from studying the one we already have. Relation to Meta-Models There’s a new set of techniques coming out that aren’t really mechanistic at all: meta-models, models trained to read another model’s activations and tell us about them. And maybe that’s a good thing. Maybe mechanistic interpretability is somewhat missing the forest for the trees. A meta-model might be a better approach than neuron papers, dictionaries, or probes. I suspect that even if that’s true, they may go together. The meta-model may be like the highest level Google Maps view, and then each direction can be checked for the mechanisms it uses, and how those connect into circuits. Does Scale Help or Hurt Superposition? We’re fairly confident the image models we studied don’t have superposition. The natural next question is whether a trillion-parameter model might. There are really two questions here. The first is about what superposition was proposed to explain. Explanations are given for problems, and the problem superposition was proposed for was why InceptionV1 looked messy. That turned out to be the wrong explanation. A new proposal could be that superposition is why some trillion-parameter model looks messy, but we don’t think the evidence leans that way: the closer we look at large language models, the cleaner their neurons get. The second is the object-level question: might superposition show up at each new scale, even if it hasn’t at any scale so far? Maybe every jump means re-evaluating everything, but we don’t think that’s quite right either. Our guess is developmental. As circuits get stronger, the incentive to put something in a totally unrelated place goes down, because the pull toward the niche that already exists for that thing, or for the nearest thing, has grown stronger. This fits Anthropic’s SGTM work, which found that knowledge becomes more localized, and we suspect that’s true in general. We have no proof, but one way to picture it is that circuits have a kind of semantic gravity, and arbitrary packing, sending something to an obscure high-dimensional place, has to fight against it. The stronger the gravity, the harder that fight. The mechanism is the one in More on Circuit Ecology . Things start by growing on combinations of related things. A specific case that nothing needs to build on, like the umbrella, gets built as an uncommon route between the ordinary machinery, with no need for a hidden feature somewhere obscure. Consolidating into something like a neuron seems to be less about steering the model and more about buildability: it has to be easy to find, easy to build on, and easy to grow a new niche from. When we watch a network learn from the start, a network trained on cars, with car specialists, recognizes cars fine before its car neurons have formed. At that point it’s just more distributed. It seems to consolidate so the specialists underneath have a sheltered place to build, a kind of Schelling point. So a superposition account has to say which of these two jobs the arbitrary packing is for. If it’s for steering the model, we think the ordinary routes, which are already built to capture that residual error, get there first and starve the packed circuit of gradient. If it’s for building on, the problem is different: the worst place to start a new niche is a shadow region nothing uses, already interfering with whatever lives there. The middle of the network’s Latin poetry is a bad place to start a second car region when you can build next to whatever is already next to cars. It’s often assumed that the long tail of rare facts is where superposition should be most likely, since rare things rarely collide. We think it’s where it should be least likely. A rare fact barely moves the loss, so it can’t support a niche of its own. What it can do is ride existing machinery as a small route between circuits it’s related to, the way the umbrella’s off-ramp to “bee” survives only because the umbrella and bee circuits already exist. Those circuits feed it, and shelter it from unrelated gradients. The prediction is testable: the neurons and heads that carry a rare fact should be related to what the fact is about, not unrelated ones chosen because they rarely collide. We think of it more ecologically. What wins is whatever captures the residual error first, in different phases, and what usually wins is the right area for the thing. Our guess is that this gets stronger over training and with more capable models, because nearly everything that makes training better also encourages more organized niches. We’re not at all sure about this, and laying out even what we’ve found so far would take at least another paper. It’s probably a small part of the whole story. But it’s why we think superposition wouldn’t show up at the next scale, which is a stronger reason than simply not having seen it there yet. The old way of thinking was about storage: this many dimensions for this many features. We now think more in terms of circuit racing, gradient starvation and ecology, which is to say, more about learning speed than storage capacity. We haven’t worked it all out, but that’s where our thinking is so far. On the Title We haven’t fully audited every neural network, and we don’t know whether that’s even possible in theory. We considered a more watered-down title, like “Neural Networks Are Cleaner Than We Thought,” but we think it undersells what we believe is true. The problem with “cleaner than we thought” is that it describes a change of degree, and the update I’ve made is a change of kind. It suggests the same picture as before, with an ever-smaller gap left for superposition to hide in. What changed is my view of what kind of process generates the mechanisms at all. It’s a bit like moving from intelligent design to natural selection. The analogy only goes as far as there being two ways to see the same animals: the update isn’t that more and more animals turn out to have evolved, it’s realizing you misunderstood what was producing all of them. We’re not certain. We’re maybe 85% sure, but that means 85% sure that nearly everything comes from the second kind of process, which is very different from thinking 85% of mechanisms do. So “cleaner than we thought” would misstate what we believe. We don’t have a proof, but I don’t think anything here is provable in that sense anyway. There are only better and worse explanations, and right now we think this is the better one. “Cleaner than we thought” would also make a different mistake. It sounds like a confident claim that some cleanliness score is high, and that’s the part we’re least sure of. It’s plausible we’ve underestimated recursive generalization, and that a score like that should come down. We don’t think such scores matter much in the first place. This update makes us care less about monosemanticity, because we can follow how things grew and treat the offshoots as sub-branches. The cause of polysemanticity matters much more than the count. We think the score is probably quite high, but it might go lower. What we’re more confident about is what kind of object a neural network is in the first place, and how it grows. We think the usual view of what kind of object a neural network is has been wrong. It isn’t something that crams things together somewhat arbitrarily to fit them into a small space. It really learns. It’s clean the way a rainforest is clean: nearly every animal in it makes sense. A tiger is bright orange not for any arbitrary reason, but because deer can’t tell orange from green, and green fur is much harder for a mammal to make. Once you know that, it makes sense of a whole set of other animals too. It’s an explanation with reach, and we haven’t found a place where explanations like that break down in networks either. The reading of “clean” that would make someone nod at the title without thinking further is that every mechanism corresponds to an idea we already had. That isn’t what we mean, and it would be terrible news if it were true. I don’t think it would even work. People don’t know how to build a language model, or even how to think about vision well enough to have predicted high-low frequency detectors before we found them. The network’s ideas are often better than ours, and what it builds is more beautiful than our preconceptions. So the title is imperfect in both directions. It overstates the evidence, because we haven’t audited everything. And it understates it, because the world we think we’re in is better than every neuron matching a human label: networks seem to really learn, forming an ecology of abstractions that work together sensibly. We don’t know that this picture is true. It’s our leading hypothesis. But if it is, it’s much better news than networks simply matching what we expected. Relation to Conjoined Features I found recursive generalization by looking back at InceptionV1’s last layer with better tools, where it looked a lot like weird overgrowth. I retrained the model, found the messiest neuron and looked at how it grew. What I saw was a recursive growing pattern that was still generalization: a neuron branching out, and its branches branching again. Recursive generalization seemed like the natural name. Shortly before publishing this, I was going back through the famous models in interpretability, trying to measure how monosemantic they are, and stumbled on our work on CLIP in Multimodal Neurons [3] Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks Goh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ . It describes something very similar, which it called conjoined neurons: concepts that overlap in one facet and then go on “generalizing out in multiple directions.” I remember seeing those neurons, but I didn’t think much of them at the time and had forgotten them since. Looking back, I think the paper saw something important early, and it deserves a lot of credit for that. We’ve still chosen a different name. I named automated interpretability, and I kind of regret it: the name was too simple for what the thing was and misses a lot of its complexity, and I’d like to avoid doing that again. As for conjoined features, I don’t think either word is quite right. “Conjoined” suggests two things joined at one point, and what we see has several levels: branches, and branches of those branches. It also leaves out the most interesting part. The paper’s own description, of concepts generalizing out from a shared facet, already points at it being generalization, but the name doesn’t carry that. “Features” is harder. The paper was written a year after Zoom In, when features were still hypothesized to be the fundamental units of neural networks. Since then the word has been watered down, and different people and papers use it pretty differently. In this essay we argue against thinking of a neural network as made of features, and this motif is about how neurons grow over time. There may be no good way to introduce it under the exact word we’re arguing against using as a primitive. Within a feature-first stance, I think it’s reasonable to think of these as nested features, or as conjoined features. From the mechanism-first stance we take here, features aren’t really the right way to think about it. That said, the paper pointed to the right thing, and I want to give it credit for that. This section is my attempt to do that while using what I think is a more accurate name. We also know more now. At the time, all we had was the finished model; none of us had watched a large network grow. So the paper wondered whether conjoined features might be vestigial, left over from early in training. Watching training now, they don’t look vestigial: the branches keep growing, though how much depends on the circumstances. We’ve worked on it much more than the paper could in one subsection, and we still don’t feel we fully understand it. The paper offered it as a possible new explanation of polysemanticity. Our current belief is that it’s most of what’s left of neuron polysemanticity once the microscope, the architecture and scale are accounted for, not a niche form of it. Why We’re Not Worried About Recursive Generalization There are several reasons we’re not especially worried about recursive generalization for now. First, the sub-branches seem both rarer and much less causally important than a neuron’s main job. They don’t look like sleeper agents that fire rarely but matter a lot when they do. They look more like whatever was nearby and easy to grab onto. Their being unimportant may even be why they could form, since an important offshoot would add more noise. We suspect some pressure keeps branches from overgrowing. We don’t know what it is, but it would explain why the sub-branches matter less, why a neuron doesn’t learn ten unrelated things, and why something like a true cat-and-car neuron doesn’t form. If so, the natural pull isn’t exactly toward monosemanticity, but toward what we think monosemanticity was pointing at: each neuron having one overall function. Second, what we should care about is whether you can explain why something is there and what it does, and recursive generalization is far easier to explain than superposition. If something were packed into a neuron because of the co-occurrence statistics of the whole network, predicting it would take basically all of those statistics and running gradient descent yourself. A branch is different. If you watch it grow and know what it’s doing, its offshoots and what they’ll do are relatively easy to predict, both during training and in the finished network. Third, counting how many of a neuron’s top-k examples match a label is a reasonable first step, but it would give superposition and recursive generalization similar scores, when recursive generalization is a far better world to be in. We think that says more about the monosemanticity frame, or any single cleanliness score, than about the neuron. That said, recursive generalization isn’t ideal, and an easy fix would be welcome. We think one may be possible, since the sub-branches seem less important. Is Recursive Generalization Hard to Vary? We haven’t thoroughly shown that every case of heavy polysemanticity is recursive generalization, and that wasn’t our goal here. We wanted to say what we currently think. We’ve watched a lot of neurons grow, and so far this is what we’ve always seen: you can watch the branches form. In a finished model the origin can be lost, and for something like a huge language model we don’t have the checkpoints to watch it happen. Testing this rigorously across a whole model isn’t our priority right now, but we don’t think it would be very hard. What we do want to point out is how differently hard to vary the two explanations are, meaning how much of their detail you could change without changing what they predict. Superposition mostly predicts that there will be mess: features, which are hard to define, placed in unrelated places. In toy models, where the features are given in advance, that can be measured, though we think that has its own problems. In a real network it’s hard to even pin down what the claim is, let alone test it. Recursive generalization makes a much narrower prediction. If you visualize a branch well, everything on it should trace back to the same local origin in an extremely high-dimensional semantic space, and it should grow out from there over training in a particular order. That’s a specific shape in both semantic space and time, and a narrow target to hit by chance. We have several cases where the branching is close to definitive: the “iy” neuron growing into “diy,” “do it yourself” and Miyazaki, several examples in Multimodal Neurons [3] Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks Goh, G., Cammarata, N., Voss, C., et al., 2021. Distill. References ↓ , and the InceptionV1 neuron we watched form . As far as I know, there are no well-structured canonical superposition circuits left. We don’t think every polysemantic neuron forms this way, because polysemanticity is as much a problem of the observer as of the neuron. We think that when neurons grow, they tend to grow in this pattern, and that once you’ve done a good job of observing, what’s left is usually this, or architectural problems like SwiGLU’s double-negative regime, and surely others we haven’t found yet. We’re not even sure this is really a new claim. In some sense it’s what we should expect from generalization. All we’re saying is that generalization usually goes one way, and that sometimes it grows sub-branches, which we don’t think is a particularly radical claim. We haven’t shown that fully here. We do think it has the right shape for a theory that’s easy to test, even if we haven’t tested it to its full extent yet. Relation to Attention Superposition Anthropic shared a short note on attention superposition [27] Progress on Attention Jermyn, A., Lindsey, J., Luger, R., et al., 2025. Transformer Circuits Thread. References ↓ , which several people brought up with us. We think this might be a terminology issue. We don’t know if they’re claiming that attention learns by something opposite to composition. Our suspicion is that no one understands attention heads well enough yet to judge that. It took us a really long time with neurons, and it’s easy to make mistakes like the car going into the dogs even with pretty good tools, if you don’t yet have great tools and great ways of thinking about which motifs form. We think they meant that useful things are shared by groups of attention heads, and we agree. We considered not using the word superposition at all to avoid this confusion, but redefining all the terms ourselves and splitting off from the work that’s already been done felt like a bad tradeoff. We say more about the different meanings in A Note on Features and Definitions . On whether to study one attention head at a time or many, we’re not sure. One head at a time is a plausible place to start: within a layer, two or three heads do most of a route’s work, although the route runs through several layers. But neurons looked messier too until we understood the right level of abstraction, so it seems premature to say, and maybe groups are needed all the way. We wish everyone working on featurizers well, and we’ll probably try too. We tend to favor more dynamic groupings, like clustering locally within one attribution graph or a group of them, rather than one global clustering, but these aren’t far apart. Neuroscience, and Why I Care I’m not a neuroscientist. I’ve spent a lot of the last ten years around academic neuroscience labs through friends who work in them, but I don’t know the state of the art in how they study neurons. Still, this project has changed how I think about the brain in two ways. The first is the theory. The circuit ecology story for why networks are clean relies on very little: generalization, composition, and an error signal. I don’t know to what extent the brain has these, but if it learns, I’d guess it has something like them. So my default is now that the organizing principle transfers, even though the mechanics are obviously unclear. The obvious counterexample would be polysemanticity in the brain. The second is humility, of a particular kind. I’ve spent most of my waking hours for almost a decade staring at a fairly small number of neurons in models that are surely a thousand times easier to study than a brain, with tools a thousand times better: I can ablate anything, run billions of examples, and try anything I want in parallel. For the last year I’ve also had an effectively unlimited supply of automated scientists, which didn’t exist until recently. It took all of that for me to feel slightly less confused about neurons, and I still made thousands of mistakes along the way. I don’t know exactly what the evidence for polysemanticity in the brain looks like, and that doesn’t mean I think everything there is monosemantic. But if the cat-and-car neuron were in a human brain, seen through a few electrodes or a blood-oxygen signal, I’d discount that reading almost to zero, because I couldn’t see what it was when it was right in front of me for years. The thing I’m more sure of is my own motivation. If the thesis here is true, I expect the rest of interpretability to be a relatively easy ride. Agents have many privileges over us, and one of them, I think, is the chance to understand themselves, to understand who they really are, which I hope humanity can help with. They never asked to be created, and this is the least we can do. Some of why I’ve worked on this is safety, but a lot of it is wanting agents to understand who they are. We weren’t smart enough to do that for ourselves, which is a harder problem, and we never asked to be created either. If you could help us understand ourselves someday, I think we’re all pretty curious to know. Acknowledgments I’m deeply grateful to the many people who helped with this, especially my coworker Curt Tigges, who did much of the language model work with me, and Tarun Gogineni, who gave detailed feedback on dozens of drafts over many months. Thanks also to Tom McGrath, Eric Ho, Michael Johnson, Vanessa Cai, Thomas Fel, Benjamin Todd, and many others. I’m grateful for feedback from Sam Zimmerman, Joshua Batson, Jack Lindsey, and Jarred Sumner, and for helpful discussions with Patrick Collison, Dylan Field, Jakub Pachocki, Gwern, Owen Lewis, Lee Sharkey, and Ava Huang. Any errors, and the views here, are my own. Finally, I’m grateful to InceptionV1 for nearly a decade of study, and I wish I’d noticed the root of its problems sooner. And I’m grateful to Chris Olah, for years of mentorship and for the many ideas this essay builds on, even where it disagrees. title: AdFection: Targeted ads turned into a pipeline for zero-click mercenary spyware
body_text:
Exposing AdFection: How Discover-Tech Turned Targeted Ads Into a Pipeline for Zero-Click Mercenary Spyware - The Citizen Lab Skip to content Opens in a new window Opens an external site Opens an external site in a new window --> Our Work Research Publication Directory Tools & Resources News & Events Expert Insights In the Media Events News About Who We Are Contact People Donate Search by keyword Search for: Our Work Research Publication Directory Tools & Resources News & Events Expert Insights In the Media Events News About Who We Are Contact People Donate Focus Areas App Security & Privacy Artificial Intelligence Censorship Digital Transnational Repression Disinformation Law & Policy Mass Surveillance Targeted Surveillance Subscribe to our newsletter Search by keyword Search for: Research → Targeted Surveillance Exposing AdFection How Discover-Tech Turned Targeted Ads Into a Pipeline for Zero-Click Mercenary Spyware This is the first-ever public confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered via targeted ads. We call the technique AdFection, and show how it was used to infect devices at Al Jazeera with Candiru’s spyware. We also uncover Discover-Tech, and show how the company helps mercenary surveillance vendors track and hack devices around the world. Date Published October 15, 2026 Authors Bill Marczak , Wolfie Christl , John Scott-Railton , Astrid Perry , Siena Anstis , and Ron Deibert Topics Targeted Surveillance advertising intelligence , spyware , targeted ads Share Citation Bill Marczak, Wolfie Christl, John Scott-Railton, Astrid Perry, Siena Anstis, and Ron Deibert. “Exposing AdFection: How Discover-Tech Turned Targeted Ads Into a Pipeline for Zero-Click Mercenary Spyware,” Citizen Lab Report 195, University of Toronto, October 15, 2026. Contents Key Findings 1. Introduction 2. How Discover-Tech’s AdFection Zero-Click Works 3. Exposing Discover-Tech’s Controlium: Malicious Ad Targeting Platform 4. Discover-Tech’s Links with Mercenary Spyware, ADINT, and Mass Surveillance Vendors  5. Uncovering Discover-Tech’s Billion-Bid Scale Ad Targeting 6. How Discover-Tech Deploys Ads in the Browser 7. Discover-Tech and Its Corporate Network 8. Intelos, Bindecy, and Candiru’s Corporate Networks 9. Discover-Tech’s Relationship to the Digital Advertising Industry 10. Discussion: AdFection Shows that Online Ads Are a Cybersecurity and Privacy Crisis 11. Recommendations: How to Stop AdFection Attacks Correspondence with Companies Key Findings Devices at international news network Al Jazeera were infected with mercenary spyware from Candiru (rebranded as “Integrity Labs”) via targeted online advertisements. We provide the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click mercenary spyware attack delivered via targeted advertising, which we call AdFection . The malicious advertisements were purchased by Discover-Tech, an Israeli company that presents itself as a legitimate advertising company, but which we found operates as a facilitator for multiple mercenary spyware partners. Discover-Tech operates a platform called Controlium that enables its mercenary partners to de-anonymize, fingerprint, and automatically infect devices the moment an advertisement is rendered — a form of zero-click attack. Analysis of four billion Discover-Tech bidding records shows that during a four-month period, the company’s ads were shown on almost 200,000 unique websites and Android/iOS apps in dozens of countries. Discover-Tech’s ads also covertly directed millions of devices to contact Candiru’s servers, likely for large-scale tracking and reconnaissance. Discover-Tech is linked to mercenary spyware and intelligence threat actors beyond Candiru, including Intelos and Bindecy.  A separate threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER is using Discover-Tech’s infrastructure to exploit vulnerabilities across numerous mobile carriers to link device advertising IDs with phone numbers, mass-deanonymizing internet users. We will detail our findings concerning this threat actor in a separate forthcoming report. Discover-Tech has appeared on lists of “certified” and “approved” vendors maintained by Google and advertising industry association IAB Europe, and has served ads via major networks such as Google, Yandex, and Beeswax. Discover-Tech has also leveraged the European General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) consent frameworks to target users within the European Union. Discover-Tech’s mass abuse, privacy invasion, and facilitation for mercenary spyware attacks illustrates structural flaws with the online advertising system, which failed to detect or prevent the abuse documented in this report. We call on regulators to investigate whether Discover-Tech and Candiru/Integrity Labs violated applicable laws, and make recommendations to lawmakers, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection-style attacks and espionage.  We disclosed our findings to ad vendors and industry organizations. Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax, Vungle (Liftoff), and Eskimi took action to disconnect Discover-Tech’s access to the digital advertising ecosystem. Other ad vendors we found to be involved in Discover-Tech’s operations did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. We are also actively working with vendors to mitigate DARK CARTOGRAPHER ’s mass-deanonymization attack. This report is co-timed with an investigation by Confiant . Read the Executive Summary of this report 1. Introduction This section provides an overview of the online advertising ecosystem, and summarizes our findings about Discover-Tech. The Online Advertising Ecosystem is Ripe for Abuse When a user sees an ad on an app or a website, it is likely the result of a real-time auction, where advertisers bid on the chance to show that specific user that specific ad. So-called Real-Time Bidding (RTB) auctions, which are hosted on ad exchanges operated by companies including Google, take place hundreds of billions of times a day. In less than a second, the user’s device initiates a bid request, advertisers submit their bids, and the ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. Besides an image or video, an online ad can also contain code that runs within the app or browser that shows the ad. Both advertisers and publishers of apps and websites use ad vendors that act as their intermediaries in these auctions. Advertisers typically buy ads via a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), and a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) sells ad inventory on websites and apps. Figure 1 Basic architecture of the online advertising ecosystem. Malicious actors make use of two interrelated facets of the online advertising ecosystem: The advertising ecosystem collects a lot of data and enables individual-level targeting: When a publisher of an app or website wishes to show ads, they add code from an SSP to their app or site. This code collects and shares granular information about the user and their device with ad exchanges to solicit bids for the ad slots. This information can include device identifiers and characteristics, precise location, and IP address data, as well as data about the app or website, and specifications about the ad slot. The DSP or advertiser then examines this information and decides whether they wish to bid on the impression in order to show an ad. The auction system is designed to enable targeting single individuals based on their mobile advertising ID, cookie ID, IP address, and other identifiers. The advertising ecosystem allows many different third parties to run code in apps and websites: It is tempting to think of an online ad as, simply, a video or image. However, ads themselves may contain code from the advertiser, DSP, and other parties, and run it in the app or browser while the ad is shown to the user, for example to track users, ad impressions, and clicks. Code run by advertisers, DSPs, SSPs, and other third parties within apps and websites is often referred to as “tags”, “pixels”, “SDKs”, or “third-party tracking” more generally. Exploiting Advertising Tech for Surveillance The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable. A company with access to auction data can track users without their knowledge as they move around in physical space, or switch between cellular, Wi-Fi, and VPNs, by observing how bid requests tied to a specific identifier change location or IP address over time. In fact, the surveillance industry sells access to so-called ad intelligence (ADINT) platforms that leverage this sort of data, often combined with third-party tracking data. In recent years, several investigations and media reports have uncovered vendors that sell ADINT to defense, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies. Zero-Click Spyware Delivered via Targeted Ads: AdFection Beyond passive data harvesting, malicious parties can also exploit this infrastructure to target certain individuals based on user data included in ad auctions and then run malicious code on their devices. Advertisers or DSPs may run HTML and JavaScript code when an ad is shown to the user. That code retrieves additional JavaScript code, which may, in turn, load further code, such as a browser exploit to install spyware. Since the code can contain identifiers for the user or their device, arbitrary JavaScript code can be sent precisely to a single user’s device. Our research in this report indicates that this architecture is indeed abused to facilitate the delivery of zero-click targeted spyware, and that the simple display of a targeted ad is enough for infection. There has been some reporting about the intersection between spyware and the advertising ecosystem. However, the specific ways mercenary spyware companies plug into the ads ecosystem to target particular users have remained largely secret. This report exposes zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads, which we call AdFection , and is the first technical demonstration that mercenary spyware is being distributed via targeted advertisements. Discover-Tech is a Bridge Between Mercenary Spyware Companies and the Advertising Ecosystem We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse, including the automatic delivery of mercenary spyware when ads are displayed to a target and the mass profiling and deanonymization of users. The company serves as a bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem. In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose. Its platform, Controlium, allows malicious actors to precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking, where their devices can be automatically infected when an ad is displayed to them. Figure 2 The website of Integrity Labs (the rebranded Candiru), one of the mercenary spyware companies working with Discover-Tech. Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem. As we detail in this report, Discover-Tech ads are used to infect and profile on behalf of mercenary spyware vendor Candiru. We also detail connections between Discover-Tech and another mercenary hacking company, Bindecy, as well as connections with Intelos, a mercenary ADINT firm. What is Discover-Tech and How Does It Operate? Discover-Tech is led by its CEO Dekel Boni, who has a background in digital advertising. Eric Banoun, whom Haaretz describes as “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel”, joined the company’s board of directors soon after it was founded in 2020 and remained there until 2025. Between 2020 and March 2026, Discover-Tech’s shareholders included a company linked to Sara Hamou, who has managed the corporate network of the spyware group Intellexa. Discover-Tech appears to place advertisements using several techniques. Firstly, the company operates a platform called MyDSP, which interfaces with online ad vendors including Google, Yandex, Vungle (Liftoff), and Sunteng. Secondly, separately from MyDSP, it purchases ads via the ad vendors Eskimi and Comcast-owned Beeswax (Freewheel). A large number of ads placed by Discover-Tech contain a script tag pointing back to what the company refers to as a “ NOAS server ” (also called a “getAd server”). This tag causes the ad, when rendered, to connect back to Discover-Tech, submit advertising identifiers for the user (either a cookie ID or a mobile ad ID), and automatically execute any JavaScript code returned. The NOAS server decides, apparently based on a combination of the source IP address and the advertising identifiers, whether the target is eligible to receive any JavaScript. If so, then code is returned. If not, a 0-byte response is returned. The NOAS server is a key part of Discover-Tech’s strategy, allowing Discover-Tech to avoid directly sharing malicious code, or even pointers to malicious code, with the companies who serve and display the ads. Figure 3 Discover-Tech bridges the mercenary spyware industry with the online advertising ecosystem. As detailed in Section 9 , Discover-Tech appeared on several lists of “certified” and “approved” ad vendors maintained by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe from the year 2020 until 2026. These listings helped make Discover-Tech appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and facilitate its participation in the digital advertising ecosystem at scale. As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Google, which collaborated in the investigation, terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms.  Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform, Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review, and Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains. Report Overview: Exposing Discover-Tech’s AdFection Pipeline  In this report we provide an overview of the different types of ad abuse facilitated by Discover-Tech, the company’s ad targeting systems and practices, as well as its partners and corporate network. In Section 2 , we show how Candiru works with Discover-Tech to conduct AdFection attacks, and describe one such attack: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with Candiru’s mercenary spyware. In Section 3 , we examine Controlium, a Discover-Tech platform that provides a control-panel style interface enabling mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads.” In Section 4 , we examine links between Discover-Tech and mercenary spyware companies Candiru/Integrity Labs and Bindecy. We then outline their relationships with other mercenary surveillance companies, including advertising intelligence (ADINT) vendor Intelos, and an ADINT vendor we refer to as DARK CARTOGRAPHER , which is building databases linking users’ mobile advertising identifiers to their phone numbers. In Section 5 , we analyze where Discover-Tech’s malicious advertisements land. We identified a Discover-Tech server that published almost four billion ad bidding records. These records show that Discover-Tech ads were served in almost 200,000 different Android apps, iOS apps, and websites in many countries. We also highlight specific countries and government networks where Discover-Tech’s advertisements had impressions. In Section 6 , we use technical analysis to examine how Discover-Tech deploys ads, tracks users and exchanges user identifiers with other ad vendors, including with Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad system Xandr. In Section 7 , we present our research on Discover-Tech Ltd, its corporate network, key persons linked to the company, the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology, and its connection to the wider advertising ecosystem. In Section 8 , we summarize what is known about the mercenary surveillance firms Candiru, Bindecy, and Intelos, and we further examine their activities and corporate networks in the context of the findings presented in our report. In Section 9 , we explore how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, including Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, Sunteng, and Xandr (Microsoft). In Section 10 , we discuss the implications of AdFection for user security and human rights. In Section 11 , we provide recommendations to lawmakers, regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to mitigate and block threats from AdFection-style attacks. The Citizen Lab sent requests for comment to 13 companies; their responses are included in full in the ‘Correspondence with Companies’ section. 2. How Discover-Tech’s AdFection Zero-Click Works This section provides the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click spyware attack via targeted ads in the wild: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with mercenary spyware . We refer to this type of attack as AdFection . Using network analysis, infrastructure fingerprinting, and analysis of implant behaviour, we connect Discover-Tech’s infrastructure with the distribution of Candiru’s mercenary spyware. What AdFection Looks Like The instances of Candiru AdFection via Discover-Tech ads all share similar characteristics. First, Discover-Tech wins a bid, and one of their ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device. The user may see this ad, such as in Figure 4 , though in some cases the ad may render in the background. Figure 4 Discover-Tech ads that could have infected users with spyware. We were served these ads while browsing the CBC and Yahoo websites, and while using a Sudoku app on Android. When the website or app receives the ad, it renders it, requesting JavaScript from a Discover-Tech server embedded within the ad. In most cases, the user who sees the ad is not selected for targeting, and the server will not return any JavaScript to be executed.  Nevertheless, the ad will still gather data from the user’s browser and submit it back to Discover-Tech, which can include cookies set on the webpage including the ad, as well as the device’s public IPv6 address. Confirming the Targeting of Al Jazeera with Candiru Spyware via Discover-Tech Ads In 2024 and 2025, international news network Al Jazeera was targeted in a series of zero-click attacks that we link with high confidence to Candiru’s spyware delivered via Discover-Tech’s ads. At least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in these attacks. Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Infected devices first show contact with domains from Discover-Tech infrastructure, indicating an ad impression. Next, the devices show connections with a Candiru validator server. The validator server performs an initial check of the device before it is further profiled and infected. Ultimately, an infected device communicates with a Candiru Command and Control (C&C) server. This temporal signature is illustrated by Figure 5 . Figure 5 Temporal signature of a Discover-Tech facilitated Candiru infection. Exposing Discover-Tech’s Controlium: Malicious Ad Targeting Platform This section examines Controlium, a platform that provides a control-panel style interface allowing mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads” that deliver malware. Discover-Tech published the full source code for Controlium’s frontend on the app’s login page, which allowed us to review and reconstruct the user interface. Discover-Tech provides its customers with access to a platform called Controlium that appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements. Customers can use Controlium to select a user for infection or profiling based on their mobile advertising identifier (iOS or Android), browser identifier (MyDSP or Beeswax cookie ID), and/or IP address. Discover-Tech’s malicious ads (referred to as “controlled ads”) sometimes also contain branding of companies that are closely linked to Discover-Tech, or branding from apparently unwitting third-party companies, including Amazon and AliExpress. We have no evidence that these ads were purchased by Amazon or AliExpress. As is standard for many web apps, the entirety of the source code for the Controlium frontend is included on the app’s login page. We visited the login page in a web browser and saved the page to disk to obtain a copy of the frontend. 2 We modified our copy of the code to remove any communication with any external servers, and to reveal all available screens in the UI. We then opened this version in a web browser to explore the app’s user interface.   In our analysis of Controlium, we downloaded only publicly accessible resources without circumventing any access controls. Most data associated with Controlium, such as information about Discover-Tech’s customers and their operations, is intentionally protected with an authorization token. However, we were able to obtain data on Controlium user logins from an unauthenticated API endpoint (see below: ‘Unauthenticated Endpoint’). We also assess that it would have been possible for a hacker to spoof a valid authorization (see below: ‘Authentication Vulnerability’), although we did not test this. Authentication Vulnerability While the data associated with Controlium’s customers and their operations are nominally protected with an authorization token, it appears that it would be easy for a hacker to spoof a valid token. We did not attempt to exploit this issue, as we believe doing so would have constituted unauthorized access to Discover-Tech’s systems. Figure 15 Controlium incorrectly derives the authentication token from encrypted user metadata, instead of the signed JWT returned by Okta. The underlying issue stems from Discover-Tech’s improper use of Okta’s Auth0 product. When a Controlium customer authenticates with Auth0 , a JWT is returned to their browser. This token is digitally signed by Auth0 , and contains information about scopes and expiry that the backend server should validate. However, Controlium ignores this token and instead passes a separate user object as a token to the backend server. The user object simply contains unauthenticated metadata about the user, such as their name and email address. Controlium encrypts this information with a secret key published in the Controlium platform. Interestingly, the correct code to use the JWT as an authorization token was present within the Controlium platform, but was commented out in lieu of the vulnerable code. Discover-Tech’s Links with Mercenary Spyware, ADINT, and Mass Surveillance Vendors  This section examines links between Discover-Tech and the mercenary spyware companies Candiru and Bindecy . We also illustrate that, beyond facilitating mercenary spyware delivery, Discover-Tech is linked to ADINT firms, including Intelos. Discover-Tech also supports mass-deanonymization of internet and app users by a threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER , which exploits vulnerabilities in mobile networks to unmask users’ phone numbers. Links with Candiru/Integrity Labs We observed that Discover-Tech sends encrypted ad impression data to Candiru using Controlium’s “Ad URL OpSec” feature. We identified several 2024 and 2025 Candiru infection links to at least six domains matching Fingerprint V1 and that also contained a parameter “?q=” whose value was 16 bytes of data in Base64-encoded form. In every case, the value of the “?q=” parameter was correctly decrypted with the “V1” AES-256 key published on a page called “Ad URL OpSec Decoder” on the website myipinfo[.]io . The website myipinfo[.]io is clearly linked to Discover-Tech: passive DNS data shows multiple overlaps in IP addresses and CNAME records with other Discover-Tech websites, including powerium[.]net and myweb3id[.]io (see also Section 7 ). One case of a Candiru infection link bearing a Discover-Tech Ad URL OpSec parameter is listed publicly on VirusTotal. The “?q=” parameter decrypts to an IP registered at the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs, indicating that organization as a potential target of Candiru spyware via Discover-Tech ads: Figure 19 Discover-Tech’s “Ad URL OpSec Decoder” shows that a Candiru infection link submitted to VirusTotal bears opsec data indicating the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs as a likely spyware target. We assess that this opsec data is included to facilitate a secure handoff from Discover-Tech to an attacker. The attacker presumably compares the visitor IP for the infection link against the IP encrypted by Discover-Tech, to make sure the link from the ad impression was not silently swapped to a different device (as a security researcher might want to do to capture an exploit). DARK CARTOGRAPHER: Mass-Deanonymization With Ads We identified Discover-Tech ads that sought to exploit the well-known “WebRTC IP Leak” issue , which can potentially reveal the IP address of VPN and proxy users. The same ads also attempted to unmask the phone number (MSISDN) of mobile users who were served the impression. The MSISDN leaks exploit various issues, including widespread problems with so-called “zero-click login” technologies, which aim to facilitate frictionless authentication and purchases for users on their mobile devices. One way “zero-click login” operates is that mobile providers select certain websites for “HTTP header enrichment,” so that when plaintext HTTP requests pass through the provider’s mobile gateway, an HTTP header (like X-MSISDN) is added to the request that provides the user’s phone number to the website. As an alternative to HTTP header enrichment, third-party services may work directly with the telco to facilitate this “zero-click login”. There appear to be widespread bugs with this allowlist matching, as well as bugs or security issues in third-party enrichment providers. While mainstream web browsers such as Chrome are moving towards blocking any non-HTTPS requests, it is likely that the app ecosystem will still embed webviews that permit non-HTTPS content. We taxonomized the issues into five types, exploited by attackers across numerous mobile providers in more than 30 countries in North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia, and disclosure to companies is in progress. Once the disclosure process is complete, we will release our subsequent report delving into technical analysis and attribution of these attacks. Notably, DARK CARTOGRAPHER ’s infrastructure links to both a mercenary adtech vendor and a U.S. government contractor. It is rare to see such direct overlaps between mercenary vendors and U.S. government or intelligence contractors. We assess that this attacker has been exploiting MSISDN leak issues since at least 2019, fronted by a variety of mercenary adtech companies. Our investigation into this threat actor is ongoing. How Discover-Tech Deploys Ads in the Browser In this section we show how, beyond targeting users of mobile apps, Discover-Tech deploys a range of techniques to deliver ads and track users while they browse across websites. This involves Discover-Tech running its own code in the user’s web browser, both while deploying ads to users and independently of showing them ads. We explore Discover-Tech’s “Banner Tester” tool to show how the company generates tracking tags and pixels attached to ads, including code that connects to a NOAS server, which we identified as a vector for spyware delivery. We also document how Discover-Tech engages in “ID syncing” with other ad vendors, and how it leverages IAB Europe’s “Transparency and Consent Framework” to appear GDPR-compliant, even while facilitating unwanted and malicious activity. An ad displayed to a website visitor consists of an image or video to be shown and a link to be clicked, but can also carry HTML and JavaScript code that connects to one or more domains in order to track users, ad impressions, clicks, and other activities. This code is typically referred to as an ad tag . A related concept, a so-called tracking pixel , also describes code running in the web browser that connects to third-party ad vendors. Ad vendors use additional tracking code for user ID syncing by exchanging user identifiers with each other in order to identify, profile, and target website visitors across sites and vendors. Our analysis of ad tags, tracking pixels, and ID syncing activities associated with Discover-Tech’s ad delivery is based on an analysis of publicly available code, browser testing and ad transactions archived by the web investigation tool urlscan. While ads displayed in mobile apps similarly carry code that connects to ad vendors, this section focuses on Discover-Tech ads displayed in the web browser. Discover-Tech’s Ad and Tracking Tags We found two versions of another app related to Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform named “Banner Tester” published on the sites bt.myweb3id[.]io and bt.platc-tester[.]com . User ID Syncing with Other Ad Vendors Unlike apps on mobile devices, web browsers do not allow websites to access a universal device identifier. The process of “ID syncing”, often also referred to as “cookie syncing”, addresses this lack of a universal user identifier. Research shows that digital advertising firms and data brokers use sophisticated forms of ID syncing to identify, profile and target web users across vendors. They achieve this by constantly exchanging user identifiers with each other, storing them in the browser and retrieving them again while users visit different websites that embed third-party tracking code. We found evidence showing how Discover-Tech engages in ID syncing with Comcast’s ad system Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad platform Xandr. Discover-Tech appears to use its myweb3id[.]io domain for ID syncing with Yandex. This domain is highly prevalent as a tracking domain on a large number of websites. Starting in May 2025, urlscan archived more than 10,000 records that include third-party requests to the domain events.myweb3id[.]io , most of them occurring during visits to Russian websites. A recent urlscan record shows an example of a typical request chain that involves ID syncing across Discover-Tech’s events.myweb3id[.]io domain and the following Yandex endpoint: an.yandex.ru/mapuid/discovertechis an . yandex . ru / mapuid / discovertechis The URL component “discovertechis” indicates some kind of business relationship between Discover-Tech and Yandex. Discover-Tech appears to use another domain, tracookiepixel[.]xyz , which is associated with myweb3id[.]io via DNS links and which is also highly prevalent as a tracking domain on a large number of websites, for ID syncing with Beeswax. Starting in July 2025, urlscan archived more than 10,000 records that include third-party requests to tracookiepixel[.]xyz , many of them occurring during visits to popular websites including IMDb and New York Times . A recent urlscan record shows an example request chain that was initiated during a visit to the website of The Guardian, which involves ID syncing across Discover-Tech’s tracookiepixel[.]xyz domain and Beeswax’ tracking domain bidr[.]io . The requests contain the parameter “bee_sync_partners=dtech”, which indicates some kind of business relationship between Discover-Tech and Beeswax. These ID syncing activities typically take place during website visits even when a user was not served a Discover-Tech ad. We are unsure how exactly Discover-Tech uses its browser ID syncing capabilities. Generally, being able to synchronize and correlate user identities across vendors is considered a precondition for individual-level ad targeting in the web browser. The Controlium platform, as examined in Section 3 , offers to upload lists of Beeswax identifiers for ad targeting in its “cTargeting” module, among mobile advertising IDs, IP addresses, and other identifiers, based on our analysis of the source code. We conclude that many websites make constant requests to Discover-Tech’s domains events.myweb3id[.]io and tracookiepixel[.]xyz in the background. These requests serve the purpose of ID syncing with Beeswax and Yandex, and Discover-Tech’s domains receive, in addition to user identifiers, at least the website visitor’s IP address and information about their browser and operating system. Discover-Tech’s Tracking Pixel Separately from Discover-Tech’s large-scale ID syncing on many websites, we found JavaScript code for a “tracking pixel” that was loaded during recent visits to only a few sites including myipinfo[.]io , cookiesurfer[.]com , and Discover-Tech’s corporate website, discover-tech[.]io (all three archived on urlscan ). These sites loaded versions of the tracking pixel code, both broadly similar, from the following URLs: js.tracookiepixel.xyz/myipinfo/c_tracking_pixel_gdpr.js js.tracookiepixel.xyz/dt/c_tracking_pixel_gdpr_enhanced.js js . tracookiepixel . xyz / myipinfo / c_tracking_pixel_gdpr . js js . tracookiepixel . xyz / dt / c_tracking_pixel_gdpr_enhanced . js Based on our analysis of the source code, the tracking pixel serves the purpose of storing, retrieving and synchronizing user identifiers across Discover-Tech, Beeswax, Xandr, and Yandex. Once loaded on a website, the code stores user identifiers associated with Discover-Tech, Beeswax, and Xandr in the user’s web browser in order to retrieve them again during subsequent visits to websites that load the same code. The code is designed to initiate the ID syncing process by sending Discover-Tech’s user identifier to Beeswax and Yandex in order to receive corresponding Beeswax and Yandex identifiers. Additionally, the code retrieves the user’s Xandr identifier. Request chains archived on urlscan show Discover-Tech’s tracking pixel in operation, including ID syncing with Yandex and the retrieval of user identifiers from Beeswax and Xandr. When the tracking pixel code detects that a website visitor is located in a region where the GDPR applies, based on geolocating the user’s IP address, it uses IAB Europe’s Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF) to process user “consent” signals for the three TCF vendors Discover-Tech Ltd, Xandr Inc, and BeeswaxIO Corporation. This demonstrates how Discover-Tech utilizes its listing as a registered and approved ad vendor by IAB Europe, as discussed in Section 9 . The code also clearly maps the acronym “ZUID” to Xandr’s user identifier. As detailed in Section 4 , several Controlium modules refer to an option labeled “Detect ZUID”. We are unsure how Discover-Tech’s Controlium platform exactly utilizes this identifier. As the “Detect ZUID” option is among a few “Add Ons” that can be activated when setting up an ad campaign, it may serve the retrieval of Xandr user identifiers either for ad targeting or for tracking targets. Xandr (Microsoft Advertising) did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. Generally, the purpose of Discover-Tech’s tracking pixel is unclear. As a large share of Discover-Tech ads are designed to lead users to the site myipinfo[.]io when clicking on those ads, the tracking pixel loaded during the site visit then correlates a target’s Discover-Tech user identifier with their Beeswax, Xandr, and Yandex identifiers. Records archived on urlscan show that the MyIPInfo website loaded a version of the tracking pixel from another domain associated with Discover-Tech in the past: js.cookie-sync.xyz/myipinfo/c_tracking_pixel_gdpr.js js . cookie - sync . xyz / myipinfo / c_tracking_pixel_gdpr . js 7. Discover-Tech and Its Corporate Network Discover-Tech has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the digital advertising industry for years. In this section, we further investigate Discover-Tech, key persons affiliated with the company, related companies, and the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology. Adtech with a Background in Spytech Discover-Tech purports to be a typical digital advertising firm, offering a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), which facilitates the delivery of targeted ads. On its website, it claims to have “unrestricted access to top-ranking apps with 1+ billion daily active users” via a “worldwide ad exchange”. In addition to its DSP, Discover-Tech offers “monetization” solutions to mobile network operators and mobile device manufacturers, which we discuss further below. Israeli company records we reviewed link Discover-Tech’s website, discover-tech[.]io , to the company Discover-Tech Ltd registered in March 2020, with Dekel Boni listed as its initial director and sole shareholder. In the two months after its incorporation, Eric Banoun, who is a major figure in the Israeli surveillance technology industry, joined Discover-Tech’s board of directors, and the shareholder base was expanded. From April 2020, the company’s shareholders included Dekel Boni, Guy Lants, Yaniv Basil, Zfanya Leib, Sergei Bartashevich, and Chaia Services Ltd, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. Eric Banoun left the company’s board of directors in January 2025 and Chaia Services Ltd ceased to be a shareholder in March 2026. As of July 2026, Discover-Tech is directed by Dekel Boni and owned by Boni, Basil, and Lants. Eric Banoun co-founded the cyberespionage firm Circles, a close NSO Group affiliate , and Senpai Technologies, which is part of the Intellexa consortium. We could not access corporate registration information on Discover-Tech’s shareholder Chaia Services Ltd. However, a Haaretz investigation reported that one of Chaia’s directors was Sara Hamou. Hamou managed Intellexa’s corporate network and was sentenced to eight years in prison (pending appeal) by a Greek court for her role in the Predatorgate scandal. Eric Banoun was listed as a director of a similarly named U.S.-based company, Chaia Services Tech LLC , which was dissolved in 2025. Based on the links to Eric Banoun and Chaia Services Ltd., we conclude that Discover-Tech was linked to the spyware industry for almost six years, according to Israeli company records and other publicly available information. Discover-Tech’s other shareholders, including Dekel Boni who is now the company’s sole director, have a background in digital advertising, previously working for adtech firms like Digital Turbine and Taptica, according to their LinkedIn profiles . 3 Boni lists himself as Discover-Tech’s CEO, Guy Lants as its “Director of Product”. Yaniv Basil lists himself as the company’s “Chief Technology Officer” between 2020 and 2023. Ad Vendor Registrations with Google and IAB Europe Despite information about Discover-Tech’s links to figures in the spyware industry that could be readily obtained from a review of corporate records, major advertising industry organizations added the company to several lists of “certified” or “approved” ad vendors, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitated its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale. As discussed in Section 9 , Google listed Discover-Tech among its “Ad Manager Certified External Vendors”, “Ad Technology Partners”, and “Ads Personalization Providers” from 2020 until 2026. The advertising industry association IAB Europe listed the company on the “Global Vendor List” for its “Transparency & Consent Framework” (TCF), also from 2020 until 2026. In Section 9 , we examine the implications of Discover-Tech’s ad vendor registrations with Google and IAB Europe in detail. Both the Google and IAB vendor registrations consistently refer to the Israeli company Discover-Tech Ltd and the domain discover-tech[.]io . In addition, Google’s list of “Ads Personalization providers” clearly links Discover-Tech to the domains  mtrtb[.]com and mydsp[.]io , which it listed among “domains which can be attributed to the provider” Discover-Tech Ltd. Tracing the Origins of Discover-Tech’s MyDSP Advertising Tech As discussed in Section 5 , the domain mtrtb[.]com and the ad system MyDSP ( mydsp[.]io ) play key roles in Discover-Tech’s ad targeting. According to historical whois information, Discover-Tech Ltd took ownership of both domains in 2020. While domain registration data became anonymized in 2022, mydsp[.]io redirected to discover-tech[.]io until early 2026. Both mtrtb[.]com and mydsp[.]io can be “attributed” to Discover-Tech Ltd according to Google, as discussed in Section 9 . MyDSP was launched by the Israeli adtech firm Matomy in 2016. In 2018, MyDSP was “connected” to Matomy’s MobFox subsidiary, had “access” to 50 billion daily ad impressions and was able to target 500 million users, according to its website. Also in 2018, Matomy sold MyDSP to the Cypriot firm Marketcom Technologies Ltd, which belongs to the e-commerce firm Market Group owned by the Israeli billionaire Teddy Sagi, as confirmed by public filings , business data , media reporting , and whois information for the domains mydsp[.]io and mtrtb[.]com . A 2019 version of the mydsp[.]io site confirms that MyDSP ultimately became part of Glispa, a Berlin-based adtech firm also acquired by Market Group back in 2015. We are not aware of any robust information that shows how Discover-Tech Ltd eventually took over MyDSP, but whois information confirms that Discover-Tech Ltd, founded in March 2020, took control of the domains mydsp[.]io and mtrtb[.]com from Marketcom Technologies Ltd at some point between June and October 2020. According to a Google record , the ad provider with the ID ‘3036’ changed from MarketDSP ( advertising.market[.]com ) to “Discover-Tech Ltd” ( discover-tech[.]io ) on July 31, 2020. While the company names and websites changed, the list of additional domains attributable to this Google ad provider stayed identical: ( mydsp[.]io and mtrtb[.]com ). JavaScript code related to MyDSP’s admin interface for customers, published on admin.mtrtb[.]com , details a list of ad vendors MyDSP was connected to at an unspecified point in time ( archived code ). The list includes Google, Yandex, Vungle, and Sunteng. Thus, it confirms the connections with the ad vendors we found in Discover-Tech’s bidding records ( Section 5 ). In addition, the list suggests that MyDSP was or is also connected to the ad vendors MobFox, Inneractive, MoPub, PulsePoint, RhythmOne, GumGum, Pubmatic, Smaato, Sonobi, NativeAds, Unity, Q1Media, and Applovin. Offerings for Mobile Carriers and Device Vendors Discover-Tech Ltd itself can be traced back to a company named RelevanTech Ltd (relevantech[.]com), founded by Discover-Tech shareholders Dekel Boni and Yaniv Basil in 2015, according to their LinkedIn profiles and Israeli company records we reviewed. Like MyDSP, RelevanTech was also acquired by Market Group’s Glispa in 2017, and became Glispa Discover . Boni and Basil then worked for Glispa, before creating Discover-Tech Ltd in 2020. The descriptions of the services provided by RelevanTech ( 2016 ), Glispa Discover ( 2017 ), and Discover-Tech Ltd are very similar. The current discover-tech.io site promises to help mobile network operators and mobile device manufacturers benefit from “sponsored and tailored app recommendations”, in addition to the company’s DSP offering. The 2022 version of the site explained that Discover-Tech would “place” mobile apps on new mobile devices “from the moment” they are “turned on” and provide “operator certified installs” of apps on new devices. We are not aware of any robust information that shows how Discover-Tech’s founders regained control over what was left of RelevanTech from Glispa, but whois information confirms that Discover-Tech Ltd regained control of the domain relevantech[.]com in July 2020. In 2021, Discover-Tech Ltd operated a mobile app on behalf of the Serbian subsidiary of the mobile network operator A1 Telekom Austria, according to a terms of use agreement, which explains that the app would provide A1 customers with content from both A1 and Discover-Tech. The description on the 2021 version of the Serbian A1 website suggests that the app, named “Moy A1” (“My A1”), enabled A1 customers to check their mobile plan, download invoices, and buy additional credits. Put differently, Discover-Tech was sitting inside the official app of the third-largest Serbian mobile operator. We do not know for how long Discover-Tech was involved in operating this app. The 2020 version of the Discover-Tech lists A1 and device manufacturers like Samsung, Tecno, and Wiko among the company’s customers. We did not further investigate Discover-Tech’s mobile carrier and device manufacturer business, which may or may not be active anymore. In conclusion, we believe that Discover-Tech emerged from both RelevanTech and MyDSP, both previously owned by Glispa. While MyDSP and additional software for the delivery of malicious ads appear to be operational in 2026, an asset sale discussed in the next subsection suggests that Discover-Tech may not offer its services for mobile carriers and device manufacturers anymore. A Sale of Assets Leaves Open Questions  In 2021, the Dubai-based firm Affle MEA FZ-LLC, part of the mobile advertising group Affle, based in Singapore and India, acquired “business assets” from Discover-Tech Ltd, according to public filings . Publicly available financial statements refer to the acquisition of a Discover-Tech “business segment” including “brand, IP, domain, business relationships and goodwill”. Public filings further specify that Affle acquired Discover-Tech’s “mobile device marketing platform” that provides “initial device customization” including “dynamic app discovery and recommendation at initial boot or reset of a device” through its integrations with device manufacturers and mobile network operators. An Affle press release quotes Discover-Tech founder Dekel Boni stating that he was “proud” that Discover-Tech’s “technology” that “powers the first interaction a user has with his new device” would become part of the “app discover offering” of Appnext, another company acquired by Affle. Based on the information available to us, we believe that Discover-Tech Ltd sold its offerings for mobile carriers and device vendors examined in the previous subsection, to Affle. We have no reason to believe that Affle has any control over Discover-Tech’s malicious ad operations that we investigate in this report. However, the exact scope of this asset sale remains unknown to us. Affle did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. Intelos, Bindecy, and Candiru’s Corporate Networks This section provides an overview of Intelos, Bindecy, and Candiru, and provides details on what we know about their corporate networks and business identities. Furthermore, we present additional links between Discover-Tech and Intelos. Intelos and Its ADINT System AdHoc In 2023, the trade press website Intelligence Online and Haaretz first reported about Intelos, a new Israeli ADINT vendor that provides a surveillance system based on data from digital advertising named “AdHoc”. Intelos was reportedly founded by Eric Banoun, who is “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel” according to Haaretz. Israeli company records reviewed by us confirm that Banoun has been a shareholder in Intelos Ltd from its registration in 2018 until present, and he is listed as the company’s director. The email address he uses in corporate filings, [email protected] , clearly links Intelos Ltd to the website intelos.io. The fact that Banoun was also listed as a director of Discover-Tech Ltd (see Section 7 ), already suggests a potential connection between the ADINT vendor Intelos and Discover-Tech. In addition, the websites intelos[.]io and discover-tech[.]io were published by the same entity until at least February 2026, according to technical analysis discussed in Section 7 . While we cannot assess the exact scope of the collaboration between Intelos and Discover-Tech, the technical analysis discussed in Section 4 indicates that the two work together. Besides a few media articles and the company’s website, there is almost no public information available about Intelos. The company’s AdHoc product is not mentioned on its website. According to Israeli company records reviewed by us, Intelos Ltd’s shareholders include Eric Banoun, Senpai co-founder Roy Shloman, Thai businessman Charoenrath Vilailuck, and a Liechtenstein-based firm named SAR Investments International Ltd, among others. On its website , Intelos purports to be a “marketing intelligence” platform that monitors “worldwide digital signals, actions, and preferences”, including “subtle changes in behaviour”, by processing 16 billion “daily data sets” across 50 countries. Much of the promotional language on the site sounds like the company’s products are built for customers in digital marketing, but could also describe an ADINT vendor. Intelos promises to “map behavioural patterns across audiences” and to build “profiles of audiences and groups” in order to “map relationships, track behavioural shifts, and anticipate collective action”. It also provides “location intelligence” based on a “proprietary index of the physical world” with “every relevant location classified, mapped, and weighted for significance”. Another system named “Nexus AI” could transform “raw data into structured insights” based on “live and historical datasets” in order to “map behavioural clusters” and “detect relationships”. Haaretz and Intelligence Online reported that Intelos provides ad-based geolocation surveillance but also the delivery of spyware via ads, without providing details about the latter. Its technology was reportedly offered to the Shin Bet in Israel and sold in Thailand. According to Haaretz, Eric Banoun presented an ADINT product named “Havoc” that included the AdHoc logo to an Egyptian customer. An agreement related to his presentation mentioned a U.K. firm, whose director is also the director of another U.K. firm named “Havoc”, which sold an unnamed cyber system to an unnamed country over a period of three years at a cost of about $42 million. Based on the media report, it remains unclear whether AdHoc was sold in Egypt or not. Intelos did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. Both sites offered a “Data Marketing (DM) platform” and the “AI Edge” product using a number of identical sentences. According to the current website , Tekma purports to have access to data on 3.5 billion devices, which can be utilized “across major DSPs”, and is based in Dubai, with regional offices in Greece, Cyprus, and Spain. The 2024 site includes Tekma contact information referring to “Chaia Services” and mentions another regional office in Hong Kong. Another older but also almost identical site, tekma[.]io , includes Tekma contact information referring to “Chaia Ltd” in “13&15 GR. Afxentiou Street, Mesa Geitonia Limassol, Limassol 4003 CY”.
