Discover-Tech Mercenary Spyware Partner: Candiru/Integrity Labs Candiru is an Israeli-founded mercenary spyware company that draws its original name from the parasitic Candiru fish, and has operated under a wide range of names throughout the years, including Saito Tech. Today, Candiru operates under the rebranded identity of Integrity Labs after acquisition by U.S.-based Integrity Partners.  Candiru: Prior Investigations, Abuses, and Discoveries Candiru is a mercenary spyware threat actor known by multiple names, including SOURGUM and Carmel Tsunami by Microsoft. First Candiru Abuse Discoveries: 2021 On July 15, 2021, the Citizen Lab published the first report exposing Candiru. That investigation included identifying a Candiru victim and recovering a copy of Candiru’s Windows spyware. We then worked with Microsoft’s Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC) to analyze the spyware, which led to the identification of two zero-day vulnerabilities ( CVE-2021-31979 and CVE-2021-33771 ). We also identified over 750 websites linked to Candiru’s infection infrastructure that masqueraded as a wide range of civil society entities ranging from media organizations to Amnesty International. On July 14, 2021, Google TAG published a report which included discussion of two Chrome exploits ( CVE-2021-21166 and CVE-2021-30551 ) that pointed to addresses matching our Candiru fingerprint. The report also linked a Microsoft Office exploit ( CVE-2021-33742 ) to the same operator. Microsoft’s own investigation into Candiru, published simultaneously with our report on July 15, 2021, identified at least 100 spyware victims across ten countries. Microsoft reported that the victims included journalists, opposition politicians, dissidents, and activists.  On November 16, 2021, ESET reported on a series of watering hole attacks observed in 2020 and 2021 targeting websites in the Middle East with what they described as a “strong focus on Yemen.” They attributed the attacks to Candiru . Further Investigations and Abuses: 2022-2025 In 2022, the Citizen Lab again found Candiru spyware targeting victims among Catalan civil society groups in Spain . In that investigation, we identified signs of a live Candiru infection on a Catalan university network, and successfully worked with system administrators to identify the victim, isolate the device, and extract the active spyware. The targeting we observed as part of this campaign included emails masquerading as official Spanish governmental messages about COVID. On July 21, 2022, Avast published a report revealing that Candiru was using a Chrome zero-day exploiting WebRTC ( CVE-2022-2294 ), and found evidence of targeting of users in multiple countries in the Middle East. On December 22, 2022, Meta disclosed that it disrupted around 130 Facebook and Instagram accounts used by Candiru to send infection links amongst themselves to “test phishing capabilities.” In the summer of 2024, during the parliamentary election campaign, Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Daniel Freund was targeted with Candiru’s mercenary spyware , according to the European Parliament’s security services.  On August 5, 2025, Recorded Future’s Insikt Group investigated Candiru infrastructure and identified multiple Candiru clusters linked to Hungary, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, and Azerbaijan, among others.  On September 2, 2025, Sekoia published an investigation into Candiru’s spyware, highlighting how Candiru and similar companies leverage complex jurisdictional structures to avoid discovery. Entity Listing On November 3, 2021, Candiru was added to the United States Commerce Department’s Entity List for malicious cyber activities. The entity listing noted that Candiru was added because “they developed and supplied spyware to foreign governments that used this tool to maliciously target government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics, and embassy workers.”  Legal Actions Against Candiru and Users In October 2024, Daniel Freund filed a criminal complaint with the assistance of German digital rights NGO GFF against Viktor Orbán and unnamed persons over his targeting with Candiru. On April 30, 2025, the NGO Sentinel Alliance filed a case against multiple Spanish governmental entities, NSO Group, and Candiru over the mercenary spyware attacks targeting Catalan civil society. Candiru’s 2025 Acquisition by Integrity Partners  In April 2025, Israeli media reported that U.S.-based Integrity Partners acquired the operations of Candiru for $30 million in a bid to bypass the U.S. Entity Listing. Research by Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified Candiru as having been rebranded to “Integrity Labs”  (אינטגריטי לאבס בע~מ) in December 2024. The current status of the acquisition is unclear. Candiru/Integrity Labs did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided. 9. Discover-Tech’s Relationship to the Digital Advertising Industry This section explores how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, and notes that Discover-Tech achieved “certified” and “approved” status by Google and the major advertising industry association IAB Europe. Our analysis indicates that Discover-Tech deployed ads via Google, Yandex, and other ad vendors including Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, and Sunteng. In addition, both Google and the advertising association IAB Europe have listed Discover-Tech as a “certified” and “approved” ad vendor since the year 2020, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitate its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale. As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review. Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains. Google listed Discover-Tech Ltd among its roughly 2,400 Certified External Vendors . These vendors, which Google also refers to as “allowed vendors” and “certified companies”, “undergo a business review,” the nature of which is not specified, so they “can serve third-party ads on the Google Ad Manager platform”. Google claims to “conduct a thorough certification process” for “vendors that are certified for third-party ads” and ensure they “meet Google’s requirements for third-party ad serving”. A listed vendor is “permitted to make third-party calls”, which may include tracking pixels. Google emphasizes that it might pause the delivery of ads when it detects “non certified vendors”. Being listed is crucial for a company that wants to interface with Google. Google also listed Discover-Tech among its roughly 1,000 Ad Technology Providers , who can receive data on website visitors and app users in Europe. In Google’s own words, these vendors “agreed to comply” with its “data usage policy” and “have shared certain information that is required by European regulations policy”. Website and app publishers “need to list these partners for [their] users.” Until 2025, Google referred to these vendors as “certified ad technology providers,” but a later redesign of the page dropped the term “certified.” In addition, Google listed Discover-Tech in its global list of roughly 1,700 ads personalization providers , which may participate in ad auctions based on “user consent”. Google, which collaborated in this investigation, removed Discover-Tech from its ad vendor registries and terminated the company’s access to its ad exchange platforms as of the first week of October, 2026. Discover-Tech Ltd was also listed in the Global Vendor List (GVL) maintained by the European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), a key digital advertising industry association. The GVL contains roughly 1,000 vendors that are “registered and approved” by IAB Europe. These vendors can participate in IAB Europe’s “Transparency & Consent Framework” (TCF), which promises to enable ad vendors to comply with European data protection and privacy law when processing personal data for digital advertising purposes. While the TCF’s ability to enable lawful data processing is controversially debated , a GVL registration has become a de-facto requirement for an ad vendor to participate in digital advertising, display ads and receive data in Europe. IAB Europe added Discover-Tech Ltd to the GVL on July 2, 2020. As a result of this investigation, Discover-Tech was removed from the GVL on October 8, 2026. According to IAB Europe, it takes “reasonable steps to vet and approve” vendor applications, including the “identity of the party or parties controlling the vendor” and the vendor’s ability to “adhere” to a number of TCF policies, and then monitors their compliance with those policies. The TCF is the basis for passing user “consent” signals for personal data processing across the digital advertising supply chain, from users to publishers to intermediaries (like SSPs, DSPs, and ad exchanges) to advertisers, including in bid requests and tracking pixels. Most ad tags and tracking pixels that connect to third-party vendors require “consent” signals, including in some jurisdictions outside Europe and the U.K. like California. Google, Xandr, and most larger ad platforms require TCF compliance. While several studies found that vendors are too often ignoring “consent” signals, an ad vendor that is not listed in the GVL, and thus cannot pass any signal, can hardly interface with other ad vendors in reliable ways. While the vendor lists maintained by Google and the IAB Europe help a company appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and are the basis to participate in the digital advertising ecosystem in a reliable way at scale, they appear to be largely based on self-attestation by vendors. They are also the basis for most of the “consent” popups shown to European web and app users every day. Discover-Tech Ltd’s inclusion in those lists potentially means that, for almost six years, hundreds of millions of Europeans were presented with a consent request that, if the recipient clicked “Agree,” could be construed as authorizing Discover-Tech to process their data under the GDPR. As of October 2026, Discover-Tech is additionally listed in a registry operated by the “Trustworthy Accountability Group” (TAG) created by major U.S. advertising associations and the IAB, which aims to increase trust in the digital advertising industry, eliminate fraud and fight criminal activity including “malware threats targeting the digital advertising supply chain”. The Verified by TAG badge held by Discover-Tech, which the company also displays on its website, is used across the industry to “determine trust and transparency” and let prospective partners know that a company has taken “actionable steps to verify their identities and adopt rigorous standards to fight online fraud, piracy, malware, and lack of transparency”, according to the TAG website. Discussion: AdFection Shows that Online Ads Are a Cybersecurity and Privacy Crisis This report provides the first-ever technical evidence of zero-click mercenary spyware attacks delivered via targeted advertising. We also confirm that AdFection was used to infect devices at international media organization Al Jazeera. These attacks were facilitated by Discover-Tech, which presents itself as a legitimate advertising business but actually serves as a bridge between mercenary spyware companies and the advertising ecosystem. Discover-Tech not only helps companies like Candiru use ads to mass-profile unwitting phone users, their ads directly enable these companies to silently infect selected targets’ devices. The combination of advertising intelligence and the delivery of spyware is extremely concerning, for several reasons. First, both the digital advertising and mercenary spyware industry are very poorly regulated, with the latter featuring numerous firms notorious for deception, a lack of transparency, and even unlawful activities. To see entities from those two industries forming an alliance should be a wakeup call to regulators and policymakers around the world. Dozens of reports by numerous organizations, including the Citizen Lab, have shown incontrovertible proof of the harms caused by mercenary spyware vendors on civil society around the globe. With the addition of the type of advertising intelligence capabilities we have documented, those firms’ capabilities will now be supercharged. Second, the combination of advertising intelligence and spyware infections provide government security agencies with highly invasive systems that span both mass and highly targeted types of user surveillance. As we show in this report, millions of devices were likely unwittingly profiled as a form of preliminary reconnaissance to enable targeting with spyware tailored to those device’s specific characteristics. Ominously, many of these infections took place without any visible indication of tampering or other clues that might have alerted them to the compromise. Also ominous is the fact that the services of Discover-Tech appear to span multiple regions around the globe. It is not known at this time exactly which governments are capitalizing on these new capabilities, but if past evidence is any indication it seems highly likely that some proportion of them are abusing those capabilities to target individuals outside of strictly criminal or national security purposes. ADINT: Journalism in the Crosshairs The hacking of Al Jazeera with AdFection is part of a longstanding pattern: mercenary spyware attacks against the media . Journalists and newsrooms are a constant target for spyware attacks , and this latest case highlights how well-resourced operators consistently seek new ways to access their private, protected communications.   The use of spyware to target the media directly interferes with the ability of the free press to hold power to account. It also threatens the privacy of journalists’ sources, and can chill reporting. Foreknowledge of movements, reporting topics, meetings, and sources does not just help powerful interests try to frustrate coverage and reporting, it can put people at physical risk. This is especially true for a news organization with reporters, freelancers, stringers, fixers and sources working in conflict zones around the world.   Investigations into mercenary spyware operations have repeatedly surfaced targeting against the media, including in the context of governmental and cartel killings of reporters. Journalists have been confirmed spyware targets , from the Citizen Lab’s earliest findings of Pegasus spyware in Mexico almost a decade ago , to cases across Africa from Angola to Morocco and Togo , to Jordan , Serbia , El Salvador, and Italy , among many others. Organizations like Reporters Without Borders provide helpful overviews of the scale of the threat which, as Access Now points out, is sometimes coupled with laws designed to authorize government access to journalists’ communications. The International Federation of Journalists, meanwhile, has a recent overview of how spyware is situated within a broader set of digital threats against journalists.  Recently, reporting from the Committee to Protect Journalists outlined the dangers posed to journalists from ADINT -style tracking. The combination of this tracking with zero-click mercenary spyware targeting presents an even more serious danger to journalists’ safety. This investigation should also serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat. This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members. We urge news organizations to immediately seek expert assistance and ensure that their systems are protected against these attacks to the fullest extent possible. We provide some guidance in Section 11 , however we urge all news organizations to systematically review their security posture (and logs) for signs of AdFection style spyware targeting and infection. The Advertising Industry: A Dangerous Lack of Due Diligence  Our findings also reveal a troubling lack of due diligence within the digital advertising industry that helped enable this inappropriate activity. Discover-Tech, which presented itself as a legitimate ad vendor but served as a bridge between the online advertising ecosystem and the spyware industry, has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the online advertising ecosystem for years. Multiple ad vendors let the company utilize their systems. The two key industry organizations, Google and IAB Europe, have helped Discover-Tech appear as a legitimate ad vendor from the year 2020 until 2026, despite information about the company’s links to figures in the spyware industry being readily accessible in corporate records. Our findings show that the digital advertising industry is ill-prepared to prevent malicious actors from exploiting its infrastructure for the distribution of spyware via targeted ads. Advertising Industry: Prioritize Security, Stop AdFection This case should serve as an alarm to the advertising industry that business as usual is no longer acceptable. The online advertising industry must get serious about tackling the distribution of mercenary spyware via targeted ads, alongside other malicious advertising practices including financially motivated fraud and cybercrime . Technical and organizational measures currently implemented by the industry, such as the SafeFrame specification or standards for supply chain transparency are insufficient or not even adopted in a meaningful way. Fix a Broken Digital Infrastructure More broadly, the distribution of spyware via targeted ads depends on the way digital advertising – and the web economy at large – currently operate. Many mobile apps and websites contain tracking software operated by dozens of third parties, which themselves may include code by additional third parties within apps and browsers. Also required for the targeted deployment of spyware, ad targeting at the individual level depends on uncontrolled data sharing via RTB auctions and third-party tracking. Automated ad selling and buying via RTB, which connects large numbers of publishers, advertisers and intermediaries across opaque supply chains, is designed to minimize human intervention. When combined with a lack of oversight and accountability, it is generally prone to abuse. This is further aggravated by the assumption that at least some ad vendors benefit from malicious and fraudulent advertising. Leaked internal documents from Meta reported by Reuters suggest that Meta estimated that it earns between five and ten percent of its annual revenue from running fraudulent ads. Industry sources suggest that ad fraud accounts for one fifth of all online advertising spend.  This broken digital infrastructure needs to be reformed at several levels, as consumer associations , regulators , and policymakers have long been demanding. AdFection: A Threat to States, Civil Society, and Everyone Else The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large. Two major U.S. security agencies, the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), have warned already in 2018 and 2020 that adversaries may leverage malicious ads to deploy malware on devices, and thus both recommended that government agencies and other organizations use ad-blocking software. Given the current threat posed by Discover-Tech’s AdFection vectors, and the evidence of wide-scale targeting, we judge that the most feasible protection is for defenders to block targeted ads at the gateway. This defensive recommendation (see Section 11 ) holds until the industry has shown that it is reliably able to block all AdFection style vectors. At the very time that state actors may be employing offensive cyber attacks, malicious ads can be deployed via apps and websites used by defense personnel, political leaders, and people maintaining critical infrastructure alike, creating national security risks for those very same states. The same structural deficits that endanger civil society, journalists, and opposition figures are potentially exploited by both foreign adversaries and cybercriminals, creating systemic risks for everyone. These security risks make it apparent that there is an urgent public-interest need to reform digital advertising. The same risks apply to the private sector and to civil society. Indeed, as prior research has made clear, a large number of governments will use these potent capabilities to undermine political opposition, stealthily target journalists and lawyers, and target refugees, immigrants, and other vulnerable populations. The mercenary spyware industry is already notorious for widespread harms; fueling that industry with digital advertising capabilities will multiply those harms immeasurably. 11. Recommendations: How to Stop AdFection Attacks The AdFection attacks and espionage described in this report impact millions of people in dozens of countries. Existing laws and self-regulation by the industry failed to catch or prevent them. In this section, we provide guidance to regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection and ADINT-style espionage. Advertising Vendors: Time to Get Serious The advertising industry uses terms like “certified” and “approved” to try and convey a veneer of effective self regulation. However, the industry appears to perform no meaningful due diligence on participating vendors, instead improperly relying on self-attestation where vendors check a box on an online form. This process allows widespread privacy abuses, including failing to prevent mass espionage via targeted ads. Ad vendors must significantly level up their cybersecurity and threat detection capacity to effectively cut off malicious advertisers across the supply chain. They must rigorously and regularly vet, screen, and audit their business partners and hold them accountable for their own supply chains. This type of more robust due diligence applies in particular to key industry organizations and dominant players who must introduce rigorous and regular audits for companies listed in ad vendor registries which they maintain and provide to many other actors in the supply chain. Business partners from countries with opaque corporate registries or where known malicious actors operate deserve specific attention. Technical and organizational measures to be taken must include both vendor-specific and industry-wide efforts. Cybersecurity agencies and other regulators in the U.S., Canada, Europe, and other regions must support these efforts by investigating risks, calling out shortcomings and taking action to ensure the implementation of effective measures by the advertising industry. Detect and block malicious ads: Ad vendors must radically increase their capacity to identify AdFection-style attacks in real-time, alongside other forms of malicious advertising such as ad fraud, across their supply chain.  Share threat data: Develop better threat sharing and clearinghouses for sharing information about malicious actors and recklessly permissive jurisdictions. Vet and screen partners : Implement mandatory know-your-customer, including due diligence and recurring vetting for all partners and other firms who transact over the provided ad and data services.  Audit vendor registries: Major advertising organizations must introduce mandatory third-party audits for “certified” or “approved” vendors.  Ban vendors in problem jurisdictions : Adopt a default-deny policy for vendors operating in jurisdictions known to be highly permissive of abuse, or without accountability mechanisms. Fix systemic vulnerabilities: Implement industry-wide measures to improve ad delivery security and to introduce full supply chain transparency, and support their adoption. Zero-Click AdFection We urge regulators to take immediate action to ensure that advertising platforms and partners stop facilitating AdFection-style attacks, and secure their populations from the security, cybersecurity, and privacy threats posed by the advertising ecosystem. Investigation and Enforcement Immediately investigate Discover-Tech and Candiru: Our research showed large-scale data collection from millions of devices involving Discover-Tech and Candiru. The data was apparently collected for the purposes of AdFection. We urge competent authorities in all jurisdictions to investigate whether the rights of their citizens, as well as applicable privacy and security laws were violated. Enforce existing laws: It is unlikely that Discover-Tech is the only enabler of AdFection-style zero-click attacks. Authorities should more closely scrutinize the advertising ecosystem to determine whether other companies are leveraging it for espionage and spyware delivery, and determine whether they have violated applicable laws and regulations. Enforcement and sanctions : Use all necessary domestic enforcement and sanctions authorities to discourage AdFection abuse. These measures can include the use of sanctions and entity-listing powers against firms that deploy mercenary spyware and conduct espionage via targeted ads, the companies that enable them, and the individuals who work in the AdFection domain. Legal and Regulatory Improvements Commission investigations: Enlist the assistance of cybersecurity agencies and regulatory bodies to evaluate the security, privacy, and national security risks from the current advertising ecosystem. Tighten privacy regulations around ad tracking and targeting data: Evaluate legislation to remove personal data from RTB auctions and work with international partners to adopt similar measures.  Real regulation of the advertising industry: It is time for regulators and lawmakers to develop frameworks based on mandatory oversight with clear enforcement mechanisms and penalties for violation.  Independent audits and KYC: Require that the advertising industry implement third-party audits and know-your-customer standards for all their business partners, as well as companies included in “certified” vendor registries. Develop meaningful penalties for failure to comply or misrepresentation. Securing National Infrastructure Requires Blocking Ads and Tracking on Official Devices Mandatory ad-blocking on government devices: Issue policy guidance aligned with relevant cybersecurity agencies (e.g., CISA and NSA in the U.S.) recommendations requiring ad-blocking software on edge devices, and ad-blocking at the gateway for all government-owned devices. (See, for example, U.S. Senator Ron Wyden’s letter to the CIO of the U.S. Department of Defense, as well as Senator Wyden and Rep. Harrigon’s joint letter to the Inspector General of the U.S. Department of Defense). Opt-out of ad targeting : Mandate the disabling of unique advertising IDs on all government mobile devices (such as through MDM), and issue guidance and policy recommendations for personal devices used in governmental spaces. Ban browsers that facilitate data harvesting: Evaluate the security risks of browsers with impossible-to-disable tracking, and consider provisionally banning them from governmental networks and devices. Defenders: Ad-Blocking Is A Cybersecurity Best Practice AdFection attacks demonstrate that online advertising is now a vector for zero-click spyware infection into your organization. Taken together with research showing that data from targeted advertising is already being used for mass espionage , and potentially for corporate espionage , this makes it clear there is currently no consistently safe way to expose your users and networks to targeted ads . You can directly block Discover-Tech’s current methods by blocking advertising identifiers, however we suspect that the AdFection attack surface may be larger, requiring more systematic measures.  Block ads and tracking on devices and at the gateway: Where possible, block online advertising at the gateway to your organization, and on work-issued and edge devices. Opting out of ad targeting (such as through MDM) on company-issued devices is also advisable. We also encourage you to develop guidance and easily actionable tools to help your personnel protect their devices. Transition towards browsers with less tracking: Browsers with built-in anti-tracking features, ad-blocking, and support for the Global Privacy Control (GPC) will improve your security posture and protect your IP. Scrutinize targeted ads: We encourage defenders to monitor traffic linked to advertising impressions for signs of malicious requests. Protecting Yourself from AdFection AdFection is a complex threat, and if you face elevated risk because of who you are or what you do, we strongly recommend seeking expert help. However, there are certain actions you can take to reduce some AdFection risks. Increase your overall security by following personalized instructions from the Security Planner . Use a trusted ad-blocking extension on your browser to reduce tracking. Consider using a privacy-respecting browser that blocks tracking and data-harvesting. Regularly reset your Mobile Advertising ID , disable ad-tracking , and use opt-out features of apps. Consider using an ad-blocking service on your network, such as at your home router, or use a trusted commercial VPN service that offers ad-blocking. Further Research Our investigation found that an attacker that we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER used Discover-Tech ads and a number of additional vendors to deanonymize users at scale since at least 2019. As these efforts rely on the exploitation of widespread security issues across numerous mobile providers, disclosure to providers is in progress. We will release a subsequent report delving into technical analysis and attribution of these attacks once the disclosure process is complete. Based on our findings, we believe that further research would be fruitful with respect to: customers and victims of the ad-based spyware deployment capabilities provided by Discover-Tech and the companies linked to it, including Candiru, Bindecy, and Intelos; additional vendors and vendor networks that deploy ad-based spyware; and, technical, organizational, regulatory, and political measures that effectively prevent the distribution of spyware via digital advertising. This report is part of an ongoing series of investigations we are doing on surveillance technologies that rely on digital advertising. We will be publishing subsequent investigations that explore areas for further research we have flagged in this report. Vungle, Liftoff’s SSP, and Ad Exchange Vungle was a mobile advertising firm that merged with the U.S.-based mobile advertising firm Liftoff, which went public in June 2026. Since the merger, Liftoff offers several Vungle-branded products including a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) named Monetize , which helps app publishers sell ads, and the mobile ad exchange Vungle Exchange , which helps marketers buy ads served in mobile apps. Both the SSP and the ad exchange rely on the Vungle SDK , which is a piece of advertising and tracking software embedded in many Android, iOS, Amazon, Windows, and Unity apps. The Vungle SDK is embedded in 150,000 mobile apps used by one billion people across 150 countries, which also describes the number of users that can be targeted via the Vungle ad exchange, according to the company. Guidelines for the Vungle ad exchange contain a rule that asks clients to “refrain from” using the platform for the distribution of “malware, spyware, and files that can harm or gain unauthorized access to a device or user information”. We did not find an explanation of how the company monitors and enforces this rule. Vungle has been controversially discussed in several papers and reports on mobile tracking and privacy. The Norwegian Consumer Council found in 2020 that Vungle received GPS coordinates and other personal data on users of Grindr and another mobile app, seemingly without a legal basis under the GDPR. As of July 2026, Liftoff’s “Monetize” and “Vungle Exchange” products are listed as approved TCF ad vendors by IAB Europe ( vendor list ). Google lists Liftoff’s DSP and Monetize products as certified ad vendors and it lists Liftoff among its “common” European ad technology partners that Google will use by default when publishers do not choose a custom list of ad vendors. Google has been deeply interconnected with Vungle from its inception. Google Ventures was an investor in Vungle’s seed, series A, and series B funding rounds. The Norwegian Consumer Council pointed out in 2020 that Google’s mobile advertising system AdMob “provides Vungle with access to extra features that allow Vungle to bypass data filters, and thus send more data to its partners than what would ordinarily be possible through Google’s regular advertising tools”. As of July 2026, Liftoff’s Vungle product Monetize is listed among a few “premium bidding partners” in Google’s mobile advertising system AdMob and among a few “ad sources” for AdMob’s advertising services on Android and iOS . Sunteng, a Chinese SSP, DSP, and Ad Exchange The Chinese digital advertising firm Sunteng provides ad buying and selling services for both advertisers and publishers, as well as a “programmatic marketplace”, i.e. an ad exchange, according to its website, sunteng.com. The site also refers to the company as “Shunfei Technology”. The link to Sunteng’s DSP offering leads site visitors to biddingx.com (“BiddingX”), an entity that promotes itself as China’s largest DSP. Sunteng appears to operate also under the brand Bidex (bidex.cn), which focuses on “overseas programmatic”, i.e. on digital advertising services for non-Chinese clients. We assume that Sunteng, Shunfei, Bidex and BiddingX are part of the same Chinese group of companies with offices in Singapore and the US. Sunteng claims to process 50 billion ad bid requests a day across 10,000 mobile apps and 60 ad vendor partners, and it lists Eskimi as a partner. As of July 2026, Google lists biddingx.com (“Shunfei Infomation Technology Corporatio” [sic]) as a certified ad vendor . IAB Europe listed bidex.cn (“Sunteng Hong Kong Holdings Limited”) as an approved TCF ad vendor until December 2025 ( vendor list ). Xandr, aka Microsoft Advertising Xandr, formerly known as AppNexus, has long been a major player in digital advertising. After Microsoft acquired it from AT&T in 2022, it became part of Microsoft Advertising in 2023. While Microsoft shut down Xandr’s ad buying system, the “Invest” DSP, in early 2026, it continues to offer Xandr’s ad selling system, the “Monetize” SSP. Ad buyers who used the former Xandr DSP were “handed” to Amazon DSP, according to trade press reporting. As shown in Section 6 , Microsoft’s user ID syncing in the browser via the domain adnxs[.]com , which assigns a Microsoft user ID to people who visit the sites of ad sellers and maps it to user IDs assigned by other ad vendors, appears to remain operational as of June 2026. Xandr has long been operating massive identity databases. In 2020, when Xandr was still owned by AT&T, it reportedly operated an identity graph linking 5 billion identifiers. As of July 2026, Microsoft’s ad system Xandr is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe ( vendor list ). Google’s list of certified ad vendors contains four records for Xandr. Google also lists Xandr among its “common” European ad technology partners which Google will use by default when publishers do not choose a custom list of ad vendors. Appendix B. Glossary Adtech vendor, ad vendor. Advertising technology intermediary such as a Demand-Side Platform (DSP), Supply-Side Platform (SSP) (both defined below) or ad exchange. Ad Slot. Designated space or position on a website or mobile app reserved to display an ad. Demand-Side Platform (DSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps advertisers buy ad placements across many different websites or mobile apps in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by ad exchanges. Supply-Side Platform (SSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps publishers of websites or mobile apps sell ad slots in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by an ad exchange, which is often operated by the same ad vendor as the SSP. Ad Exchange. Automated marketplace operated by an adtech intermediary that hosts real-time auctions which facilitate the selling of ad slots and the buying of ad placements across many publishers, advertisers and intermediaries like DSPs and SSPs. Ad exchanges are often operated by SSPs. Real-Time Bidding (RTB). Automated high-frequency auctions hosted by ad exchanges where advertisers (or DSPs on their behalf) bid on ad placements offered by website and mobile app publishers (or their SSPs). When a user visits a website or uses an app that sells targeted ads via RTB, the publisher’s SSP initiates a bid request that transmits data about the user and the ad slot to several DSPs, who submit bids on behalf of advertisers. The ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. Bid Request. RTB auction record that describes an ad slot and the user who currently visits a website or uses a mobile app. Bid requests are initiated by publishers and sent via an SSP and an ad exchange to several DSPs, which place bids in order to show ads to specific users on behalf of advertisers. Bid requests typically contain personal data about users in order to facilitate targeted advertising. Mobile Advertising ID (MAID). Unique identifier for a mobile device used for advertising and tracking purposes, assigned by the device’s operating system such as Google Android or Apple iOS. While users can reset or delete mobile ad IDs in the settings, they are activated by default. Advertising and data companies use mobile ad IDs to link user data across contexts and vendors in order to track, follow, profile and target users. Cookie ID. Unique identifier for a user’s web browser, typically stored and retrieved in the browser by third-party code operated by adtech vendors during website visits. Appendix C. Domains linked to Discover-Tech and Controlium General We assess that the following domains are – or have been – linked to Discover-Tech and Controlium: *.discover-tech[.]io *.mtrtb[.]com *.mydsp[.]io *.controlium[.]net *.powerium[.]net *.platc-tester[.]com *.myweb3id[.]io *.myipinfo[.]io *.akedo[.]gg *.volasim[.]com * . discover - tech [.] io * . mtrtb [.] com * . mydsp [.] io * . controlium [.] net * . powerium [.] net * . platc - tester [.] com * . myweb3id [.] io * . myipinfo [.] io * . akedo [.] gg * . volasim [.] com N OAS Servers According to our analysis, Discover-Tech operates – or has operated – the following NOAS servers as part of its Controlium platform: noas.mtrtb[.]com/getAd infinoas.mtrtb[.]com/getAd ppv2.mtrtb[.]com/getAd pqv2.mtrtb[.]com/getAd events.platc-tester[.]com/cplatform/getAd events.myweb3id[.]io/cplatform/getAd noas.powerium[.]net/getAd qa-noas.powerium[.]net/getAd noas . mtrtb [.] com / getAd infinoas . mtrtb [.] com / getAd ppv2 . mtrtb [.] com / getAd pqv2 . mtrtb [.] com / getAd events . platc - tester [.] com / cplatform / getAd events . myweb3id [.] io / cplatform / getAd noas . powerium [.] net / getAd qa - noas . powerium [.] net / getAd Additional NOAS domains that appear to be associated with Discover-Tech: noas.adtimizer[.]co noas.impchkdsp[.]com noas.trakking[.]co noas . adtimizer [.] co noas . impchkdsp [.] com noas . trakking [.] co Ad Tracking Domains We assess that the following additional domains are – or have been – associated with Discover-Tech’s ad tracking or targeting: tracookiepixel[.]xyz cookiesurfer[.]com cookie-sync[.]xyz ads-monitor[.]xyz checkmyimp[.]com ads-impressions[.]com nutralove[.]co tracookiepixel [.] xyz cookiesurfer [.] com cookie - sync [.] xyz ads - monitor [.] xyz checkmyimp [.] com ads - impressions [.] com nutralove [.] co Note that the “?” after the date header is due to a 2022 Censys bug and does not relate to server behaviour. Anyone seeking to write signatures over HTTP banners on Censys, who wishes those signatures to be applicable to the 2022 timeframe, should make a similar modification to their signatures. ↩︎ We also submitted several of the bundle.js files containing the frontend to the Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine ( 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 ) to assist in future investigations by other researchers. ↩︎ Accessed on June 17, 2026 ↩︎ Not available on the web anymore, but archived by the authors of this report on 18.8.2025: https://api-docs.freewheel.tv/advertiser/v2.0/discuss/60a53c1531fb4d001c01435e ↩︎ Accessed on June 17, 2026 ↩︎ More in: Targeted Surveillance LATEST research → Brief Pegasus Spyware Infection of Serbian Pro-Democracy Student Activist In collaboration with the SHARE Foundation, the Citizen Lab confirmed that the iPhone of a member of Serbia’s student protest movement was infected with Pegasus spyware. title: FLUX 3 Image Klein
body_text: FLUX 3 Image Klein: open weights, 5.6B parameters | Black Forest Labs Models Research API Open Weights Pricing Enterprise Resources Contact Sales Back to blog Models News Research FLUX 3 Image Klein October 15, 2026 4 min read Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area. FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world. The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License. Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters. Parameter counts are for the image generator, as each publisher reports them; text encoders are not counted. Krea 2 does not support image editing and is not included in the image editing comparison. FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI. Generation time by GPU: Step-distilled model, 16 steps. Seconds per image, one image per run. Lower is better. Measured by NVIDIA; RTX results in ComfyUI; data results are the best-performing framework for each configuration. Each GPU shows its quickest build. Generation time on the GPU itself; API latency in Section 02 also includes queueing, network and prompt upsampling. Generation time by GPU: Base model, 50 steps. Seconds per image, one image per run. Lower is better. Measured by NVIDIA; RTX results in ComfyUI. Each GPU shows its quickest build. The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints. For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch . On the speed–quality frontier FLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier. Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image. Get started FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API . Try it BFL API: the distilled model is available as flux-3-image-klein, with prompt upsampling and pixel restoration, which preserves unedited regions of an image exactly. Pricing starts at $0.009 per 1K image. Playground or Hugging Face . Build with it Weights on Hugging Face: base and distilled . Reference inference code , including a Gradio demo for bounding-box control. Try it out on Hugging Face Spaces . Day-one support in ComfyUI , Hugging Face Diffusers , TensorRT-LLM , SGLang Diffusion and vLLM-Omni . LoRA training with Ostris's AI Toolkit and recipes in NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel . Trained on NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and optimized for NVIDIA's accelerated computing platform, serving through NVIDIA TensorRT LLM, vLLM-Omni and SGLang Diffusion . On NVIDIA GB300, the distilled model generates a 1MP image in under 0.6 seconds in NVFP4. Serving a LoRA adds around 5% to generation time. License The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API. Safety In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here . FLUX 3 Image Klein is the second open weights release from the FLUX 3 family, following FLUX 3 Action. More will follow. Learn more FLUX 3: Real World Models , the research behind the FLUX 3 family FLUX 3 Action , our open weights 7B model for robot control Citation If you use FLUX 3 Image Klein in your work, please cite: @misc{bfl2026flux3imageklein, author = {{Black Forest Labs}}, title = {{FLUX} 3 Image Klein}, year = {2026}, url = {https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3-image-klein}, } Copy ← Previous article Introducing FLUX 3 Action Models FLUX 3 Video FLUX 3 Image FLUX 3 Image Klein FLUX 3 Action FLUX Tools API Documentation Dashboard Status Open Weights Licensing Hugging Face GitHub Resources Documentation Help Desk Blog Creator Program Brand GitHub Company About Us Careers Trust and Security Contact Us ISO 27001:2022 SOC 2 Type II Enterprise Learn More Contact Sales Legal Imprint Terms of Service Usage Policy Privacy Policy Intellectual Property Policy Developer Terms of Service FLUX API Service Terms Self-Hosted Terms of Service Non-Commercial License Terms Responsible AI Development Policy All rights reserved. © 2026 BLACK FOREST LABS.

See RELEASE-NOTES.md . I've created a Discord server! You can also report bugs and submit ideas for new features here! link : https://discord.gg/xR5f7Xs49 DEsk is D esktop E nvironment and desk in one word -- a name that came from the Reddit community. It used to be called DeskWM: the commands are now desk , desk-session , desk-settings and so on, and what was set up for DeskWM (its settings, its data, DESKWM_* variables) carries over by itself. A Wayland desktop for Linux in realistic skeuomorphism -- the kind iOS 6 had, where everything on the screen is drawn to look like the real thing. Here the desktop is a desk. Windows are sheets of paper on a walnut desk. The dock is a drawer, your apps are filed in binders on a bookshelf behind the desk, notifications arrive in a post box, and the system controls are a panel built into the back of the desk. The room is ray-traced, and one desk lamp lights all of it. Status: beta. DEsk is used day to day on its author's machines and has been checked carefully (see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md , section 9), but this is its first release: expect rough edges, and expect things to change. Your settings and data will be carried forward. Install Download the latest release from the Releases page and unpack it (or clone this repository). Then, in its folder, run the line for your system: Debian 13 sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 (and Linux Mint, Pop!_OS) sudo sh scripts/install_ubuntu.sh Arch Linux (and EndeavourOS, Manjaro) sudo sh scripts/install_arch.sh Fedora 43 / 44 (and Nobara) sudo sh scripts/install_fedora.sh Then log out and choose DEsk on the login screen. It shows what it will install and asks first. --yes takes the suggested answers; --no-apps installs DEsk without the recommended programs. The first login draws the room once: a few seconds on a GPU, longer without one. After that it starts at once. To update, get the new release and run the same line again. Your settings are kept. Something went wrong? See Reporting a problem . More options, building by hand and running DEsk in a window are under Build and Run . What's on the desk Nothing here is a symbol for a thing on a desk. As in the realistic skeuomorphism of iOS 6, each is drawn to look like the real thing set down there -- its material, the light on it, its shadow and the wear of use. Windows are paper. Each window sits on a cream sheet with real fibre, thickness and a dog-eared corner. Hold the pointer on the corner and it lifts to show what is printed on the back: Fold (minimize: folded like a letter and left on the desk, under the windows as paper put down is), Unfold / Refold (maximize and restore), and Discard (close: crumpled into a ball and tossed). Dragging an edge pulls more paper out from behind the sheet. The drawer is the dock. Pull the brass handle (or press Super+D ). It holds the things you put in it: any app, or a folded window. Out of the box it holds DEsk's standard programs (below) and a screwdriver that opens Shell Settings. The bookshelf holds your apps ( Super+A , or the ALL APPS plate). Each category is a ring binder whose sheets fan from a single ring. Take a sheet and it is carried down to the desk, where the app's window opens on it. At the end of the row stands an ALL APPS index book : every program from A to Z, with thumb tabs and a line at the top of the page to type into (input methods via IBus work). The post box is the notification centre ( Super+N ). Letters show the sender and subject, and a letter taken out lies on the desk. The Control Panel ( Super+C ) is a valve-era machine built into the back of the desk: real meters, a volume knob, network and Bluetooth levers, a fader for the room's lamp and one for the screen's own backlight (on a laptop, through logind; the brightness keys work too), a key to unlock the power buttons, and the system tray as paper slips under it (more than fit, and the wheel slides the row along). A desk calendar, a desk memo pad and a clock stand on the shelf. The calendar has a notebook of plans and to-dos, and notes are peeled off and stuck onto the day. The memo pad is taken down the same way and written on (IBus works there too); its sheets turn over the wire. The clock shows the seconds small beside the minutes, under two lamps that light only while a camera or a microphone is in use. The front door is out in the real world. The lock screen's door has the hour's light -- the sun worked out from your time zone's city, the porch lamp coming on at dusk -- and, if you let it ask open-meteo.com for that city's weather (only its latitude and longitude are sent), the weather: rain darkening the brick and streaking past the lamp, snow settling on what faces up, fog, lightning. And on certain days of the year the door and the clock have something more for you -- there is no setting for it; what it is, you will see on the day (give Shell Settings your birthday, and that is one of them). Esc stops it. Light. The room (desk, shelf, console, post box) is ray-traced on the GPU (GLES 3), with a CPU tracer as the fallback, and cached per screen size. Everything drawn over it is lit by the same lamp. At login the room starts dark and the lamp comes up as the room is made, while the clock counts how far in glowing red. Sizes are in points. A bigger screen is a bigger desk, not bigger things. More than one screen. The desk is on one screen; every other shows more of the desk's boards, running on from it, for windows to lie on. A new window comes onto the screen the pointer is on, Unfold and full screen fill the screen the window is on, and nothing the desk's own screen does -- the drawer, turning to the bookshelf -- moves what lies on the others or takes it out of reach. A screen taken away puts its windows on one that is left. X11 apps run through Xwayland, and windows that draw their own frames sit on paper too. The screen lock is the front door ( Super+L , or logind): you walk up to it at night, close enough to touch, traced in 3D with its own lamps and soft shadows. Your picture and name are on the board hung on it, the password goes in at the brass plate, the key beside it; on Return (or a click on the key) you lean in and turn the key. Let in, it goes round, the door swings open, you walk through into the room and sit down at the desk; told no, it will not turn. Locking is the same run backwards -- out of the room, the door shut, the key turned -- from Super+L or the blue LOCK button on the Control Panel. Checked with PAM, as at login. Seven languages. Everything DEsk prints itself, and the names of programs, are in English, Japanese, Chinese (simplified), Korean, Spanish, French or German: the locale's, or language = en | ja | zh | ko | es | fr | de in ~/.config/desk/shell.conf (or the Shell Settings app), and switch live. The calendar is printed as one sold there is, and Chinese and Korean are set in their own cut of the CJK faces. Standard programs DEsk is meant to be installed as a whole desktop, like GNOME or KDE, so it picks a standard program for each job the desk has: a terminal, a web browser, a file manager and a text editor. The drawer's things and Super+Enter open them. For each job, the first of these that is there: app.terminal , app.browser , app.files , app.editor in shell.conf (a .desktop id), the default-applications lists in the freedesktop.org order: ~/.config/desk-mimeapps.list (DEsk only), ~/.config/mimeapps.list (what Shell Settings' Default programs, xfce4-mime-settings, writes), and the same two in the system's folders, ending with the desk-mimeapps.list installed with DEsk -- the same answers xdg-open and GIO give, the standard set, classic GTK programs first: Xfce Terminal, Firefox ESR, Thunar, Mousepad (then MATE Terminal, Caja, Pluma, and so on), any program filed under the right category. A tour The corner of every window: Fold, Unfold, Discard. The drawer: the dock. A folded window, lying on the desk under the others. The bookcase behind the desk. ALL APPS, every program from A to Z ... ... and a line to type into. The Control Panel. The post box: notifications. The desk calendar and its notes. Shell Settings. Documentation docs/ARCHITECTURE.md -- how DEsk is built: the programs, the compositor, the ray-traced room, threads, files. docs/MODDING.md -- changing DEsk: words and languages, settings, borrowed programs, sounds, the room, things on the desk. docs/CONFIGURATION.md -- every setting, file and environment variable. RELEASE-NOTES.md -- what is in v0.1.2 and what is known not to work yet. docs/design.md -- the full development log (in Japanese). As a desktop DEsk draws the desk; the work done on it is done with free software that already exists. It reaches completeness by borrowing, and keeps a firm line between what it makes and what it borrows: DEsk makes both: DEsk draws it, something else does the work borrowed what what is drawn as the room and handled as its things; what only the compositor can do programs, system settings panels, background helpers examples windows as paper, the drawer, the bookcase, the clock, the Control Panel, the post box, the front door, the calendar and memo pad; keyboard, pointer and their keys (volume and media keys too), the screens and their power, remembering their arrangement, going idle, the lock; Shell Settings volume knob and mute (PipeWire/PulseAudio), brightness (logind), Wi-Fi and Bluetooth levers, the post box (the desk is the notification daemon), the tray's slips (the applets' own items), the clock's MEDIA page (MPRIS), screenshots (grim), the input method (a bridge to IBus) network connections, Bluetooth devices, sound devices, display arrangement, printers, the look of other programs, default programs, disks, polkit agent, keyring, portals -- and the programs themselves The rule for new cases: make only what is drawn as part of the room or can only be done inside the compositor; otherwise find an existing program that works as it is under a wlroots compositor, and make something only as a last resort. KDE's System Settings and kcmshell (which do not work outside Plasma), Xfce's and MATE's X11-only dialogs, and Xfce's display and appearance dialogs (which need xfsettingsd, and xfsettingsd overwrites GSettings with Xfce's defaults as it starts) are not used. sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh # DEsk and the whole set (install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh) sh scripts/install-desktop.sh # only the programs (shows them, then asks for sudo) sh scripts/install-desktop.sh --extras # and the office suite, mail... install-desktop.sh works with apt, dnf, pacman and zypper. On Debian and Ubuntu the same set is also one package: equivs-build packaging/debian/desk-desktop.equivs . For What comes terminal, files, text Xfce Terminal, Thunar (with tumbler and thunar-volman), Mousepad the web Firefox (Firefox ESR on Debian, the snap on Ubuntu) pictures, documents, music and video Ristretto, Atril, Parole tools Engrampa, GNOME Disks networks, Bluetooth, sound NetworkManager with its applet and editor, Blueman, PipeWire, pavucontrol displays, looks, defaults wdisplays, nwg-look (GNOME Tweaks on Ubuntu 24.04 and Fedora), Xfce's MIME settings printing system-config-printer, CUPS notices udiskie (memory sticks mounted, with a letter), poweralertd (low battery; batsignal on Arch; none on Fedora), package-update-indicator (updates; Debian and Ubuntu) looking after the machine QDirStat (disk usage), LXQt's date and time and users, Mugshot (your name and picture), Seahorse (passwords and keys), gnome-packagekit (adding and removing programs), Back In Time (backups), Xfce Task Manager, hardinfo2 (about this computer); baobab and Deja Dup on Arch; no Mugshot on Fedora passwords MATE's polkit agent, GNOME Keyring plumbing xdg-desktop-portal (wlr, gtk), Xwayland, xdg-user-dirs, xdg-utils, wl-clipboard, grim, curl looks Qt's GTK platform theme, so Qt programs match the GTK ones typing and fonts IBus (and Mozc for Japanese), Noto (CJK, emoji), the URW base 35, Klee One (not on Arch or Fedora) --extras LibreOffice (drawn with GTK), Thunderbird, Galculator, Xfce Task Manager, Simple Scan The classic GTK programs of Xfce and MATE come first because they are the kind of window the desk's paper is cut for -- a menu bar, plain tools and the document -- and they are light, start quickly and run on Wayland as they are. GTK 3 asks the compositor for its frame through KDE's server-decoration protocol, so they lie on DEsk's paper with its printed heading and no GTK title bar. Windows with a header bar (GNOME's programs, Firefox) keep their own frame, inside a paper margin. Shell Settings ( desk-settings ) holds DEsk's own settings -- windows, the size of things, how much is drawn, language, clock, your birthday and the weather, when the screen goes off and whether the desk locks then -- on its Shell tab, and on its System tab rows that open the borrowed programs (network, Bluetooth, sound, displays, printers, the look of other programs, default programs, disks, disk usage, colour profiles, the input method, date and time, your name and picture, users, passwords and keys, adding and removing programs, backups, what the computer is doing, and the Experience Index), classic-looking programs first, each with the program's own icon and its name -- "Displays (wdisplays)" -- so you can see what does the setting. A row whose program is not installed is printed faint with the package to install, by this distribution's name. The two tabs sit on the sheet like a folder's index tabs, and in each pocket is a wire-bound pad with a sheet to each part of the form and a sticky note on each sheet's edge; taking hold of a note turns the sheets over the wire to it, as on the desk calendar (Page Up and Down too). Changing tab (a click, Ctrl+Tab or Ctrl+Page Up/Down) draws the other pad up out of the folder from below, and the pad comes up the same way when the window opens. Started as a session ( desk-session , from a login screen), DEsk tells D-Bus and systemd where its display is, runs the XDG autostart entries (leaving out the ones that would fight it, such as another notification daemon or an X screen locker), and starts an authentication agent, the keyring, the input method and the network applet with whichever free program for each is installed. The input method's candidates come up under the text being written -- in a program's window as on the desk's own pages -- and leave the keys where they are. It turns the screen off when nobody is at the desk (locking first, by default), lets video players keep it on, and speaks wlr-output-management (wdisplays, wlr-randr, kanshi), remembering a display tool's arrangement for each set of screens. Logging out, restarting and powering off ask every window to close first, so a program with unsaved work can ask about it; a window that does not close holds it up and is put in front. Shell Settings also sets what only a Wayland compositor can: tap to click, natural scrolling, pointer speed and left-handed buttons (through libinput), the keyboard layout, a second layout and the keys that change to it, and key repeat -- applied at once to what is plugged in. How much the desk draws is a setting too, Graphics: Ultra (the room traced finer, and wider where a GPU can, and nothing drawn coarser while it moves), High (as made, the default), Medium, Low, and 2D Fallback -- for a machine without a GPU or a virtual machine rendering on its CPU: no shadows, nothing fading, blurred or moving, nothing ray-traced as it moves, and the room traced once, small and plain. On two CPU cores without a GPU the first start goes from nearly ten minutes to about a quarter of a minute, and a frame from 2 ms to 0.5 ms. The installer takes a quick look at the machine ( desk-index --suggest : the graphics, or the processor, for a couple of seconds, the threads and the memory, and how long the processor takes to draw a sheet of paper folding) and picks the level for it, as the machine's default ( /etc/xdg/desk/shell.conf ); each user's own choice wins. Where the screen is drawn by the processor -- no GPU, a virtual machine without 3D, a GPU without its driver -- the desk runs in 2D Fallback unless you choose a level yourself, and says so: a letter in the post box (check the graphics drivers, or the virtual machine's settings) and a line in red beside Graphics in Shell Settings. 2D Fallback is the same desk with its effects off, not a second one, its room traced at a sample a pixel and softened. And a first start, which traces the room from nothing, leaves a letter in the middle of the desk saying it may take a minute or two, more on some machines, and that the desk can be used meanwhile. It is meant to stay light on old machines. Measured on a machine held to about a 2010 laptop's pace (a quarter of a core each on two cores, 2 GB, no GPU for the room): a later login shows the desk in under half a second and has the light on in 1.4 s; the very first one, which has to trace the room on the processor, shows a soft first look and the light within seven seconds instead of a minute and a half in the dark; folding a sheet costs 5 ms a frame at Low. The traced room is kept across updates, and paper in motion is drawn finer or coarser by the level (whole at High, half at Low). Programs on the desk are dressed for it too: DEsk's own icons, drawn to look like the real things set down on the desk, the way iOS 6 drew them -- manila card folders with papers in them, a typed page with its corner turned down, a letter signed in blue ink, a ledger, slides in their mounts, instant photos, a record sliding out of its sleeve, a film slate, a taped carton for an archive, a deck of punched cards for a program, a block of wood type for a font, a wire wastebasket you see through, a brass globe for the network, a drive in its aluminium case -- with the grain of paper, card, wood and brushed metal and the shadows they cast; and a GTK theme of paper, ink and brass. They are set in a dconf layer of DEsk's own over the user's, so another desktop on the same machine keeps its look. When something on the desk gets stuck: Ctrl+Alt+Del twice puts everything of the desk's own away and draws it all again (the windows stay as they are); three times logs out. desk-ctl reset and desk-ctl logout do the same from a terminal or another VT. The DEsk Experience Index desk-index rates the machine at what the desk asks of it, the way the Windows Experience Index did: processor, memory, 2D graphics (the desk's own drawing), 3D graphics (the room's shader, checked against the CPU) and disk, each 1.0-9.9, on brass-rimmed meters; the base score is the lowest. desk-index --text prints the same in a terminal. Requirements The simplest way is the installer for your distribution (below), which brings everything. To build it yourself: wlroots 0.18 (Debian 13 has it, and Fedora 43 and later as wlroots0.18 ; Ubuntu 24.04 has 0.17, Ubuntu 26.04 only 0.19 and Arch only 0.20, so the installers build 0.18.3 from its release into /opt/desk-wlroots , used by DEsk alone through its run path) wayland, wayland-protocols, xkbcommon, cairo, pixman, fontconfig, libdrm, PAM libsystemd (optional): the notification daemon and the system tray. Build with -Dpost=disabled to leave them out. libpulse (optional): the desk's sounds ( -Dsound=disabled ) libinput (optional): touchpad and mouse settings EGL, GLES, gbm (optional): ray-trace the room on the GPU. Without them the CPU does it. Xwayland and xcb (optional): X11-only apps. Fonts: the URW base 35 ( fonts-urw-base35 ) and Noto CJK ( fonts-noto-cjk ); fonts-klee for the memo pad. At run time: grim for screenshots, curl for the weather at the door. Minimum and recommended Measured with the CPU, GPU and memory cut down ( systemd-run CPUQuota and MemoryMax, taskset ; nested, 1440x900, the same hand moves every run). Once the room is traced, even one core without a GPU dropped no frames; a frame costs about 2 ms. Only the first login traces the room: 6-9 s on a GPU, about 10 minutes on two cores without one (then it is cached). minimum recommended CPU 2 x86-64 cores (1 works) 4 cores or more memory 4 GB (DEsk itself 200-450 MB) 8 GB or more GPU none needed (a long first login) OpenGL ES 3.0 with GBM (Mesa Intel, AMD, Nouveau; VMware's SVGA3D) screen 1366x768 1440x900 or more disk about 1 GB ( --bare ; --no-apps adds what Shell Settings opens) 2-2.7 GB with the whole set system Debian 13, Ubuntu 24.04 / 26.04 LTS, Arch Linux, Fedora 43 / 44 the same Build meson setup build meson compile -C build Run Inside your current session, as a window: ./build/desk -s foot As a session of its own, picked from the login screen (GDM, SDDM, LightDM), use the installer for your system ( Install ). All four take the same options: sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh # or install_ubuntu.sh, install_arch.sh, install_fedora.sh sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --no-apps # DEsk, what it needs and what Shell Settings opens sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --bare # DEsk and what it needs, no programs (containers) sudo sh scripts/install_debian.sh --prefix /opt/desk sh scripts/install_session.sh picks the right one by itself and keeps what it says in ~/.local/state/desk/install.log . Each installer does the same (derivatives such as Mint, Pop!_OS, EndeavourOS, Manjaro and Nobara are recognised): packages, a release build in build-install , the PAM file, the login entry, and the removal of what the old name, DeskWM, left behind (after asking). Every program Shell Settings' System tab opens is installed, --no-apps or not, and at the end desk-settings --check lists what each row opens (or which package would bring it). On other distributions, install the requirements and run scripts/install.sh . Or from a TTY: desk-session . To update, get the new copy and run the installer again the same way ("this updates it", it says): what is installed is replaced, the last build is reused (or made afresh when it cannot be), and your settings and the traced room stay. All the installer says is also kept in ~/.local/state/desk/install.log (the last run's) -- the thing to look at, or send, if it stops part way. A copy made for passing round carries SHA256SUMS, and the installer checks every file against it before building: a copy damaged on its way says which files are wrong and stops (copy it again; if a fresh copy is damaged too, suspect the machine's memory or disk -- memtest86+). A Japanese locale gets the Mozc converter among the suggested programs; IBus itself is installed for everyone but only runs for languages typed through an input method, or when one is set up. The first start at a new screen size spends a little while ray-tracing the room, on the GPU the screen is drawn with: the desk first, then the bookcase, the Control Panel and the post box, each there to turn to as soon as its picture is, and last the films of the camera moves to them (until a film is done, the move to its view is a cut). Each part is cached as it is done, so a first start cut short picks up where it stopped. What DEsk says as it runs is kept in ~/.local/state/desk/session.log (the session before in session.log.old ); its desk: room: lines say what the room was traced on and how long each part took -- the thing to send if a start is slow. A GPU is tried once, in a child process, before the room is traced on it; one that fails says why ( failed its trial: ... ), and the processor traces the room instead -- at High's quality even where Ultra is chosen, Ultra's being a GPU's to trace. Keys Key Super+Enter terminal Super+Q / Alt+F4 close the focused window Super+M fold / unfold the focused sheet Super+D open / close the drawer Super+A look up at the bookshelf Super+C the Control Panel Super+N the post box Super+Tab / Alt+F1 cycle windows Esc back to the desk brightness keys the screen's backlight (or, with none, the lamp) volume, mute and media keys the mixer and the player playing (as the clock's MEDIA page) Print / Alt+Print screenshot of the screen / of the window in front Super+L lock the screen: the front door; type the password, Enter (or click the key) Super+Esc / Alt+Esc log out (asking the windows to close first) Reporting a problem The quickest way: run this in a terminal (any desktop, or a console -- DEsk need not start), and attach the file it writes, ~/desk-report.txt : desk-report It gathers DEsk's version, your Linux, your graphics card and driver, the last session's log and whether DEsk crashed, with your user name, home folder, machine name and network addresses taken out. Read it through before sending it. Say too what you did and what happened. Without it (an older DEsk, or one not installed), attach by hand: ~/.local/state/desk/session.log (and session.log.old if the problem was in the session before) -- what DEsk said as it ran; if the installer stopped, its last lines from the terminal (or ~/.local/state/desk/install.log when it was run through install_session.sh ). Both are plain text; look them over before sending them. If the desk is stuck, desk-ctl reset from a terminal (or another VT) draws everything again without closing your windows. How it was made DEsk was built with the help of AI. Much of the code and the documentation was written by Claude (Anthropic's AI model) under the author's direction: the author decided what DEsk should be and how it should look, tested it on real machines, and reviewed what went in. Reports and patches are welcome all the same. License MIT About No description, website, or topics provided.
